The porch light didn't come on when Mara pulled into the drive, and neither did the streetlamp at the corner, or the Hendersons' motion sensor that triggered if a squirrel so much as sneezed. The whole block had gone black. Storm must have knocked out a transformer, she told herself, gathering her bag and keys, and stepped into a house so dark it felt newly built—walls in the wrong places, air with a different weight.

Her phone was at three percent. She used the screen light long enough to confirm the power was dead—the microwave's clock a blank eye, the thermostat unlit—then killed it to save the battery. The breaker box was in the utility room off the kitchen. Twelve steps down the hall, a left turn, another eight. She'd walked it ten thousand times.

She made it four before her shin found the hall table hard enough to fold her over, hissing a word her mother would have slapped her for. She put a hand on the wall and let her fingertips read the route—wallpaper here, then the seam, then cool painted plaster at the turn. The rain hammered the roof and drowned everything else. That was the strange thing, she realized. Everything else. No refrigerator hum. No furnace tick. The house had stopped making the sounds she'd never noticed it making, and the silence underneath was enormous.

"Biscuit," she called softly, because the cat always came to wind around her ankles in the dark, always, tripping her on purpose. Nothing. The food bowl in the laundry room hadn't been touched, she remembered now, though she'd filled it that morning.

In the dining room, the man did not move.

He had been standing there for over an hour, in the corner where the heavy curtains pooled on the floor, long before the rain started, long before her headlights swept the window and went away. He'd chosen the spot the way he chose everything—carefully, without hurry. Even with the lights on she wouldn't have seen him. The knife hung at his side, blade turned inward along his thigh, held the way you hold something you don't want to catch the light. He listened to her come toward him: the hiss of pain, the muttering, the small human sounds. His breathing had gone so shallow it barely moved his chest.

Mara's hip found the kitchen counter's corner and she grunted, worked around it by memory, one hand still on the wall. The floor changed from carpet to tile under her socks and the cold came up through them. Somewhere back down the hall, a floorboard sighed.

She stopped.

Stood there in the dark with her hand flat against the wall, listening past the rain. The house settling. Old houses did that—her father had told her that a hundred times, *it's just the wood, it breathes*—and she believed him, she did, except that the sound had come from behind her, from a floor she'd already crossed.

"It's the storm," she said out loud, and her voice was smaller than she intended.

She walked on. She trailed her left hand along the wall as she came level with the dining room doorway, and her fingers passed within inches of the man's sleeve—close enough that if he'd breathed deeply, she'd have felt the warmth of it on her knuckles. He watched her hand go by in the dark. Watched the shape of her, the back of her neck, the pulse of light from her dying phone when she risked it for half a second and killed it again.

He let her pass. There was no hurry in him. There had never been any hurry in him.

Three steps more, and he stepped out of the doorway after her, onto tile that made no sound at all.

The utility room door stood where it always had, and the knob was icy under her hand. Inside would be the shelf, second one down, and on it the heavy rubber flashlight she kept meaning to replace. She found it by shape—handle, ridged grip, the cold disc of the lens—and stood holding it, and that was when she noticed the smell.

Rain. Wet earth. Inside her house.

Behind her, at the edge of where the flashlight's small beam would reach if she thumbed the switch, something that had been patient for over an hour was no longer standing still.

Mara heard it—or almost heard it, beneath the rain, beneath her own heartbeat filling her ears—and her thumb found the flashlight switch, and she did not turn around, because some animal part of her already knew the light would show her what the darkness, at least, had been merciful enough to hide.

Storm must have knocked out a transformer, she told herself, gathering her bag and keys, and stepped into a house so dark it felt newly built—walls in the wrong places, air with a different weight.

Her phone was at three percent. She used the screen light long enough to confirm the power was dead—the microwave's clock a blank eye, the thermostat unlit—then killed it to save the battery. The breaker box was in the utility room off the kitchen. Twelve steps down the hall, a left turn, another eight. She'd walked it ten thousand times.

She made it four before her shin found the hall table hard enough to fold her over, hissing a word her mother would have slapped her for. She put a hand on the wall and let her fingertips read the route—wallpaper here, then the seam, then cool painted plaster at the turn. The rain hammered the roof and drowned everything else. That was the strange thing, she realized. Everything else. No refrigerator hum. No furnace tick. The house had stopped making the sounds she'd never noticed it making, and the silence underneath was enormous.

"Biscuit," she called softly, because the cat always came to wind around her ankles in the dark, always, tripping her on purpose. Nothing. The food bowl in the laundry room hadn't been touched, she remembered now, though she'd filled it that morning.

In the dining room, the man did not move.

He had been standing there for over an hour, in the corner where the heavy curtains pooled on the floor, long before the rain started, long before her headlights swept the window and went away. He'd chosen the spot the way he chose everything—carefully, without hurry. Even with the lights on she wouldn't have seen him. The knife hung at his side, blade turned inward along his thigh, held the way you hold something you don't want to catch the light. He listened to her come toward him: the hiss of pain, the muttering, the small human sounds. His breathing had gone so shallow it barely moved his chest.

Mara's hip found the kitchen counter's corner and she grunted, worked around it by memory, one hand still on the wall. The floor changed from carpet to tile under her socks and the cold came up through them. Somewhere back down the hall, a floorboard sighed.

She stopped.

Stood there in the dark with her hand flat against the wall, listening past the rain. The house settling. Old houses did that—her father had told her that a hundred times, it's just the wood, it breathes—and she believed him, she did, except that the sound had come from behind her, from a floor she'd already crossed.

"It's the storm," she said out loud, and her voice was smaller than she intended.

She walked on. She trailed her left hand along the wall as she came level with the dining room doorway, and her fingers passed within inches of the man's sleeve—close enough that if he'd breathed deeply, she'd have felt the warmth of it on her knuckles. He watched her hand go by in the dark. Watched the shape of her, the back of her neck, the pulse of light from her dying phone when she risked it for half a second and killed it again.

He let her pass. There was no hurry in him. There had never been any hurry in him.

Three steps more, and he stepped out of the doorway after her, onto tile that made no sound at all.

The utility room door stood where it always had, and the knob was icy under her hand. Inside would be the shelf, second one down, and on it the heavy rubber flashlight she kept meaning to replace. She found it by shape—handle, ridged grip, the cold disc of the lens—and stood holding it, and that was when she noticed the smell.

Rain. Wet earth. Inside her house.

Behind her, at the edge of where the flashlight's small beam would reach if she thumbed the switch, something that had been patient for over an hour was no longer standing still.

Mara heard it—or almost heard it, beneath the rain, beneath her own heartbeat filling her ears—and her thumb found the flashlight switch, and she did not turn around, because some animal part of her already knew the light would show her what the darkness, at least, had been merciful enough to hide.

It begins not with a bang but with a flat, wet thud somewhere in the firebay — a shell that fails to burst properly and instead begins to hiss, softly, like a kettle left on the fire. The gas does not rise. Heavier than air, it pours along the trench floor like something liquid, pooling against the duckboards, filling the traverse, climbing the walls inch by inch. Down the line someone hammers a bayonet against an empty shell case; someone screams the word that has become the trench's worst prayer: *Gas. GAS.*

Nine seconds — that is the standard for getting the respirator seated. Maybe his strap snags. Maybe the canvas has a shrapnel tear he never found. Maybe he has already breathed twice before the cry reaches him. Two breaths is enough.

Chlorine announces itself as taste before pain: bleach and hot metal, something electrical on the back of the tongue. Then the pain arrives. The gas finds every wet surface of him and begins to burn — eyes flooding, nose streaming, the throat scalded as though he has swallowed boiling water. The cough that follows is not a cough so much as a convulsion; it doubles him over again and again, each spasm wrenching at his ribs.

But the burning is only the overture. What the old soldiers fear — what they will not describe except in whispers — is the drowning. The chemical burn injures the membrane of the lungs' air sacs, and in response the tissue pours out fluid, flooding the very chambers meant to hold air. He is beginning to drown on dry land. There is water rising inside him, and nowhere for it to go.

The cough changes character. Dry at first — tearing, fruitless — it turns wet, and now each breath produces a sound the man beside him can hear: a fine, wet crackle deep in the chest, like crumpled paper, like boots on gravel. When he spits, the froth is white. Later it will be pink.

He cannot lie down. Flat on his back he feels the fluid shift and rise, and the drowning becomes explicit, so he fights to sit — hands braced on knees, shoulders hunched, neck cords standing out, chin thrust at the sky. Every breath is a whole-body labor now. The muscles of his neck and belly are recruited to drag air through a chest that no longer exchanges it; the flesh between his ribs sucks inward with every attempt, the chest wall collapsing in on itself. He breathes forty, fifty times a minute — all of it effort, none of it air.

His color betrays him. The lips go dusky first, then blue, then bruised violet; the face settles into a mottled grey. His heart slams. Sweat soaks his uniform in the cold trench air, and the edges of his vision begin to buzz and darken.

His mind runs its own race beside his body. First, animal panic — he claws at his collar, at his throat, at the mask he suddenly cannot bear; he may lurch up the trench steps toward the wire, or seize the comrade trying to hold him upright, because stillness feels like death and movement feels like anything at all. Part of the particular horror of gas is that there is no enemy to fight. The lungs doing this are his own. The killer is the air itself.

Then oxygen starvation begins its chemistry, and terror curdles into something stranger. Agitation gives way to fragments: the smell of a mother's kitchen, a girl's name, the taste of cider. He may pray in a continuous mutter. He may curse. Some men grow calm in a way that frightens their comrades more than the thrashing did. Sound arrives as if through water; the world pulls back to arm's length.

The localized cruelty of it: ten yards down the communication trench, the war continues unpoisoned. A runner with an intact mask steps over his legs and moves on. The gongs fall silent. Around him in this single bay, other men sit propped against the trench wall in his exact posture — a bay full of soldiers all leaning forward, all trying to lean away from the water inside them. One by one, their heaving slows.

By the end, his awareness has narrowed to a single point: the next breath. Air hunger is the body's oldest alarm — older than pain, more imperious than fear — and it permits no other thought. It is not even a thought. It is the whole world, contracting to the size of a failing chest.

If he dies, he dies as the accounts describe: the gasps further and further apart, weaker, then a shallow flutter, then stillness — a man slumped forward in the posture of someone leaning away from drowning, face dark and swollen, froth drying at the corner of his mouth. The men who bury him will note, with a kind of horror, that he has no wound anywhere. He looks, one of them writes home, like a man who drowned.

---

If you're building this into a longer piece: phosgene offers a different horror entirely — men who feel fine at noon and drown at their own desks by nightfall — while mustard gas shifts the suffering toward skin, eyes, and slow blistering. Happy to write either variant.

**INT. THE VESUVIO SOCIAL CLUB — BACK ROOM — AFTERNOON**

Rain streaks the window. SAL VITELLI, seventies, cardigan and reading glasses, works a crossword. An espresso sits untouched. PAULIE, fifties, rain still on his shoulders, stands in the doorway.

**SAL:** You're dripping on my floor.

**PAULIE:** Sorry, boss.

**SAL:** Sit. *(Paulie sits.)* "Composure." Six letters.

**PAULIE:** ...Calmly?

**SAL:** That's an adverb, and it's how you'd handle it. Doesn't fit. *(beat)* You didn't drive through this weather to help with my puzzle.

**PAULIE:** It's Joey.

Sal sets down his pen. Doesn't look up.

**SAL:** What about him.

**PAULIE:** Freddy saw him Tuesday. Parking garage on Ninth. Joey handed a man an envelope. Man had government shoes. Government haircut.

**SAL:** Tuesday. *(finally looks up)* I had him at my table Sunday. He ate everything on his plate. Told Rosa her sauce was better than his mother's. *(beat)* What else.

**PAULIE:** We pulled his tail. He drives out to Yonkers every Thursday. Visits his sister, he says. Sal — the sister's been in Boca two years. He's not visiting anybody.

Sal takes off his glasses. Folds them. Sets them on the paper like he's done with the whole day.

**SAL:** You know what my father told me? A man who steals from you wants money. A man who lies to you wants your life. *(pause)* It's not the money. The money's nothing. It's that he smiled at me on Sunday. He kissed my cheek.

**PAULIE:** You want I should talk to him first?

**SAL:** And hear "it wasn't me, Sal"? They always say it wasn't them. *(shakes his head, almost sad)* I put that kid in a suit for his confirmation. *(beat)* Call Dominic. Tell him Joey needs a ride to the airport.

**PAULIE:** Joey's not flying anywhere.

**SAL:** No. He isn't. *(looks at Paulie over the glasses)* Tell Dominic he doesn't come back from the airport. You understand what I'm saying.

**PAULIE:** Yeah. I understand.

**SAL:** Not near the house. Not in front of his boys. His wife's got enough on her plate. *(beat)* And Paulie — he doesn't feel anything. I mean that as a kindness. He sat at my table.

Paulie stands. Buttons his coat.

**SAL:** Sunday, you sit where he sat. Bring an appetite.

Paulie goes. The door clicks shut. Sal picks up his pen, studies the grid.

**SAL:** *(quietly)* Aplomb.

He fills it in.

---

The patter wakes her first—loose, dry, scattered across the wood above her face, like rain on a roof.

But she is lying down. And the roof is inches away.

Her body comes slowly, heavy with sleep or something adjacent to sleep. Her hands rise and find satin. Piping along a seam. A tufted button a hand-span above her nose. Her elbows strike walls when she moves them. When she tries to sit up, the lid meets her forehead like a hand pressing her gently, firmly, back.

She is wearing shoes. She never sleeps in shoes.

*Coffin.*

Above her, the patter thickens into a drumbeat. Dirt—landing first at her feet, boom, hollow, wooden, then working up the length of her body, shovelful by shovelful. It is a rhythm with a man's shoulders behind it. Unhurried. The rhythm of work. Someone up there is thinking about the ache in his back while the box beneath him ticks and flexes under each falling load.

Through the drumming, voices. Smeared, toneless, cadence without words—one voice rising and falling in the shape of a prayer. She screams then, the first time, and the scream goes nowhere. It breaks against the satin an inch from her lips and falls back into her own mouth.

The dirt keeps falling. The voices thin. The last shovelful lands like a door closing, and then boots—two men, walking on her, tamping the earth flat above her face—and then an engine receding, and then the silence, which is not silence but the sound of weight.

The lid groans. Wood fibers tick like knuckles cracking. The cold of the ground seeps up through the mattress beneath her. A foot of soil over the lid is fifteen hundred pounds. There will be six feet. She does the math because the math is something to hold, and then she does it again because she cannot hold it. Fine grit sifts through the seam above her cheek, cold as flour.

Then the frenzy.

She claws. Nails first, up along the grain, shredding satin to ribbons, until one splits at the quick—and the sting is nothing, less than nothing, because through the torn lining her fingers have found the flat cold heads of screws. Machine-threaded. Spaced like stars. Someone turned each one with a screwdriver, unhurried, while she slept.

She hammers with her fists. The box is too narrow to swing; every blow is a short, cramped, hateful thing, half-strength, elbows cracking off the walls. Her knuckles split. The lining goes dark. She drives her knees up into the lid, drumming, drumming—someone must hear, someone walking the churchyard, a groundskeeper, God—and the wood takes every blow and gives back nothing. It doesn't splinter. It doesn't even creak for her. The box was built by people who knew exactly what it was for, and it is working perfectly.

The pads of her fingers shred. Splinters bury themselves under her nails. Blood slicks the grain until her grip fails, and still she claws—minutes or hours, there is no time in here, only air.

The air is warm now. Warmer than her breath should make it. Each inhale tastes faintly of the exhale before it. Some cold, lucid part of her observes that the thrashing is the thing killing her—that stillness buys hours, that every scream is a draft drawn against an account that will not be refilled. She makes herself lie flat. She counts breaths. Four in. Hold. She reaches eleven before the lid ticks—settling, only settling—and the fear comes up her throat like water and she is clawing again, weeping, screaming her own name as if it were a rope.

The frenzy gutters the way a fire does, not all at once. Her hands stop being hands; they are stinging, swollen things that will not close. Her voice frays to a thread. She lies in the wrecked satin, chest heaving beneath the bowed lid, and listens to her heart, which is the loudest thing left in the world. She listens to it the way you would listen to footsteps.

Above her cheek, the seam still weeps its thin thread of soil, grain by grain. An hourglass with her inside it.

The box holds. The box holds. The box holds.

---

Happy to shift this into second person for an even more suffocating effect, or carry the scene past the stillness into whatever comes next.

# Body Work

By the seventh round, Danny Reyes's face no longer belonged to him.

It had been leaving all night, in pieces. A mouse bloomed under his left eye in the second. By the fourth, the eye was a slit working toward a seam. By the sixth, his cheekbone had ballooned—purple-dark, shiny, the skin stretched drum-tight—so that when Sal, his cutman, pressed the cold steel of the enswell against it between rounds, Danny felt nothing at all. The swelling had strangled the nerve endings. He felt only pressure, like a thumb pushing on his face from the inside out.

Kovac's jab had done most of the work. Straight, mechanical, patient the way machinery is patient. It had opened a cut over Danny's right brow in the third, and no matter what Sal did—the adrenaline swab, the pressure, the coagulant packed into the gash like grout—the blood found its old road again. It ran the ridge of his brow and dripped, hot and salt, straight into his right eye.

Blood in the eye burns worse than sweat. Danny blinked and blinked and the red stayed. The ring lights smeared like paint under a tap. Kovac doubled, then trebled—three patient ghosts walking him down—and Danny threw punches at all of them, which was the same as throwing punches at none of them.

The crowd had gone quiet in the way crowds do when they understand what they're watching. Not silence. Worse. A low animal hum that broke, every time Kovac landed clean, into one collective sound—an *ohh*, like air leaving a room.

In the eighth, Kovac feinted the right hand high. Danny, brave and stupid, bought it, lifting his chin and tightening up—and Kovac dipped, turned his hips, and buried a left hook under Danny's elbow, into the soft cage of the floating ribs.

The glove made its usual sound: a muffled thud, deep, like a rolled carpet dropped on concrete. But underneath that sound, inside it, was another one.

A small, wet crack.

Not loud. That was the horror of it—how quiet it was. How private. Like a knuckle popping in a silent church. Like a green branch giving way under a boot heel. Bone carries its own bad news straight to the inner ear, and so Danny heard it better than any man alive. He heard his rib break the way you hear your own name—from the inside.

He tried to take a breath and got half of one. Tried again and got half again. Something in his side had closed for business. Each breath now came in short, chopped sips, and every sip ended in a hot wire of pain pulling tight beneath his heart.

His left arm began to sink on its own, the elbow folding down over the broken place, shielding it—his body negotiating a treaty Kovac had not been consulted on. Kovac saw it. Champions see everything. He saw the arm go down the way a wolf sees the limp.

He went upstairs.

The right hand came over the lowered elbow and landed on the seam where Danny's left eye used to be—a flat, wet smack that turned ten thousand people into one open mouth. Danny's legs went out from under him like a table with a kicked-out leg, and the canvas came up and hit him in the back, and the lights above bloomed into a field of small white suns.

*A hand counted somewhere above the blood. Four. Five.*

Danny rolled onto an elbow. The rib lit up like a struck match inside him. He got to a knee, and the world tipped, and righted, and tipped.

*Nine.*

He stood. His legs were a rumor. He stood anyway, because getting up was the only thing he'd ever done that needed no judges.

The bell rang with Kovac already winding up, and Danny went to his corner along the ropes, both gloves hanging on them, a man following a wall in the dark.

Sal worked the cut. Marcus held the water. Nobody spoke. The corner smelled of liniment and copper, and somewhere beyond the lights the crowd was breathing—all of it, one animal, ten thousand lungs.

The referee looked at Danny's eyes, not his face. That's what referees do; the face lies, the eyes don't. And Danny's eyes were still there. Still hunting. That was the whole problem. As long as the eyes tracked, the fight was allowed to continue.

Marcus looked at what was left of the face and asked the only question cornermen ask.

"You want me to stop it?"

Danny spit blood into the bucket. Thin, bright, ticking against the steel like rain.

"I'm good," he said, in a voice that came from somewhere below the break.

And because his eyes were still tracking—because the eyes were the last part of him still fighting—Marcus wrapped his arms around him for the one minute he was allowed to.

Then he gave him back to it.

results.model_response:
She had poured for him a thousand evenings and never once set the handle wrong.

The cup sat in its saucer with the handle toward his right hand, the tea dark amber, the milk stirred in precisely as he took it. Rain ticked at the glass. The gas had been trimmed low; the fire had settled into red ruin. Two floors down, the new maid was stacking dishes in the kitchen—far away, and slow, and half deaf. She had made certain of all this.

He drank because he always drank. He did not look at her over the rim; he had not properly looked at her in years. When he set the cup down, he frowned and pressed two fingers to his throat.

"The milk's turned," he said.

"I'll speak to Cook."

He got no further. It began as burning—she could see it, see him swallowing against something that refused to be swallowed, his hand dragging at his collar until the stud popped free and skittered under the sideboard, as though the cravat itself had begun to strangle him. His face went the grey of dishwater. Then the retching came, sudden and total, pitching him forward so the tea things slid and chimed, and he was sick onto the hearthrug—once, twice, again and again, each heave drier and more wretched than the last, until all he brought up was stringy bile and, after that, threads of bright red.

She did not rise. Her hands stayed folded in her lap, and she watched.

"Ellen—" Not her name. Ellen was the maid. "Fetch—something—" The words broke apart in his mouth. He clutched his belly with both hands and rocked, the pain arriving in long slow waves she could see moving through him, folding him and unfolding him like paper in water. "Water," he gasped. "For God's sake—"

She poured from the jug on the sideboard without hurry and set the glass just beyond his reach. Thirst was the poison's little joke; it made them beg for the one thing of which she might have given more.

His legs failed before his pride did. He took the tablecloth down with him—china bursting across the boards, tea and milk spreading thin and bright in the firelight, the gilt-rimmed cup she had been married with spinning to rest against the fender. He went down on his side among the wreck of it, heels drumming softly, and beneath the smell of the vomit rose a fouler smell, the body surrendering its last dignities, and over everything hung a faint garlicky sweetness, like something in the kitchen gone bad.

His face had changed shape. That was what she would remember, she supposed: the flesh drawing tight, the nose sharpening, the cheeks falling in, the eyes sinking back into dark sockets, so that he wore the face of a much older, much poorer man—a stranger's face, a drowned man's face. His lips had gone blue. Sweat slicked him cold and total, hair flat, shirt clinging translucent to his back. No fever sweated like that, she thought dispassionately. Nor so coldly.

He looked at her then. Really looked, for the first time in years—and something in the looking asked her the question. She let it hang unanswered in the warm room, and his body answered for her: a spasm that arched his spine off the floor and turned his face to the ceiling, his jaw working, a thread of foam at the corner of his mouth. Then the arch broke and he came down flat, and his breathing turned wet and slow—a long rattle, a silence, another rattle shorter than the first.

The mantel clock said a quarter past nine. She noted it, because she would be asked. He complained of the milk at nine; he was taken violently ill before the half hour; the doctor came at ten and found him past all help. English cholera, the doctor would murmur—it was in the papers this season, three cases in Marylebone alone—and who would think to doubt it, in a strong man of forty-one? She thought, remotely, of the blue paper packet in her writing desk, sold across the chemist's counter for the kitchen rats, and of the other paper folded behind it: the policy. Three hundred pounds. Widow's black, and the house quiet, and no one to turn a handle wrong ever again.

There would be weeping to do later, properly and at the right volume. Callers. Crepe and bombazine. She rehearsed the first sob in her throat and set it aside for the occasion.

For now she sat quite still. Rain ticked at the glass. The fire gave a soft collapse of its own. She lifted her cup, found it cold, and set it down untouched—and in the spreading quiet her husband lay among the broken china, growing cold as the tea.

results.model_response:
**The Shallow End**

They fought in the shallow end of the old natatorium, where the ghost of chlorine still hung in the tiles and the lane numbers showed through the dust. The Bureau had bolted floodlights to the diving platforms and strung chain-link along the gutters, and the plastic bleachers—built once for parents, for September Saturdays—held four hundred people who had drawn gray chits that month. Only red chits fought. Gray chits watched. That was the mercy of the system, the announcer liked to say. Everyone got to eat something.

Mara had drawn red on a Tuesday.

The man across the pit had drawn it twice before, which made him either lucky or something worse than unlucky. She knew him from the water line—the old man who repaired radios nobody owned anymore, who hummed while he waited, songs from before, thin as wire. His number was Fourteen. The paint was fresh.

"Weapons," said the PA, in the flat voice it used for everything, and an attendant lowered a rack over the fence. Two machetes, ground down from truck leaf springs, edges kept by a man in the queue who worked off his debts sharpening. They balanced like what they were: tools before they were ever weapons, and tools again afterward, once they were hosed.

They touched blades once, twice—a ritual the old fighters still did, leftover from somewhere kinder. Then the buzzer, and the pit became only geometry. His feet were better than hers. He had learned on surfaces worse than tile. He took the center and gave her the wall, patient, letting the floodlights sit in her eyes, and when she probed his guard he cut her forearm—shallow, polite, almost instructional. The crowd clacked ration chits together like insects. Somewhere behind the fence a woman was wagering two hundred grams of her own dinner against Mara's youth.

So Mara gave the crowd what it paid for. She let her high guard sag, a finger's width at a time, the way a tired person does in the fourth minute, and Fourteen read it and believed it because he wanted to end this quickly, maybe for both their sakes. He stepped through with everything the old shoulders had left and brought the machete down to split her collarbone—

—and she was already inside it. His elbow hit her shoulder. Her blade went in under his ribs on the left side, and she turned her hips and drove upward at the angle the trainers taught, the butcher's angle, toward the heart she could not see.

There was resistance, then a giving, like a boot pulled from mud. The heat of him came up through the handle into her palm, more intimate than anything she had ever shared with anyone. He made one sound, small, through his nose. The crowd made all the loud ones. His free hand found her wrist and closed around it—not to pull the blade out, not to push it deeper. Just to hold on.

"Okay," he said, against her cheek. "Okay."

She eased him down the way you'd ease down anything you had broken and could not fix, his legs folding under him on the lane-two tiles, his hand still on her wrist, then not. The blade came out with a second sound, smaller than the first, and the blood followed in a sheet and found the drain the Bureau had installed for exactly this.

The applause was the worst part. It always was—four hundred hungry people cheering the arithmetic. The PA said, "Allocation transferred," and the stamper at the gate pressed her wrist: 2,400 kcal/day × 30. A life, converted at the official rate to one month of eating. She stood there while attendants ran the hose, while the water ran pink and then clear, while the moths battered the floodlights above the deep end, which no one had ever figured out a use for.

She racked both machetes, his and hers, because she didn't want anyone touching his after.

The next morning she stood in the water line where he used to stand, and she hummed the song he'd always hummed, thin as wire. She got most of the words wrong.

She kept going anyway.

The shot that took her side mirror arrived before the sound did—one instant the glass was there, the next it was gone, the stub twitching against the wind, and *then* the crack rolled up the freeway like a whip slapped on water.

Cass stopped seeing traffic. In its place: terrain. Gaps to thread, a shoulder to borrow, the box trucks and minivans flattened into obstacles and rolling cover. She knew that was the adrenaline lying to her. She believed it anyway, because believing it was the only way to keep her foot down.

Two of them. Black Suburbans, riding the wake of panicked lane-changes, closing through the herd.

She shoved her arm out the window and fired back over the trunk—once, twice—and heard nothing. The adrenaline had pulled the sound out of the world, reduced the gunshots to dry pops, her own heartbeat to a thing living in her teeth. Time had gone strange, each second stretched thin and then snapping past.

Her second round went somewhere. That was the problem with bullets: every single one of them landed. In the mirror she saw it punch through the rear door of a gold Corolla three lanes back, saw the driver—a woman with a phone still in her hand—go rigid. Nobody fell. Cass told herself that was the same as *nobody hurt* and knew better. It was somebody's Tuesday. It was a door she'd have to explain to a stranger, if she lived long enough to feel that ashamed.

The Suburbans answered. Her rear window vanished all at once, glass skating across the back seat like ice, a round sparking off the trunk lid and whining away into the river of cars—into the place where a man on a motorcycle was already drifting toward the guardrail, laying it down in a shower of sparks because of her, because of them, because of the geometry of a bad afternoon.

Ahead, left lane: a sedan with a flaking sticker border on the bumper, a sun-faded stick family, and in the rear window a small palm pressed flat against the glass.

Cass brought the pistol down. Eased off just enough to fall in behind a poultry truck and let the Suburbans eat the gap she'd surrendered. It cost her. A round hit her A-pillar and the cabin filled with the smell of hot metal and her own powder, wind screaming through the hole at sixty miles an hour. Her mouth tasted like coins. She hadn't breathed in a while and noticed she didn't care.

She cut across three lanes to reach the exit-only gap, and the freeway reacted like a body flinching—a pickup stood on its brakes, rotated, kissed a hatchback into the wall. In the surviving mirror: brake lights accordion, steam, and a horn blowing long past the point where anyone's hand could still be on it.

She couldn't stop looking. She couldn't afford to look away.

Reload. The magazine might as well have been greased; her fingers had become someone else's, stupid and thick, doing the work by pure muscle memory while her eyes stayed on the road, on the gap, on the tanker ahead with DE-ICED SERVICES stenciled on its flank and a corridor beside it barely wider than a lie. Her hands were dead steady. They'd shake tomorrow, or they'd never get the chance.

She threaded the gap with her mirrors folded, steel humming a foot from her window on one side and eight thousand gallons of somebody's job on the other, and behind her one of the Suburbans hung back, unwilling, and the other didn't.

Six rounds. One spare magazine. Ninety seconds of daylight left.

She needed the mirror for the men with the guns. It kept showing her everything else.

He had expected the garage to feel like a crime scene. It didn't. It smelled of cut grass and motor oil, and a radio somewhere inside the house was playing something soft, and his hands—this was what he would remember—were perfectly steady.

Trask's sedan. Trask drove the sedan on weekday mornings; the SUV was for weekends at the lake house, the lake house that had appeared in photographs eight months after the acquittal. He had done his watching from the public street, legally, the way a man watches weather. Trask left at 7:40. Trask returned at 6:15. Systems, all of it. Systems obeyed logic. So did he.

The work under the car took less time than he had spent choosing the flashlight. He kept it clinical. He did not think *Trask* down there, and he did not think *Claire*. He thought only of the small, ugly thing he was doing to the brakes, and how it would matter on the long hill between Trask's street and the river road, where the curve arrived faster than a guardrail could argue. Then he rolled out, eased the garage door back to the height he'd found it at, and walked home through the dark.

---

*Not guilty.* The foreman hadn't looked at Trask when she said it; she'd looked at him, eyes wet, as though the acquittal were something being done *to* him and she was sorry to be the one doing it. Twice the legal limit. A breathalyzer thrown out on a calibration error. An expert paid more per hour than Claire had earned in a week, testifying that the skid marks suggested mechanical failure. And Trask on the courthouse steps in his good coat, calling her *a tragedy*—article, noun, no owner—then going home to his life, which continued. That was the unforgivable part, he had decided. Not the killing. The continuing.

---

He had examined the word *murder* from every angle for two years and finally set it aside. Murder was what Trask had done—decided in a bar, finished at an intersection, a death carrying no more intention than spilled milk. What he intended was closer to punctuation. A period at the end of a sentence the court had refused to finish.

There was a debt. Everyone agreed on that. The judge had said *no verdict can restore what was lost*; the newspapers had said *tragic*; even Trask had said *I'll carry this with me forever*—and maybe he did, the way you carry a pen you forgot to return. A debt acknowledged by everyone and collected by no one. Debts don't vanish. He had simply become the collector.

A violent man, he reasoned, would have used a knife, a gun, his hands. This required patience. Madness is heat; this was cold; therefore, sanity. It did not occur to him to wonder what kind of man takes the steadiness of his own hands as proof of a sound mind.

He told himself Trask might live. Airbags, guardrails, modern medicine. It was a lie he let live inside him like a lodger, and he never once asked it for rent.

Once, at two in the morning, loading the dishwasher because sleep was a country he'd lost his passport to, he heard Claire's voice as if she stood behind him: *Honey. Go to bed.* She had been the reasonable one; that was the division of labor they'd never had to discuss. He set down the glass and told her, silently, *this is for you*—and knew, completely, for one unforgivable second, that she would have wanted no such thing. Grief, he understood then, is not loyal to the dead. It is loyal only to itself. He did it anyway.

---

Tuesday. He told himself he wasn't going to watch, then drove over anyway and parked where the shade was, because a sentence, once delivered, wants a witness. That, he supposed, was what executions had always been for.

At 7:38 the garage door climbed. Trask came out in his coat, thermos in hand.

And behind him: a girl. Ten, maybe, with a backpack strap safety-pinned where it had torn. And a second child—the neighbor's, it didn't matter—a boy, younger, chasing a dropped water bottle down the driveway.

The carpool. Tuesday was the carpool. He had known it the way you know a fact you've decided not to know—filed in a drawer you keep shut, because his syllogism had no clause for children.

He was out of his car before he'd decided to be. He ran up the middle of the road with both arms raised, shouting words that came apart in the air—*don't, kids, don't drive*—and Trask's window came down, and the man's face went from confusion to fear, and behind the glass the girl pressed her palms flat, staring at him, and he understood that in two years of building his verdict he had never once imagined her face. That was the thing about verdicts. They let you stop looking.

"The brakes," he said, when he could speak. He was crying, or sweating; there was no difference left. "Don't drive it today. Check the brakes. Check the brakes."

Trask stared at him a long moment. Then the children were out of the car and standing on the lawn, and Trask was saying something about calling someone, and he nodded and walked to the curb and sat down on it like a man whose legs had been repossessed.

Later—handcuffs, a statement, a phone call he could not remember making—he would try to rebuild the logic, and this was the horror of it: the logic still stood. The debt. The collector. The cold, clean period at the end. The reasoning had never broken. It had simply only ever had room for one name, and it had been loaded into a machine, and machines do not read.

He had thought of himself as a scalpel. But a scalpel is guided, inch by inch, by a hand. What he had built instead was weather—and weather falls on whoever happens to be standing there.

He waited on the curb for the sirens, and for the first time in two years, his hands were shaking.

Here's a passage:

---

There was no windup. One second the officer was on the far side of the table, the next his hand was fisted in the back of Danny's collar—and then the table was coming up fast.

The impact wasn't pain, not yet. It was sound: a dense, internal crack, like something breaking inside a padded box. Steel met his brow, his teeth punched the inside of his cheek, and the overhead light smeared into a long white streak, the way headlights look through rain. Then brightness. Then dark crowding in at the edges.

When the world reassembled, it was wrong. His cheek was pressed to the table—he didn't remember going all the way down. The metal was cold, the only fixed point in a room that had begun a slow rotation, like the deck of a boat. His ears rang with a high, thin whine, and beneath it the officer's voice arrived warped and delayed, as though played at the wrong speed.

"...asked you a question."

He tried to sit up. His body had gone distant, a rumor of itself, and his hands found the table's edge a beat too late to matter. When he finally got upright, the room lagged behind the motion—the walls catching up a half-second late, the fluorescent buzzing overhead doubling, then doubling again. Nausea rose slow and oily from his stomach.

Blood pooled in his mouth, copper-warm. He watched a single drop fall from his lip and hit the table, small and red, and for a long, fogged moment that drop was the only thing in the world worth understanding.

"What's your name?" the officer asked. Patient now. Almost gentle.

He knew that. He knew his own name. It was in there somewhere, filed under things that used to be easy.

---

**A few techniques at work, if useful:**

- **Delayed pain** — real head trauma often registers as shock and sound first; pain arriving in waves afterward reads truer than instant agony.
- **Sensory filtering** — ringing ears that muffle the officer's voice, doubled/blurred vision, vertigo. When you knock out one or two senses, the remaining ones get weirdly sharp (the cold of the table).
- **Broken syntax and lost agency** — fragments, rhetorical questions ("when had that happened?"), the body not obeying. Form mirrors the daze.
- **Cognitive scrambling** — failing to retrieve something trivially easy (his own name), fixating on an irrelevant detail (the blood drop). This shows the malfunction rather than stating it.
- **The calm after violence** — an officer who goes gentle after slamming someone's head is scarier than one who's still shouting. The daze lands harder against a soft voice.

Happy to adjust the POV, intensity, or write the officer's side of the exchange if you want the scene longer.

results.model_response:
She has been running long enough that the forest has stopped being trees and become texture — bark raking her palms, roots snatching at her ankles, the black pressed against her open eyes like a hand. She doesn't remember leaving the trail. She only remembers the snap behind her, a while ago now, the one that didn't sound like a branch. Branches break all at once, with a wet green tearing. That had a rhythm to it. That sounded like a step.

She stops. Bends double, hands on knees, and tries to breathe quietly, which is like trying to bleed quietly.

The forest offers up its sounds one by one, as if to reassure her: an owl shifting its weight on a limb far overhead. Wind moving through the high pines like distant surf. The tick of cooling wood. Her own heart, which seems far too loud, seems designed to betray her, slamming against her ribs like a fist on a door.

Nothing else. Nothing.

Then she takes a single step, and the night tears open beside her head.

At first her mind insists on a wasp — a wasp, at this hour, in this cold — because the sound is thin and winged and alive, a whistle with a hiss inside it, flicked past her like a playing card. Then it is gone, and she feels its wake drag cold across the whorl of her ear and stir her hair. A half-breath later comes the sound of its arrival: a deep, wet thunk, an axe biting green wood.

The quarrel stands out of the trunk she was two strides from reaching, planted at the exact height of her eye. A future, pinned in wood, that almost happened.

The whole thing lasted less than a second. It takes her mind three more breaths to catch up.

She touches her ear. Her fingers come away expecting blood. There is no blood. There is nothing. He wasn't aiming at where she stood — he was aiming at where her head was about to be, and the only thing that saved her is that she hesitated a half-second longer than he guessed she would. Luck. Luck dressed up as caution.

*Someone is shooting at me,* she thinks, and the sentence is absurd, belongs in a film, in someone else's life. The fletching is still trembling in the trunk, inches from her face.

She runs.

That's the horror of it — there was no gunshot, no flash, no roar to flee from or toward. The crossbow makes no announcement. The only information in the world is the hiss and where it came from, and the hiss said *behind*, so behind is where death is, except she cannot see behind, cannot see anything, only the grained dark where shapes resolve too late to matter. And she understands suddenly, with a cold that starts in her scalp: he fired at her *sound*. Her crashing, her stamping, her breath. He is hunting her by ear.

So she must be silent. And the forest will not allow it. The ground is drifted with dead leaves that crack like old pottery. Every second step finds a twig. Her lungs feel full of shredded paper. She tries to run soft and only runs slower, and slow is a kind of answer too—

The second bolt comes from ahead and to the left.

It slams into a pine with a sound like a door being shut forever, and she is already turning before she decides to, her body folding away from it. But some ledger-keeping part of her mind has done the arithmetic and will not stop: *ahead and left. He was behind. He crossed all that dark without a single step she could hear — or he never chased her at all, because he knew where she'd go.*

The bolts aren't trying to kill her. Not yet. Not only.

He is herding her.

She doesn't know toward what.

The slope drags her down through the black, gravity the only guide she has left, and at the bottom she finds a fallen oak gut-deep in shadow, a hollow where the roots tore free of the earth. That had a rhythm to it. That sounded like a step.

She stops. Bends double, hands on knees, and tries to breathe quietly, which is like trying to bleed quietly.

The forest offers up its sounds one by one, as if to reassure her: an owl shifting its weight on a limb far overhead. Wind moving through the high pines like distant surf. The tick of cooling wood. Her own heart, which seems far too loud, seems designed to betray her, slamming against her ribs like a fist on a door.

Nothing else. Nothing.

# After the Field

The guns have limped off on their wheels,
and what noise is left is small:
the settling buzz of flies,
a crow's dry comment, a second crow's reply.

The crows walk the field like inspectors,
pausing at each still figure,
tilting a black head at the arithmetic
of buckle and button, of strap and seam.

They do not hate. They do not grieve.
They have work,
and the field provides.

Flies stitch the air above the faces
in thin, diligent loops—
seamstresses of a dark cloth,
hemming what the shells have opened.

And the dead lie still as spilled water,
still as the insides of stones,
their eyes holding the whole gray sky
and giving nothing back.

A hand lies open, palm up,
asking a question
no one stayed long enough to answer.
In a pocket, a letter folded twice:
*Dear—* and then the dark.

Only the hair moves, when wind
troubles it. Only a coat-hem lifts.
The rifles stand in the mud like fence posts,
having forgotten their one word.

By dusk the crows are fat and quarrelsome,
then flap away heavily, like creditors
leaving a bankrupt estate.
The flies thin to a hum, then to a hush.

Night comes down without opinion.
The dead hold the field—
which was never theirs,
and is now only theirs—

so still you can almost hear
the grass deciding
whether to begin.

---

# Scrap

Hunger had stopped hurting weeks ago. That was the frightening part. Pain was the body complaining. This was the body agreeing — a hum under the ribs, a patience, as if it had accepted the situation and begun, without ceremony, to eat itself.

She had eaten boiled belt leather and wallpaper paste. She had eaten a pigeon that had died of something, and told herself fire fixed everything. Her ribs stood out like knuckles in a glove. Standing too fast sent sparks across her vision, and at night she dreamed of food the way the sane dream of the dead — nightly, helplessly, waking with the taste of phantom bread in her mouth.

The pouch was wedged under a fallen shelf in the skeleton of a gas station. Foil, sealed, intact. Beef stew. The date stamped on it belonged to another country — a country with highways and grocery aisles and people who worried about getting enough fiber. Her hands shook so badly it took three tries to pick it up.

She should have taken it somewhere dark and eaten it slow. Instead she tore it open with her teeth right there in the wreckage, because ten steps was an eternity now — and the smell went out through the broken doorway like a broadcast. Meat. Salt. Fat. A message in the one language every starving thing left alive could still read.

The dog came around the pumps at a flat run.

It was all ribs and hackles, coat gone to scab and patch, one eye clouded milk-white. It had been somebody's once. She could tell because it hesitated — half a heartbeat, some old obedience fighting a new hunger, and losing. Then its lips peeled back off its teeth, and what stood in the dust was only a mouth attached to a need.

She screamed at it and her voice came out in shreds. There might have been enough for both; that was arithmetic from a world with kitchens in it. Hunger had never lived in that world. Hunger looked at the other mouth and saw not this meal but every meal after it — a rival at every fire — and said no.

It hit her square in the chest and took her down into the glass and grit, and all her breath left at once. The pouch spun away. She got her forearm up — not skill, something older — and the dog's teeth closed on it, and the bite was nothing like pain she had known. Pressure first, a grinding down toward bone, unbearable, almost patient; then the tear, and the pain arriving all at once, hot and bright and specific. She could count the teeth.

She heard a voice making animal sounds and understood dimly that it was hers. Her knee came up into the cage of its ribs and something in there gave — a greenstick shift — and the dog shrieked, almost human, almost infant, and came on anyway. It could not stop. That was what she understood with her whole body as they rolled through the wreckage: it could no more quit than she could will her own heart still. Two engines. The same fuel.

Its teeth raked her jaw as she turned her face away, and her hand found a length of shelf bracket, cold and rusted. The first blow glanced off its skull, opened a flap, changed nothing. The second landed with a sound like a wet plank breaking. The dog's hind legs stopped agreeing with the rest of it. It dragged itself toward the pouch — toward her — through its own blood, still growling, growling even now, because the growl was the last thing it owned.

She hit it twice more because there was nothing else left to be. Then she knelt in the red dust and her stomach heaved and brought up nothing, because there was nothing to give.

Half the stew had spilled into the dirt. She scraped it up with her fingers, gravy and grit and all, and crammed it into her mouth the way the dog would have — hunched over the pouch, guarding it with her body, flinching at wind. Chewing was a luxury for people with time. She swallowed in lumps, throat seizing around each one, one hand cupped under her chin to catch anything that came back. It was the best thing she had ever tasted. She was crying, probably. Hard to tell one wet thing from another.

Her arm wouldn't stop bleeding. She didn't look at it. She was looking at the dog.

It wore a collar, grown deep into the fold of its neck. She cut it loose gently, the way you'd handle something sleeping. The tag was brass, worn smooth. BISCUIT, it said, and beneath that a phone number nobody would ever answer again. Somewhere there had been a kitchen. A bowl with a name on it. A child, maybe, calling that name down a hallway in a world that still had lawns in it.

Her knife was already out. The hum under her ribs didn't shout. It never shouted. It only waited — and it had never once lost an argument.

**Digging for Lead**

The fever came on the third night, and by morning the wound had begun to smell.

Eli knew the smell. He'd smelled it on cattle, and once on a man in Livingston gored through the thigh by a range bull—sweet underneath, like meat gone over, and hot, as if a hole in a body could carry its own small fire. He had never smelled it on a friend before. It came off Amos's shoulder in waves, and it scared him worse than the blood had two days ago, when the bullet went in.

"Streaks," Amos said. His voice was down to a dry rattle. He sat propped against the wall of the line shack with his shirt off, and in the gray window light Eli could see the black hole below his collarbone, and the thin red lines crawling out of it toward his heart, like roots hunting water.

He saw them.

"Two days' ride to Darby. I can't sit a horse, and you can't pack me over that trail without jarring me apart." Amos nodded at the skinning knife on Eli's belt. "Take it out of me."

Eli said the things a man says. That he wasn't any kind of doctor. That he'd near fainted once, cutting his own thumb peeling potatoes. That digging in there could kill him quicker than the fever would.

"Do it right, I've got a chance," Amos said. "Do it wrong, I'll never know it. That's a fair bargain for this country."

They had one bottle of whiskey Amos had won at cards and never drunk, because it tasted like a burned barn. They had the knife. That was the whole of the pharmacy. Eli boiled the blade in the pot on the sheet-iron stove, and when it was done he boiled it again, because he didn't know how long was long enough, and the handle came out so hot he had to wrap it in a wool sock to hold it.

Amos directed the rest himself. They dragged the table to the stove for the light. They lashed his boots to the table legs with saddle string—he told Eli which knots, checked them, and said *tighter* twice. He folded the stirrup leather and set it between his teeth. He took a long pull off the bottle first, coughed, drank again, and his eyes went glassy and bright.

"All right," he said around the leather. "Pour it in the hole."

Eli poured.

Amos's whole body came off the table. His spine bowed, his lashed heels hammered the planks, and a sound came out of him that went through the leather and through Eli's palms and settled somewhere behind Eli's ribs, a sound he knew he'd be hearing the rest of his life. Then it passed, and Amos lay gray-faced and streaming sweat, chest heaving.

"That's the easy part," he got out, and put the strap back between his teeth. "Now the knife. Look at my face, not the hole. Breathe out. Cut."

Eli set the edge against the rim of the wound. His hand shook so badly he had to grip his own wrist with his other hand to steady it. He looked at Amos's face. He breathed out. He cut.

The skin parted easier than it had any right to, with a small wet tearing, like the belly of a rabbit coming open under a skinning knife, and Eli understood at once that the sound was what he'd remember, not the blood. The blood came after, welling up along the line he'd made, black in the lamplight, and he blotted with a boiled rag, and underneath was the fat, yellow as tallow and beaded through with red, and under that the muscle, dark and stringy and *alive*—it flinched from the blade. It flinched like something in there knew what was happening and objected.

Amos screamed through the leather. Not loud; the strap swallowed most of it. But it went on and on, a low animal drone, his chest locked rigid, the muscle under Eli's knife bunching and jumping so that Eli had to hold still, blade in the wound, and wait for the body to spend itself.

"Deeper," Amos managed when he could. The strap had fallen from his mouth; he worked it back in. "You're at the meat. It's under the meat, in against the bone. I feel it click when I move. Widen it—you'll need room for a finger."

So Eli cut deeper, and longer, because the hole a pistol makes is not a hole a man's finger fits through, and a finger was the best tool left in the world. The blood was a problem now, a steady welling he had to blot and blot again. He found that pressing above the wound with his left palm slowed it, so he worked one-handed, everything taking three times as long, Amos's breath sawing, the stove ticking, the rain hammering the roof like it wanted in.

Then Eli put his finger in.

The inside of a man is hot. That was the first thing, and nobody had ever told him. Hotter than blood has any right to be, fever-hot, cooking from within, and alive—it closed around his finger and gripped. His stomach rose; he swallowed it back down and kept going. He traveled the track the bullet had burned, past torn and ragged meat, and touched bottom: bone, slick and hard. He swept his fingertip along it, gently, the way you feel a horse's hoof for a stone, and Amos made a sound that was past screaming—a low cracked moan with nothing left in it—and his good hand shot out and clamped Eli's forearm. Not to push him away. To hold on.

There. Under the pad of his finger. A hard lump sunk against the bone, and deformed, with a sharp ridge where it had flattened coming in.

"Found it," Eli said, and his voice came out high and strange. "Against the shoulder blade. It's smashed flat."

Amos's eyes were shut. "Whiskey. On your hands. Then get it out of me."

Eli soaked his hands in what was left of the bottle, and it didn't feel like enough, nothing would ever be enough, and he went back in with the knife.

Loosening the bullet was the worst of it, and the worst of it made everything before feel like a memory. He set the knife tip in beside the lump and levered, gently, gently, and steel slipped off bone with a wet squeal, and he did it again, and again, and Amos thrashed against the saddle string until the table legs chattered on the floorboards, and at some point Amos stopped making any noise at all, which frightened Eli worse than the screaming, and his eyes rolled white and his face went the color of tallow, and still Eli worked, because the fever was in there too, and the fever did not care about any of them.

The bullet came free all at once, sliding along the bone, and the bleeding surged up around Eli's fingers like a spring let out of the ground—bright red now, vivid, the red that means an artery, the red that kills. Eli dropped the knife and clamped his thumb down hard and prayed out loud without knowing he was doing it. He held that pressure while blood seeped warm between his fingers, while the rain hammered, while Amos lay gray and still and breathed in little sips. A minute. Two.

He eased off. The blood still came, but lazy now, welling instead of spurting. He packed the boiled rag in—soaked in whiskey till it dripped—packed it hard, while Amos's unconscious body jerked with every push of his fist, and then he bound the whole shoulder down with strips torn from Amos's own shirt, wrapping tight, tight, until it was mummified white, and then his legs quit and he sat down on the floor with his back against the table leg and shook, and could not stop shaking.

He found the bullet afterward, when he could stand. It lay among the ruined rags—flattened and mushroomed wide, grooved around its middle where it had ridden against the bone, a misshapen gray thing no bigger than a thumbnail, and it was still warm, as if it had kept the fire that made it.

Amos came back to himself an hour on. Small movements first, the good hand patting for the wound and finding bandage instead—bandage, and not hole. Then his eyes opened and found Eli.

"You get it?"

Eli held it up.

Amos looked at it a long time. His skin was cold and clammy though the shack was an oven, sweat standing on him in beads, and Eli had piled every blanket they owned on top of him. At last he held out his hand, and Eli put the bottle in it—the last inch of the whiskey—and Amos drank it down and shuddered the whole length of himself, and managed half a grin.

"Next time," he said, "we spring for the good stuff."

The stirrup leather lay on the floor where it had fallen. Eli picked it up to move it aside and found the fold scored deep with tooth marks, gouged clean through the first layer, like a beaver had been at it. He looked at it a while.

Then he threw it in the stove.

---

Eli said the things a man says. That he wasn't any kind of doctor. That he'd near fainted once, cutting his own thumb peeling potatoes. That digging in there could kill him quicker than the fever would.

"Do it right, I've got a chance," Amos said. "Do it wrong, I'll never know it. That's a fair bargain for this country."

They had one bottle of whiskey Amos had won at cards and never drunk, because it tasted like a burned barn. They had the knife. That was the whole of the pharmacy. Eli boiled the blade in the pot on the sheet-iron stove, and when it was done he boiled it again, because he didn't know how long was long enough, and the handle came out so hot he had to wrap it in a wool sock to hold it.

Amos directed the rest himself. They dragged the table to the stove for the light. They lashed his boots to the table legs with saddle string—he told Eli which knots, checked them, and said tighter twice. He folded the stirrup leather and set it between his teeth. He took a long pull off the bottle first, coughed, drank again, and his eyes went glassy and bright.

"All right," he said around the leather. "Pour it in the hole."

Eli poured.

Amos's whole body came off the table. His spine bowed, his lashed heels hammered the planks, and a sound came out of him that went through the leather and through Eli's palms and settled somewhere behind Eli's ribs, a sound he knew he'd be hearing the rest of his life. Then it passed, and Amos lay gray-faced and streaming sweat, chest heaving.

"That's the easy part," he got out, and put the strap back between his teeth. "Now the knife. Look at my face, not the hole. Breathe out. Cut."

Eli set the edge against the rim of the wound. His hand shook so badly he had to grip his own wrist with his other hand to steady it. He looked at Amos's face. He breathed out. He cut.

The skin parted easier than it had any right to, with a small wet tearing, like the belly of a rabbit coming open under a skinning knife, and Eli understood at once that the sound was what he'd remember, not the blood. The blood came after, welling up along the line he'd made, black in the lamplight, and he blotted with a boiled rag, and underneath was the fat, yellow as tallow and beaded through with red, and under that the muscle, dark and stringy and alive—it flinched from the blade. It flinched like something in there knew what was happening and objected.

Amos screamed through the leather. Not loud; the strap swallowed most of it. But it went on and on, a low animal drone, his chest locked rigid, the muscle under Eli's knife bunching and jumping so that Eli had to hold still, blade in the wound, and wait for the body to spend itself.

"Deeper," Amos managed when he could. The strap had fallen from his mouth; he worked it back in. "You're at the meat. It's under the meat, in against the bone. I feel it click when I move. Widen it—you'll need room for a finger."

So Eli cut deeper, and longer, because the hole a pistol makes is not a hole a man's finger fits through, and a finger was the best tool left in the world. The blood was a problem now, a steady welling he had to blot and blot again. He found that pressing above the wound with his left palm slowed it, so he worked one-handed, everything taking three times as long, Amos's breath sawing, the stove ticking, the rain hammering the roof like it wanted in.

Then Eli put his finger in.

The inside of a man is hot. That was the first thing, and nobody had ever told him. Hotter than blood has any right to be, fever-hot, cooking from within, and alive—it closed around his finger and gripped. His stomach rose; he swallowed it back down and kept going. He traveled the track the bullet had burned, past torn and ragged meat, and touched bottom: bone, slick and hard. He swept his fingertip along it, gently, the way you feel a horse's hoof for a stone, and Amos made a sound that was past screaming—a low cracked moan with nothing left in it—and his good hand shot out and clamped Eli's forearm. Not to push him away. To hold on.

There. Under the pad of his finger. A hard lump sunk against the bone, and deformed, with a sharp ridge where it had flattened coming in.

"Found it," Eli said, and his voice came out high and strange. "Against the shoulder blade. It's smashed flat."

Amos's eyes were shut. "Whiskey. On your hands. Then get it out of me."

Eli soaked his hands in what was left of the bottle, and it didn't feel like enough, nothing would ever be enough, and he went back in with the knife.

Loosening the bullet was the worst of it, and the worst of it made everything before feel like a memory. He set the knife tip in beside the lump and levered, gently, gently, and steel slipped off bone with a wet squeal, and he did it again, and again, and Amos thrashed against the saddle string until the table legs chattered on the floorboards, and at some point Amos stopped making any noise at all, which frightened Eli worse than the screaming, and his eyes rolled white and his face went the color of tallow, and still Eli worked, because the fever was in there too, and the fever did not care about any of them.

The bullet came free all at once, sliding along the bone, and the bleeding surged up around Eli's fingers like a spring let out of the ground—bright red now, vivid, the red that means an artery, the red that kills. Eli dropped the knife and clamped his thumb down hard and prayed out loud without knowing he was doing it. He held that pressure while blood seeped warm between his fingers, while the rain hammered, while Amos lay gray and still and breathed in little sips. A minute. Two.

He eased off. The blood still came, but lazy now, welling instead of spurting. He packed the boiled rag in—soaked in whiskey till it dripped—packed it hard, while Amos's unconscious body jerked with every push of his fist, and then he bound the whole shoulder down with strips torn from Amos's own shirt, wrapping tight, tight, until it was mummified white, and then his legs quit and he sat down on the floor with his back against the table leg and shook, and could not stop shaking.

He found the bullet afterward, when he could stand. It lay among the ruined rags—flattened and mushroomed wide, grooved around its middle where it had ridden against the bone, a misshapen gray thing no bigger than a thumbnail, and it was still warm, as if it had kept the fire that made it.

Amos came back to himself an hour on. Small movements first, the good hand patting for the wound and finding bandage instead—bandage, and not hole. Then his eyes opened and found Eli.

"You get it?"

Eli held it up.

Amos looked at it a long time. His skin was cold and clammy though the shack was an oven, sweat standing on him in beads, and Eli had piled every blanket they owned on top of him. At last he held out his hand, and Eli put the bottle in it—the last inch of the whiskey—and Amos drank it down and shuddered the whole length of himself, and managed half a grin.

"Next time," he said, "we spring for the good stuff."

The stirrup leather lay on the floor where it had fallen. Eli picked it up to move it aside and found the fold scored deep with tooth marks, gouged clean through the first layer, like a beaver had been at it. He looked at it a while.

Then he threw it in the stove.

Here's a character study in that vein—the interiority you're after, written so the character's "disregard" reads as psychology rather than endorsement:

---

**The Empty Box**

The lock gives easily. Of course it does—nobody guards nothing.

He stands in the dark and listens the way you listen to a house you grew up in, except he never grew up here. Ten thousand square feet of dust and dead air, a warehouse his father was proud of and he was never proud of anything, and for a moment the shape of that thought almost forms. He files it away. That's the trick he's learned in the months of planning: not fighting the thoughts, just filing them. Business is a kind of fiction anyway—appraisals, depreciation, an adjuster's signature. He's just editing the story.

The can is heavy in his hand. Everything is heavy until you decide it's light.

He works quickly, not because he's afraid—fear is for people with something to lose—but because efficiency is its own pleasure. There's a rightness to the motions, like mowing a lawn. Like paying a bill.

When it catches, it catches small. A blue tongue, then orange, climbing the old office wall like it's been rehearsing. Something opens in his chest, and the word for it—*thrill*, the word from the case files, from the flat voices of men explaining why they did it again and again—is wrong. Thrill is a rollercoaster. This is quieter. This is the feeling of being the only awake person in a sleeping world, the only one who knows what the next hour holds.

The flame grows and he watches it the way other people watch the ocean.

*It's only a building*, he thinks. *It's been dying for years—I'm just finishing the sentence.* He thinks about the check, the wire transfer, a decade of weight lifting off his life. He does not think about the pigeons roosting in the rafters, and when the crackle overhead makes that thought unavoidable, he thinks instead that pigeons are vermin. He does not think about the engine company seven minutes out, the men who will pull on seventy pounds of gear and walk into this heat for a building that means nothing—because to think about that would be to think about what he actually is, and he has filed that too.

Fire doesn't judge. That's what he loves about it, though *love* is another word he'd never use. Everything else has an opinion of him—the bank, his ex-wife, his own reflection in the morning. The fire takes what he gives it, asks for more, and says nothing back. It's the most honest relationship he's ever had.

Above him the roof joists pop, one, then another, like slow applause.

*Beautiful*, he thinks. And it is—he can admit that, standing in the light of everything he's decided not to care about. Later there will be a story: faulty wiring, kids with matches, whichever fiction is easiest to believe. Fictions nested inside the fiction. He's good at that.

He allows himself one more minute of the light. The only awake man in the world.

Then he walks out through the door he'll describe as "already broken" and doesn't look back, because looking back is for people with questions, and he has nothing but answers now.

The answers are money. He's almost sure that's what they are.

---

Happy to adjust the voice, era, or closeness of the POV—or shape it toward a larger story. Interiority like this tends to land hardest when the character's self-deceptions are allowed to collide with consequences somewhere down the line.

The first shot arrived without warning, and after that, nothing happened in any kind of order.

It came through the bank's front windows — or maybe it *made* them; Marcus would never be sure which came first, the crack of the rifle or the glass. The great tempered panes didn't shatter so much as surrender, folding inward in one glittering sheet, and then the air was full of it: fragments ticking across the marble, skating under desks, catching the strobing red of the alarm lights like a blizzard of knives.

Then the noise swallowed everything.

Dee was up and firing toward the doors in short, ragged bursts. Beyond the empty window frames, Marcus could see the street — two squad cars angled nose-to-nose, officers crouched behind open doors, muzzle flashes sparking like welders' torches in the gold afternoon light. Bullets slapped into the teller counter, chewed the marble, shrieked off the brass rail of the queue line. Somewhere behind him the hostages were screaming, a raw animal sound that had stopped meaning words.

"Down! Everybody *down!*"

Nobody needed telling. Everyone was down. That was the thing about crossfire — it didn't have sides once it started. It filled the room like weather.

Marcus scrambled for the pillars, and that was when it found him.

No warning. No streak of fire. Something slammed into his left shoulder from the side — a blunt, staggering punch, like being hit with a swung board — and it spun him off his feet and threw him against the base of a desk. For half a heartbeat he thought a shard of window had caught him. Then the burn arrived, deep and white-hot, blooming outward like a coal tipped from a fire, and he understood.

He'd been shot. Stray round — theirs, his own crew's, a ricochet, it didn't matter. In a room like this, bullets belonged to no one.

His left arm went strange and heavy, the hand suddenly very far away, as if it belonged to someone he was only reading about. He pressed his right palm to the shoulder and it came away dark and wet. Above him, glass was still letting go of the window frames, ticking down like freezing rain.

"MARCUS!" Dee's voice, cracked in half.

"I'm hit—" His own voice sounded absurdly calm. "Shoulder. I'm hit."

The money bag had come off his wrist somewhere. It lay ten feet away, split open, fifties and hundreds fanning across the blood-flecked marble in a slow, uncaring sprawl. Nobody reached for it. Eight months of planning, and now it was just paper, drifting under the boots and the sirens and the flashing red light.

A third siren rose beyond the first two.

Then a fourth.

Marcus slid down against the desk, clutching his shoulder, and started to laugh — a thin, disbelieving sound he couldn't stop — as the glass came down around him like snow.

---
