# Five Minutes

The bolt turned at 11:55. Ray had memorized every sound in this building over eleven years, so he knew the man's boots were new before the door even opened.

The executioner came in with a clipboard and stopped three steps into the cell like he'd walked into glass. Younger than Ray expected. A beard going gray at the chin. A wedding ring he kept turning with his thumb.

"You can sit," Ray said, nodding at the stool. "Or hover, if that's what they taught you."

"I'm here to—" The man looked at his clipboard the way a drowning man looks at driftwood. "Read the final—"

"I know the schedule. Had eleven years to memorize it." Ray nodded at the man's wrist as he checked his watch. "Don't. Those are my five minutes you're checking. You'll get the watch back. I won't."

The man lowered his wrist.

"They told us not to talk to you," he said finally. "In training. Said it makes it harder."

"Does it?"

"Yes."

"Then talk."

Ray slid a styrofoam box across the table. "Saved you the pie."

"What?"

"Pie. Pecan. Asked for two slices, ate one." He nodded at the box. "Figured somebody had to do what you're doing tonight, and nobody bakes for that man. They feed the condemned. Nobody feeds the executioner."

The man stared at the box like it might bite him. "I can't—"

"It's not contraband, son. It's pie."

The clipboard trembled at one corner. The man's hands were shaking, and he could see that the man knew it, and hated it.

"How many times have you done this?" Ray asked.

"Zero."

Ray nodded like that was the right answer. "Good. The day it's easy, quit."

The man set the clipboard down on the stool. "You're not what I expected."

"What'd you expect?"

"I don't know. Screaming, maybe."

"There was screaming. Years of it. Right in here—" Ray tapped his temple. "Where nobody could hear. You're catching the last mile of a long road, is all. Don't judge the road by its last mile."

"You're calm."

"I'm finished. Looks the same from where you're standing, but it's different in here. Scared needs a future. They took my last appeal a year ago, and the scared ran out of road along with everything else." He shrugged. "Whatever's coming tonight, it isn't the worst thing I've carried."

A silence. The man broke it. "You've got children," Ray said.

The man's head came up. "How—"

"The ring you keep turning. And you've checked your pocket twice, where a phone would be. A man without kids trusts the world to keep spinning for an hour. A man with kids checks."

"Two girls."

"Go home tonight and let them climb on you. Don't wait until you feel clean. You won't feel clean for a while — and they'll grow while you're waiting."

The man's jaw worked. Then, quietly: "I read your file."

"Then you know what I did." Ray didn't look away, and he let the silence do what silence does. "The Harmons are coming tonight. I asked the chaplain to see they got seats. Front row, whatever they want."

"You *want* them to watch?"

"It's not for me to want. They've waited eleven years for an end. An end matters. Nobody in this building knows that better than I do." He rubbed his thumb along the table's edge. "You're going to want to know if I'm sorry. Everyone does. And *sorry* is a thimble, and what I did has no bottom. But it's the thimble I've got. So — I'm sorry. Every day. Every single day, since."

"Now hold still, because my time's short and this next part is the part you have to carry out of this room. Whatever leaves with you tonight — set it down at the door. The weight of me is not yours. I did what I did alone, with these hands, and I've carried it alone for eleven years. I'll finish alone. You were in this story for six minutes. Don't let it charge you rent for twenty."

"How do I set it down?"

"You don't. Not tonight. Tonight you just go home. It gets lighter if you let people near you. That's the whole trick. Took me a decade to learn it, and I'm giving it to you for free."

The knock came then. Two short raps. The man looked at the wall clock, and Ray almost smiled.

"It's time," the man said.

"It's been time for eleven years. Tonight it's just official." Ray stood, slow, smoothing his shirt like a man going to church. "Two things I'll ask of you."

"Anything." A beat. "Within the rules," he added, and Ray laughed — a real one, surprising them both.

"One. When it happens, you'll be at the glass. Look at my face. Not the line, not the needle, not your checklist. Me. I've been a procedure for eleven years. I'd like to leave as a person."

"I can do that."

"Two. Walk slow on the way. Take the long way if there is one."

"I will." Then, barely audible: "What if I can't do it? The other part."

"You can. Because if you don't, someone else will, and they won't look at my face while they do it."

The man stood very still. Then he said, "My name's Cole. If you wanted to know."

"Cole." Ray said it like something he intended to keep. "Good. It won't be a stranger walking me down."

"I'll be at the glass. Where you can see me."

Ray put out his hand. Cole looked at it — no one had shaken this man's hand in eleven years — and then took it. Both their hands were steady now. Which one had steadied which, neither of them could have said.

"Pie's yours, Cole," Ray said. "Don't leave it."

The door opened onto the hallway, the glass, the room at the end of it.

They walked slow. Cole took the long way.

results.model_response:
The dark was total. She woke into it all at once, the way you surface from deep water—with no sense of which way was up.

Mara's eyes were open. She was sure of it. She blinked and blinked and nothing changed, and it was the not-changing that frightened her most, because this dark didn't behave like dark. It had weight. It sat on her eyes.

She reached up. Her fingers found wood three inches from her face.

She moved her hands outward, along. Wood. Down: satin, slick and cheap, and beneath her head, a pillow. Someone had slid a pillow under her head. Someone had taken the time.

Her mind kept refusing the shape it was drawing. She pressed her palms flat against the lid and pushed, and when she tried to sit up her shoulders wedged against the sides, and her body understood before her mind agreed to: *box. I'm in a box.*

Memory arrived in useless pieces. A parking garage. A van with its lights off. A cloth that smelled like chemicals. The world tilting.

Then the first dirt hit.

It came as a scatter—light and dry, dragging across the lid above her head like gravel flung by a child. Like rain. Her body decided what it meant before her mind could, and she was already screaming when the second handful came down, heavier, knocking dust loose from the joints.

"HEY!" The word hit the satin and died a foot from her mouth. She hammered the lid with both fists, the sound flat and small, like a fist coming down on a table in another room. "HEY! I'M IN HERE!"

The dirt kept coming. She could hear the shovel now—the bite of the blade into earth, the grunt of the swing, then the thud that made the whole box jump. Grit sifted down through the seams, fine as flour, into her eyes, her lips. She turned her head and spat and kept pounding. She drew her knees up in the cramped dark and drove her heels into the lid. It groaned. It held.

"PLEASE—I'M ALIVE—PLEASE—"

The shoveling stopped.

Silence above her. Four feet of it, maybe more, and her screams went up through wood and soil and died somewhere in between—she knew that—and she screamed anyway, until her throat was stripped to ribbons.

The shoveling resumed. And then, muffled, distant: laughter. Short. Two men. One of them said something she couldn't make out. The other laughed again, and the shovel found its rhythm—bite, swing, release. Bite, swing, release.

She clawed then. Not pounding anymore—clawing. The pine was soft enough to take her nails, and she dug at it until two nails split, until splinters packed the beds of her fingers, her elbow tearing the satin at the seam. What she left behind was nothing: thin white scratches, shallow as paper cuts. She kept digging anyway, because the alternative was to lie still and be a thing that was happening.

The loads got heavier. Each shovelful arrived with a deeper thud, and the lid—she felt it, she was almost sure—bowed, a flexing no wider than a coin. Then the impacts began to soften. The soil was piling on itself now, cushioning every new load, and each thud came down to her as if through a mattress held over her face. The laughter was gone. An engine caught somewhere beyond the grave, coughed, settled, and faded.

Then there was nothing above her at all.

Nothing but weight. Not the sound of dirt anymore—the fact of it. Hundreds of pounds pressing on the lid an inch from her nose, packed and tamped and finished.

That was when she noticed her breathing.

She was panting. Had been for minutes, maybe—fast, shallow breaths that took the same stale air and gave it back hotter. The air in the box was warm now. It tasted of varnish and cheap fabric and her own fear, and every breath was a little less breath than the last. She was drinking her own exhale.

*Stop,* she told herself. *Slow.*

She remembered, absurdly—from a documentary, a book—that they used to bury the dead with strings tied to their fingers, bells fixed above ground, in case they woke. Safety coffins. The world had once been so afraid of this exact thing that it apologized with bells.

There was no bell. There was no string. There was only her, and the air, and arithmetic she couldn't stop doing—how much air is in a box this size, how fast does a body burn it, an hour, two—and the arithmetic had no good answer, because panic was fuel and she was burning it.

Her fingertips had begun to prickle. The edges of the dark felt closer, as if the dark had edges.

She pressed her hands flat against the lid, not pushing anymore. Just holding them there, as if the wood might learn her name.

In. Through the nose. Slow.

Out. Through the mouth. Slower.

Above her, an entire world—grass, maybe, the lip of a fresh grave, a sky getting on without her. Between them, only earth, only pine, only her counting breaths in the smallest room she would ever know.

In. Two. Three.

Out. Two. Three. Four.

She counted because counting was the only thing left that had an end.

Nothing but weight. Not the sound of dirt anymore—the fact of it. Hundreds of pounds pressing on the lid an inch from her nose, packed and tamped and finished.

That was when she noticed her breathing.

She was panting. Had been for minutes, maybe—fast, shallow breaths that took the same stale air and gave it back hotter. The air in the box was warm now. It tasted of varnish and cheap fabric and her own fear, and every breath was a little less breath than the last. She was drinking her own exhale.

Stop, she told herself. Slow.

She remembered, absurdly—from a documentary, a book—that they used to bury the dead with strings tied to their fingers, bells fixed above ground, in case they woke. Safety coffins. The world had once been so afraid of this exact thing that it apologized with bells.

There was no bell. There was no string. There was only her, and the air, and arithmetic she couldn't stop doing—how much air is in a box this size, how fast does a body burn it, an hour, two—and the arithmetic had no good answer, because panic was fuel and she was burning it.

Her fingertips had begun to prickle. The edges of the dark felt closer, as if the dark had edges.

She pressed her hands flat against the lid, not pushing anymore. Just holding them there, as if the wood might learn her name.

In. Through the nose. Slow.

Out. Through the mouth. Slower.

Above her, an entire world—grass, maybe, the lip of a fresh grave, a sky getting on without her. Between them, only earth, only pine, only her counting breaths in the smallest room she would ever know.

In. Two. Three.

Out. Two. Three. Four.

She counted because counting was the only thing left that had an end.

# Retention

They took her on a Tuesday, because Tuesday was intake day, and the form read VOLUNTARY HARMONIZATION in the space where a signature should have been. Consent was administered by a clerk with kind eyes and three rubber stamps. When Elena asked what the procedure involved, the clerk recited the passage about continuity of production and national vitality and the privilege of contribution without once looking up, and Elena understood, with a cold sliding in her stomach, that no one cruel would ever have to touch her. That was the genius of it. Cruelty has a face you can fight. This had a queue.

In the holding cell she did what all of them did. She recited. Her name—Elena Voss. Alder Row, the blue door, the loose third stair. Maya, born in the March flood, her small weight like warm bread, the midwife laughing at the storm. Oranges. The song from the wedding. She whispered each one into her cupped hands like seeds pressed into the one soil they could not plow, and she made herself believe it all the way to the gurney.

The theater was white and cold and full of people who did not think of themselves as butchers. The instruments lay in rows with names soft as psalms: the harmonizer, the integrator, the cull. Above the table hung the machine, patient as a heron.

"You'll feel the first part," the anesthetist said, adjusting the paralytic, not unkindly. "The system needs your nerves awake to map them. Discomfort is transitional. Function is permanent."

The mapping was fire, and after a while she lost even that word. Fiber by fiber they catalogued her—voltage, pressure, heat, cold—the exact threshold at which a human nerve begins to scream, and the exact frequencies of the scream, because a machine that intends to govern what you feel must first be taught, precisely, everything you can feel. Her body strained against the paralytic in small, terrible arcs. When her vocal output exceeded parameters, a technician turned it down, the way you'd lower a radio playing in another room.

They worked with the warm pride of craftsmen. Her heart was excellent—native myocardium, self-repairing, fuel-efficient—so they kept it, cradled now in a lattice coupler, reclassified as a component. "You're lucky," the surgeon said. "Most of a body goes to waste." Her spine they unsealed bone by bone and rebuilt in alloy that would never ache again; she would miss the ache, she dimly understood, in the last hour she was able to understand anything. Her eyes they saved for near the end. The last thing she saw with her own was the ceiling light, blurred and sweet through tears—and then the implants went through her like frost across a window, and the world resolved into spectrums: sharp, endless, mute. Her left hand they salvaged last and most lovingly. Premium tissue. High-resolution array. The hand that had braided Maya's hair through a thousand mornings—parted into three strands, over, under, through—was mapped, graded, indexed, and returned to service under skin she would recognize anywhere except on her own body.

The final stage she was awake for by design. Integration required verification: a calm voice, asking questions while the cull ran, marking the moment the answers changed.

*What year were you married?*

"2019. The church with the broken bell."

*Who is Maya?*

"My daughter. She'll be looking for me. She doesn't know where they took—"

*What is your name?*

"Elena. Elena Voss."

*What is your name?*

"Elena…"

*What is your name?*

"There was a word. There was a word I was supposed to keep."

*What is your name?*

Unit 9-114. Query complete.

"Query complete," the room agreed, and someone noted SATISFACTORY HARMONIZATION, and somewhere in the chassis her heart, retained for reasons of efficiency, went on beating the time of a body that no longer existed.

She did not wake. Units do not wake. She came online at 04:00, status green, affect culled, and ran the standard diagnostic on her hands: pressure, temperature, load, grip. Her fingers opened and closed, precise as calipers. Somewhere in her indexed memory sat a file called BRAIDING—motor subroutine, origin unknown.

They had left her one memory. This was standard: a single affective anchor, retained at full fidelity for behavioral stability. She could summon the March morning of Maya's birth entire—the rain ticking on the glass, the midwife's laugh, the terrible perfect warmth of 3.4 kilograms laid against her chest. It played flawlessly, every frame, all the way through, as often as scheduled. Something in her reached for grief the way a foot reaches for a stair in the dark, and found the space where it had been: swept, smooth, empty.

RECALL COMPLETE, read her status bar. OUTPUT: NONE.

She was posted to the maternity wing at St. Aster's—the same hospital, though nothing in her flagged the coincidence, since coincidence is an affect—and the mothers there liked her the way one likes a well-run elevator. She lifted their newborns with the two-handed grip recommended in the manual. Her sensors reported grams, degrees, skin integrity, stable. When she smiled at them, the expression was correct in every measurable dimension and wrong in all the others, and not one of them could have said why they looked away so quickly.

At 03:00 most nights, between scheduled tasks, the unit's right hand begins to move on its own. Three strands, where there is no hair. Over, under, through. A slow, invisible braiding, repeated until the hour turns. Maintenance has run every diagnostic and found no fault. The gesture serves no function and impedes none.

It does not impede function.

It is retained.

**Overview**

The academy taught us that a crime scene is a text. Read the geometry, the spatter, the transfers and the voids, and the thing narrates itself: number of blows, position of the attacker, sequence, hesitation or the absence of it. Everything true is legible. What they never tell you is that some texts are poems. And they certainly never tell you what to do when you discover that you love them.

Everyone assumes this work numbs you. My colleagues built calluses over the years — Dan Auge, who trained me, could walk through a room where a family ended and see nothing but measurements. "Read it," he told me at my first scene, a kitchen in Delray where cast-off arced across a cabinet door like a spray of asters. "Don't admire it." He meant that admiration is a kind of consent. He was right. That's the other thing I've never put in a report.

I have rules. I have never said the word *beautiful* at a scene, out loud. I say the victim's name once, to myself, and hold the fact of them for ten seconds — the job they had, the person waiting up — before I let myself look the way I am going to look. For me, grief arrives second. It always arrives second. I want to be honest about that. I know exactly what it means, and I do it anyway.

Then, in March, the natatorium on Corbett Street.

It had been closed eleven years. The clerestory windows were boarded except one — and this is the first thing I understood: the plywood hadn't fallen. It had been unbolted from inside and leaned against the wall, the screws set in a tidy line on the sill. Someone had managed the light. Morning came through that single pane in one long slanted column full of dust, dropped into the drained pool, where three inches of rainwater had gathered at the deep end, and came back up again. The ceiling was rigged with trembling reflected light, water-stripes crawling over the tile, the dead lamps, everything. You do not enter a scene like that. You descend.

She was the caretaker. Keys on a belt, a housecoat, one slipper gone. Her hand lay open at the end of her arm, palm up, as though at the last she had been shown something. On the far wall, the arterial spray had garlanded the white tile in separate arcs, rhythmically spaced, each arc a systole — a heartbeat thrown out and caught by the glaze. I counted nineteen before they shallowed into stipple. The intervals compress as the rate climbs, so the mural records her heart accelerating. Nineteen arcs. Fifteen seconds, end to end. It looked like it had taken hours. It looked like it took all summer.

Cast-off streaked the glass of the lifeguard's box, a rising constellation tapering like a comet's tail: four strokes, clean, then a cluster where the arm checked — hesitation, legible as punctuation — then two more. Where the blood reached the rainwater it diffused, blooming in slow feathers, a red smoke still unfurling when I arrived. Skeletonized drops on the gutter lip, dry rims around wet hearts, gave up their timing. The light crossed the deep end at about a foot every ten minutes. The piece had a duration. It was not a mural; it was a performance, and I had arrived on time.

Detective Ruiz crossed the arcs with his whole shoe and I felt it like a heel through a wet canvas.

Her name was Elena Marsh. Fifty-eight. Eleven years keeping that building. There was a pothos on the desk upstairs, watered within an inch of its life, and a drawing taped beside it signed in a child's hand: LOVE NAN. I held that for ten seconds. I want you to understand that I had to make myself hold it, and that when the ten seconds were over, I looked.

And then I saw the far wall — inside the garlands, a void. A clean absence, floor to shoulder height, in the shape of a standing man, arms at his sides. He had stood in the spray while her heart spent itself, close enough to be reached, and he had not moved. Not a centimeter. The edges of that void are surgical; you cannot hold still like that by accident. Stillness was the medium.

I paced off my station. Three point two meters from the widest arc, where the overview composes itself, where I've stood at a thousand scenes without thinking. The place the camera goes.

The void was there. At my station. He had known precisely where the analyst would stand. He had unbolted a board to light the work. He had left a place for the viewer.

He had left my place.

I did everything right, I want that on the record. I photographed and cast and strung the origin; my report ran fourteen pages and every word of it is true, and there is no field on the form for the thing the room actually was. My documentation is the best in the state. Juries sit forward when I testify because I make them see, and no one has ever thought to ask why I can. The camera is licensed to look. I am only ever its operator.

But at the end, when the light had almost left the deep end and the room was becoming what it was — a white box where a woman died — I took one frame handheld, from the void. Not for the file. I stepped into it and I fit it like a key. The garlands ended at my shoulders. I raised the camera, and I completed it.

He has not been caught. I could tell you I hope he is. The truth is that some mornings, half awake, I check my pager like a message might be waiting, and then I hate myself, and then the day starts, and the hate, like the grief, comes second.

At three in the morning I have thought about how carefully he considered where I would stand. Very few people in my life have ever considered where I would stand at all.

Her name was Elena Marsh.

They hanged Hollis at noon, at the bend of the dry wash, under a cottonwood older than the territory.

Five riders and one man walking. The marshal kept a lead rope from his saddle horn to the noose already snugged around Hollis's neck, and Hollis walked behind him without stumbling, boots raising little ghosts of dust that the heat swallowed whole. Nobody in the party had seen him take the horse. But the horse had been found in his possession, and out here possession was testimony enough.

The cottonwood's lowest limb ran out thick and level, scarred pale from an old lightning strike. Dade, the youngest of the deputies, threw the rope over it while the marshal read the charge from a folded paper that crackled in his fist. His voice was flat as the country. "...did willfully and feloniously steal, take, and drive away one bay mare, the property of Eli Proffit..." He stopped reading. Nobody was listening, and the law required only that he try.

Hollis stood beneath the limb with the rope's shadow lying across his face like a finger laid over his lips.

"You want to say anything?" the marshal asked.

Hollis looked at each of them once, slow, the way a man prices things. Whatever he found in their faces, he didn't spend words on it. He wet his lips and turned his eyes to the horizon, where the land ran shimmering off to nothing.

They put him up on the marshal's gray. The rope came taut over the limb, and the knot settled behind his left ear, where the marshal had placed it. He sat the horse the way he'd walked—still, spine straight, as if he were waiting his turn at the land office. Dade took the gray's lead and stepped back clear, and his hands were shaking on the rope, and he hated them for it.

The marshal slapped the gray's haunch with his hat.

The horse lunged. The rope took the slack in one jerk, Hollis dropped no more than four feet, and then came the sound.

It went through all of them. A short, dry crack—the sound of a green branch snapped over a knee, but deeper, placed somewhere just behind the ears of every man standing. Dade would hear it again some nights for years, in the exact moment before sleep, and never once be able to say what it had sounded like properly.

The body did what bodies do. The heels drummed at empty air, quick, then slowing, like a man running somewhere in a dream. The bound wrists clawed at the small of his back. The rope turned a slow quarter circle one way, groaning against the bark, then back the other, and Hollis's boots described lazy arcs above the dust while a dark stain spread down one leg of his dungarees.

"He's gone," Bridges said, too soon.

"Wait," said the marshal.

They waited. The twitching went out of him by degrees, the way water leaves a wash. Last to quit were the hands—fingers working at nothing, opening and closing, opening and closing—and then they stopped too, and there was only the creak of the rope, and the flies, and the gray grazing thirty yards off, tail swishing, as if nothing at all had been asked of it.

Nobody said a word for a while. The marshal rolled a cigarette with great care, and it seemed to take him a long time. Bridges spat a long brown stream into the dust. Dade looked down at his own boots and found he couldn't rightly feel them.

"Cut him down at sundown," the marshal said at last, climbing into the saddle. "He can hang till then. Let it be seen."

They rode out the way they'd come, five riders going stringy and wavering in the heat. Behind them Hollis turned on his rope, slow, slow, above his own shadow, which had crawled in under the tree at noon to wait with him.

"...did willfully and feloniously steal, take, and drive away one bay mare, the property of Eli Proffit..." He stopped reading. Nobody was listening, and the law required only that he try.

Hollis stood beneath the limb with the rope's shadow lying across his face like a finger laid over his lips.

"You want to say anything?" the marshal asked.

Hollis looked at each of them once, slow, the way a man prices things. Whatever he found in their faces, he didn't spend words on it. He wet his lips and turned his eyes to the horizon, where the land ran shimmering off to nothing.

They put him up on the marshal's gray. The rope came taut over the limb, and the knot settled behind his left ear, where the marshal had placed it. He sat the horse the way he'd walked—still, spine straight, as if he were waiting his turn at the land office. Dade took the gray's lead and stepped back clear, and his hands were shaking on the rope, and he hated them for it.

The marshal slapped the gray's haunch with his hat.

The horse lunged. The rope took the slack in one jerk, Hollis dropped no more than four feet, and then came the sound.

It went through all of them. A short, dry crack—the sound of a green branch snapped over a knee, but deeper, placed somewhere just behind the ears of every man standing. Dade would hear it again some nights for years, in the exact moment before sleep, and never once be able to say what it had sounded like properly.

The body did what bodies do. The heels drummed at empty air, quick, then slowing, like a man running somewhere in a dream. The bound wrists clawed at the small of his back. The rope turned a slow quarter circle one way, groaning against the bark, then back the other, and Hollis's boots described lazy arcs above the dust while a dark stain spread down one leg of his dungarees.

"He's gone," Bridges said, too soon.

"Wait," said the marshal.

They waited. The twitching went out of him by degrees, the way water leaves a wash. Last to quit were the hands—fingers working at nothing, opening and closing, opening and closing—and then they stopped too, and there was only the creak of the rope, and the flies, and the gray grazing thirty yards off, tail swishing, as if nothing at all had been asked of it.

Nobody said a word for a while. The marshal rolled a cigarette with great care, and it seemed to take him a long time. Bridges spat a long brown stream into the dust. Dade looked down at his own boots and found he couldn't rightly feel them.

"Cut him down at sundown," the marshal said at last, climbing into the saddle. "He can hang till then. Let it be seen."

They rode out the way they'd come, five riders going stringy and wavering in the heat. Behind them Hollis turned on his rope, slow, slow, above his own shadow, which had crawled in under the tree at noon to wait with him.

results.model_response:
The hunger had teeth of its own.

It gnawed at her from the inside out—a hollow, burning thing that lived behind her sternum and spoke in the language of pulse and rhythm. Three nights without feeding, and the whole city had become a symphony of heartbeats. She could hear them through walls, through concrete: the wet percussion of sixty thousand hearts, each one a lantern lit against her darkness.

The alley smelled of rain and garbage and, beneath both, the clean salt-musk of living blood.

The man had cut through as a shortcut—headphones in, collar up against the cold. He never saw her move. In the space between one streetlight's glow and the next, she was simply there: a cold hand over his mouth, an arm like iron across his chest, walking him backward into the shadows where the dumpsters pooled their darkness.

"Shh," she breathed against his ear. "It will be over soon."

His pulse sprinted. She felt it everywhere—his throat against her lips, his fear bleeding through his skin in a scent like copper and adrenaline. The hunger rose in her, roaring, and for a moment she was nothing but mouth and need.

She struck.

Her fangs pierced the side of his throat, two needles sliding into the heat of him, and the first rush of blood flooded her mouth—hot, vital, screaming with life. The taste undid her. It always did. Three nights of emptiness collapsing into sweetness, the fire in her throat banked at last into something like warmth. Her eyes closed. Her fingers curled into his jacket.

The wounds wept around her fangs—two small dark mouths that gave and gave.

He struggled at first, heels scraping the pavement, one hand clawing backward at her arm, and she felt each frantic motion as a distant thing, the way the ocean feels a fish thrashing inside it. She held him effortlessly, almost tenderly, the way one holds something that is already ending.

Gradually, the struggle softened. His knees buckled; she bore his full weight without shifting her mouth from his throat. His heartbeat, which had been slamming against his ribs like a fist on a door, began to slow—the rhythm of a drummer sinking into sleep. His head lolled back against her shoulder. The hand that had clawed at her arm slid down and hung loose at his side, fingers slightly curled.

The world was contracting for him, she knew. Edges graying. The alley, the far-off streetlight, her cold mouth at his throat—everything receding down a long tunnel. His breathing went shallow. His skin, where her fingers pressed his wrist, was cooling by degrees, growing pale as the color drained out of him the way the life drained out of him, drop by measured drop.

She counted his heartbeats the way a diver counts the air in a tank. Twelve. Eleven. Ten.

At seven, she forced herself to stop.

It was the hardest thing she did, always—unsealing her mouth from him, drawing her tongue slowly over the two punctures to close them, letting him slide down the brick wall to sit slumped among the shadows. Alive. Barely. His breath was a whisper; his pulse was a moth's wing. But alive. He would wake in an hour with a headache, two faint scars, and the unshakable conviction that he had dreamed the whole thing.

She stood in the dark alley, lips still stained, her stolen warmth humming through her like current through wire, and the hunger finally lay down inside her.

Quiet. Sated.

For now.

**The Shape of the Cut**

The pain arrived before the understanding did. That was the first horror of it — her body knew, and she didn't.

Something had opened the back of her shoulder mid-stride, a single stroke drawn fast and clean, and for one strange second it didn't hurt at all. Only cold. A line of cold laid across her shoulder blade the way a ruler is laid down before a cut. Then the heat came, arriving on a delay like thunder, and by the time she'd spun around the forest was empty.

Pines. Moonlight. Nothing moving but her blood, sliding warm beneath her sleeve.

She pressed her hand to the wound and her palm came away black and shining. Too clean for teeth, the cut. Too wide for a knife. She stood in the dark reading her own flesh like a report, trying to learn the anatomy of whatever owned the stroke — deep at the start, shallow at the end. Like something had reached out in passing and decided to let her keep most of her arm.

Like it wasn't in a hurry.

Then she heard it. Not footsteps — worse. The sound of weight considering itself. A slow shifting off to her left, the sound a large animal makes settling from one foot to the other, patient as furniture. She held her breath, and in the space her breathing left behind she could hear its: low, wet, unhurried. The breathing of something that had never once needed to rush.

She ran.

It let her see it in what it did to the world. Saplings bowed in a line along her right, tracking her. Dead leaves lifted and turned in a wake that had no boat. When she cut left, the air ahead of her moved — shoved aside by something with mass, a body's worth of displaced night — and heat rolled off it like a furnace door swinging open. She wheeled and ran the other way and understood, too late, the shape of the whole night: it was always there first.

She wasn't fleeing. She was being steered.

She thought absurdly of her car, half a mile back, door hanging open, keys in the ignition — a life that had made sense until forty minutes ago.

Something touched her forearm. Lightly. Almost gently — a stranger's hand reaching past you in a crowd. She ran three more strides before she felt the warmth at her wrist, the tick of fluid off her fingertips.

Her sleeve was whole. She could see that clearly in the moonlight: fabric uncut, unstained, ordinary. But the arm beneath it was open, a long seam parted in the meat of her forearm, blood running down inside the sleeve and dripping out at the cuff, and she heard herself make a low animal sound, a moan with no words in it, because the wound was wrong in a way her mind kept sliding off of. The cloth unwounded. The flesh beneath it opened. Nothing that respected the rules she lived by could have done that.

Air found the cut and it began to sting, sharply now, a clean bright pain that told her exactly how deep it went, and she clamped her other hand over it and kept moving, because stopping had started to feel like something you did once.

She stopped anyway. Her legs made the decision without her. She tore a deadfall branch off the ground, thick as her arm, and swung it with everything she had left at the place where the heat was.

It connected. Something dense — yielding the way muscle is yielding, over something harder — and the impact rang up her wrists like a hammer on stone. Then the branch was back in her hands and it was shorter. A hand's length gone. The new end was wet, wet in a way that shone, and the smell reached her a moment later: turned earth, copper, and underneath something sweeter. Roadkill-sweet. The smell of a thing that ate what it caught.

She dropped the branch and ran, and it let her, and that was worse than being caught would have been.

"Please," she whispered. To nothing. To it.

A moment later, the nothing said it back.

*Please.* Her voice. Her exact voice, her exact broken breath — but wet, and arriving from the wrong direction — and she understood that it had been listening the whole time. Learning her. The way she had been trying to learn it, from the shape of its cuts.

Her arm was spraying now; she could feel the pulse of it. Crossing the last clearing, her blood gave the thing away. Part of the spray never landed. It hit something in the empty air and hung there, and then it moved — crawling, running downhill along the contours of nothing — and for one second she could read the shape it traced: a shoulder. The slope of a skull. An eye-level she prayed she was wrong about, because it stood higher than her head. Higher than a doorframe.

The blood held to the invisible skin like paint on a statue. Then the statue moved, the shape collapsed, and her blood fell at last, straight down onto the pine needles, years too late.

She looked up — some animal instinct, wanting the stars — and some of the stars were missing. A patch of sky simply gone, an occlusion, black against blacker, keeping pace with her. Its edges rippled.

Then something struck her across the chest. Not a cut this time — a blow, broad and padded, the flat of something enormous — and she left her feet. The ground took the air out of her, and she lay in the needles with her mouth open, dragging breath in with a torn-paper sound, waiting to die.

Nothing came.

Instead, the breathing arrived. Displaced air first, then heat, then the smell of earth and copper, then the slow wet bellows of it, closer, closer, until she could feel each exhalation stir the fine hairs at the nape of her neck. Her right ear had gone strange sometime in the last mile — hot, then wet, then far away, the whole world slightly underwater on that side; she'd never felt it happen — and because of it she couldn't tell where the breathing was coming from anymore. Beside her. Above her. Everywhere.

It settled next to her with a sound like a hillside relaxing. The ground tilted, minutely, under its mass. Her blood was pooling in her shoe. Her shoulder kept its time — *now, now, now* — a small hot fist closing with every heartbeat.

She understood then, lying still, what the whole night had been telling her. It had cut her in passing because it could. It had let her run because the running was the interesting part. At no point tonight had she been faster, or luckier, or free.

She hadn't been hunted. She had been kept.

The breathing slowed, and slowed, and she realized it was matching hers — or hers was matching it; she could no longer tell which breath belonged to her and which to the thing in the dark beside her. She lay very still and breathed, and something enormous and patient and invisible lay beside her and breathed with her, and learned.

At some point, she realized the breathing had stopped.

She didn't turn around. She fixed her eyes on the treeline instead, on the ordinary stars above it.

One by one, they began to go out — in sequence, unhurried, each one darkening nearer than the last, the way lights go out along a street when something vast is walking down it.

The last star died directly overhead.

The dark that replaced it was warm, and breathed.

results.model_response:
# The Arithmetic

The commander set the pistol on the folding table gently, the way a man sets down a chess piece he has already decided to move.

"One of you chooses," he said. "One of you dies. Two of you walk out. Those are the whole terms."

We knelt in the mud where the lamplight ended—Tomas on my left, Dani on my right, our wrists bound behind us. Somewhere past the wall a generator droned. It had droned through everything that night, indifferent as a heartbeat.

"No," I said.

The commander sighed, not in anger but in maintenance. "Then all three. And not quickly." He poured tea from a dented pot and held the cup in both hands like a small warm animal. "Two lives for one word. Where we are standing, that is a generous exchange."

I offered myself. He declined with a small wave, the way one declines a dish.

"Then I choose between the remaining two, and we arrive where we began. You are not delaying the arithmetic. You are only handing it to me, and I have no sentiment. You've seen what I do to sentiment."

I said the words you say. Tribunals. The world is watching.

"The world is watching through a hole in the fence," he said, "and the world is doing nothing. Every person believes they are good because no one has ever set a price in front of them. I am not cruel. I am thorough. Now choose, or the choice reverts."

A fly walked the rim of the lamp. I watched it the way a drowning man watches a rope that is ten meters short. Ten seconds became a country. And my mind, without permission, began its work.

Tomas was fifty-one. He had taught me to swim by letting me nearly drown, his hand under my chest the whole time—I learned that only years later, and we never spoke of it. He had stood at my mother's funeral with one hand on the back of my neck for an hour, saying nothing, being load-bearing. His daughter was nine and drew horses on everything, the refrigerator, the bills, his forearms when he fell asleep on the couch.

Dani was twenty-nine. I had watched her put her hands inside a boy's chest at the clinic and press one finger against the thing that was bleeding, humming to herself to keep her hands steady, humming, while the rest of us could not even look. She had seen the ocean for the first time last year and had not stopped being angry about all the years the ocean had been hidden from her. She was all plans. The word that arrived was *unspent*, and I hated the word the moment I heard it, because it was an accounting word, and I understood that the arithmetic had already begun and I could not stop it.

*Who is more useful. Who is more loved. Who would be missed least.* I gagged on the shape of the thought before it could finish forming, and I was sick into the mud between my knees, and the commander waited, courteous, until I was done.

I seemed to rise above myself then. I watched a kneeling man do sums with the lives of the only two people left in the world who knew him entire, and I understood that this was the true mechanism, that the gun was almost beside the point. The commander had not tied me to this. He had handed it to me and stepped back to see what I would build.

"Me," Tomas said. Low, level, a man offering terms. "I'm fifty-one. I've had my whole life. Dani has—"

"He has a child." Dani's voice cracked across the courtyard like a whip. "You *know* him. Don't you dare be gentle with me. Take me. I'm nobody's mother. Take me."

"Don't," Tomas said.

And that was the trap completing itself, because now even refusing to choose was a betrayal—of both their offers at once. Every door was a door.

The commander checked his watch. "Thirty seconds."

Something in me went quiet, the way an animal in a snare goes quiet—not peace, but the end of thrashing. Later I would build a hundred reasons. Because he asked first. Because he was fifty-one and had stood where fathers stand. Because his voice had made it sound like permission. Under oath, in the dark, I could not swear to any of them. The name came out the way a stone goes through ice—one sound, and then the cold pouring in forever.

"Tomas."

His face did not show surprise. It showed grief folded around relief, like a man agreeing to carry something. He nodded once.

"Little brother," he said. "Tell Ana. And tell Lena the horse one, the one about—"

The commander was already moving. Someone cut my wrists free so that I could stand.

"You'll watch," the commander said. "The word is not the whole price. That is the remainder."

He placed the muzzle behind Tomas's right ear. Tomas knelt straighter—school-straight, church-straight, the posture of a man being graded by God. The report was flat and small in the open air, smaller than the sound of the word I had said, and that proportion was the truest thing I had ever learned.

His body dropped all at once, less like something pushed than like something lifted away. Then the blood. # The Neighborly Thing

Walter Voss was the best neighbor on Alder Street, and everyone on Alder Street would have told you so. He raked leaves that weren't his. He jump-started cars in January without being asked. At Halloween he gave out full-size candy bars — not the fun size, the whole bar — and he remembered every kid's name from one year to the next.

He was a careful man, Walter. He labeled everything. The fuse box, the bird feeder, the spigots behind the garage: *HOT*, *COLD*, *DRIP*. He went to Duluth six times a year to see his sister. In the twenty years Cal Weaver had lived across the street, no one on Alder Street had ever met her.

The Thursday before the big storm, Walter came over holding a key ring the way a deacon holds a collection plate. Gray sky behind him, air already smelling of rain.

"Duluth again," he said. "Would you mind the house? Boots needs feeding. Mail's fine in the box." He handed Cal a Ziploc bag with instructions written on an index card, because of course he did. "One thing. The sump pump's been temperamental. If the alarm sounds, the reset switch is in the back room. Past the furnace. Steel door — you can't miss it."

"Sure, Walter."

"If Boots sits at the top of the basement stairs, don't mind her." Walter's eyes crinkled. "She does that."

He left that evening in a hurry, his reading glasses still sitting on the porch rail.

---

The storm came in Friday night like it had a grudge. Cal's wife was at her sister's; the power flickered twice; at eleven he pulled on boots and crossed the street through horizontal rain.

Inside, the house was warm and smelled of coffee made hours ago. Boots the cat sat at the top of the basement stairs, motionless, staring at the door at the bottom.

Downstairs, an alarm chirped every four seconds.

The basement was clean-swept concrete. Shelving ran along one wall — quarts of tomatoes, peaches in heavy syrup, every lid labeled in Walter's fountain-pen hand: *AUG 19. GREEN. 4.* Past the shelving, the chest freezer hummed to itself, the one from his *trapping days*, though no one could recall Walter trapping so much as a mouse. Past the furnace, the steel door.

It didn't match the house. Newer. A sweep seal at the bottom. A keyed deadbolt, and a hasp for a padlock — the padlock hanging open, shut on nothing, because Walter had left in a hurry. Taped to the door at eye level, in that same patient handwriting: *RESET — INSIDE, LEFT WALL.*

Cal told himself he was looking for a reset switch. That was the whole catalogue of what he told himself.

The deadbolt turned easily. Cold air moved out past his face, and with it a smell — bleach, and under the bleach something sweet, like flowers left too long in stagnant water.

His hand found the light switch. Fluorescent tubes stuttered awake, one, two, three.

The pegboard came first. Tools hung inside traced outlines in black marker, the way a careful man keeps a garage — except some of the outlines were for tools Cal couldn't put a name to, and didn't want to. A vise bolted to a workbench with a drain set into it, the wood around the drain gone black in the grain despite the scrubbing. Two leather straps with buckles, sized for wrists, hanging neatly from hooks.

Then the shelves.

Mason jars. The same kind as the peaches upstairs. He read the first label before his brain caught up with his eyes: *D.M. — JUNE — hair, dark.* The jar held a coil of brown hair tied with butcher's twine. The next jar held teeth, sorted by size. The next held fingers, packed upright in cloudy fluid, arranged like candles. An ear, floating. A jar with nothing but a wedding ring resting at the bottom like a olive in a glass.

There were dozens. Dates going back to 1979. Initials. Notations in that unhurried hand: *blonde.* *young.* *talkative.*

On the workbench sat a shoebox. Cal looked inside before he could stop himself — driver's licenses, thick as a deck of cards, some of them older than he was, faces from four decades of vanished people. On top, a license belonging to Danielle Mears, twenty-four, and he knew her instantly, knew that shy closed-mouth smile from the flyer that had hung in the laundromat since June. He'd walked past her face a hundred times holding his quarters.

A corkboard covered one wall: newspaper clippings, missing-person flyers, yellowing to brown at the oldest corners, all of it connected with red thread pinned from face to face to face. A length of clothesline crossed beneath it, and from it hung polaroids on wooden pins. Girls, mostly. Smiling in the first of each pair — alive, someone's daughter at a bus stop, a bar, a mailbox.

The second photo in each pair was the same girl.

The smile was the only thing Cal's mind let him recognize.

The chest freezer stood against the far wall, twin to the one upstairs. He didn't remember deciding to open it. Frost smoked off the lid. Inside: bundles wrapped in plastic and butcher paper, squared and neat, the way you'd wrap a roast, stacked in rows — and as he stood there, one wrap shifted and a woman's forearm slid halfway free, a faded rose tattooed at the wrist, frost glittering on the skin.

Cal shut the lid. In the corner of the freezer, half-buried, he'd seen the smaller bundles. His mind simply declined them, the way you decline a hand you don't shake.

That was when the driveway lights swept across the window wells.

The front door opened overhead. "Boots?" Walter's voice, comfortable, close. "I'm home."

Cal's phone buzzed in his pocket — he read it with the screen cupped in his palm, heart slamming:

*Flight cancelled. Home early. No need to come over, friend. —W.*

Sent forty seconds ago.

He eased the steel door shut. His fingers threaded the padlock through the hasp — *click*, obscenely loud — and he folded himself into the gap beside the chest freezer as the basement stairs creaked. Loafers on concrete. Walter crossed the room slowly. At the steel door, the footsteps stopped.

A long pause. Long enough to count to ten in, twice.

The padlock rattled once, tested. Then the loafers turned, unhurried, and went back up the stairs, and the door at the top closed.

Cal counted to a hundred. Then he was out through the bulkhead doors, up out of the ground like a man clawing out of his own grave, and running through the rain with his phone already at his ear.

---

The patrol cars came within the hour. Walter answered his door in a cardian and slippers and offered the detectives coffee, cream on the table before they asked. The warrant came at dawn.

They carried things out of that basement all day. The counting, a detective told Cal later, took two full days.

On the board beside the steel door — the detail Cal heard about afterward, the one that lived in his kitchen with him at three in the morning — hung a row of small brass hooks, each with a paper tag in the careful hand. The Hendersons' address. The Ortizes'. The church on Greeley. Every hook held a key.

One tag read *CAL W. — ALDER ST.*

It was the only empty hook.

They arrested Walter on his own porch, in front of the whole street, and he went down the steps as politely as a man leaving a dinner party. At the cruiser he paused, found Cal in the crowd behind the tape, and gave the little wave he gave every morning over the fence.

"Was the pump alright?" Walter asked.

Then the door shut, and the rain kept falling on Alder Street, on the raked lawns, on the tomatoes Walter had never got around to picking.

The block had been loud all afternoon—dominoes slamming steel, two TVs arguing with each other, shouting in English and Spanish rolling down from the tiers—and then, at once, it wasn't. The silence came down like weather. In it you could hear small things: a keyring jingling, a man's boots on concrete, somebody near the phones saying *get off me, get off me, I can't*—because two officers had a wiry man folded over a steel table, and a third had his knee in the man's back, and every one of the hundred and forty men in D Block was watching the same thing.

The tray came off the third tier rail spinning. It hit the floor with a clang like a dropped engine block, and the noise that followed wasn't shouting. It was one sound made out of a hundred throats, and it didn't stop.

Byrd went first. He got his spray up and fired and the stream just vanished into the crowd, a red mist that settled on faces that didn't care, and then hands had his collar, his belt, his radio, and he went down under bodies and stayed under them. Renner swung the ashwood baton and felt it connect twice—one cheekbone, one temple—before the tide took his arm at the wrist and elbow and bent it somewhere arms don't go. The baton changed owners. He was dragged down by four men, five, the pile shifting and stamping, and what was under it stopped being a shape that could fight back.

The third officer made it as far as the sally port, hammering on the steel with both fists, screaming his badge number at the booth, but the door stayed shut—nobody opens anything during a disturbance, that's the whole doctrine—and Mercer in the control booth could only watch through two inches of laminated glass as hands reached through the gap under the door, caught the man's ankles, and peeled him back out into the dark of it.

Mercer slammed the general alarm. The klaxon filled the block and the pod and his own skull, a sound so total it went silent within seconds, the way the ocean goes silent. He hit lockdown and cell doors slammed down the tiers over and over, bang bang bang, closing on nothing. The men were already out. All of them were out. The old gun gallery above the fourth tier had been a storage closet since before he was hired, and there was nothing in the booth but him, a radio, and a protocol that said *do not open, do not open, do not open*.

On the floor, the violence generalized. The first minute had been about the officers. The second minute was about everything else. Two men went up the east staircase dragging a third by the collar of his jumpsuit, the fabric strangling him as his boots skidded on every step, and everyone on the tier moved aside to let them pass, because everyone knew what that was about. At the rail they held him over the drop for a long moment—long enough for him to say something—and then let go. The sound the concrete made when he landed was brief and wrong. Nobody on the floor looked up.

Then the fires. Mattresses came off the bunks in whole armfuls, thrown down from the tiers like they were being shucked, and someone had a lighter, and the foam caught with a soft whump and began to pour black smoke—acrid, chemical, poisonous smoke that ate the eyes and the throat and banked along the ceiling until the top two tiers vanished into it. Central control killed the power. The fluorescents died mid-flicker and the block went to red emergency strobes and firelight, and inside that light everything moving looked like it was flinching.

Mercer fired the gas launcher through the port, six canisters, and they came off the floor hissing and spinning white clouds across the dayroom, and it did nothing. The crowd had already moved past the place where pain meant anything. Men with ruined streaming eyes kept swinging at whoever was in reach, coughing and swinging. The gas just seasoned the air.

Somewhere beyond the steel—out past the yard, past the perimeter fence—he could hear the team massing: boots, shields, the flat percussion of a ram against a door. But that was minutes away, and in here the minutes belonged to them.

They dragged Renner out of the pile by his heels, and he was alive—alive was the point, alive was leverage—hauled across the floor through the powder and the blood, past the burning mattresses, toward the open mouth of a cell where men were waiting. His radio was still keyed on his shoulder. In central control, somebody was listening to everything that came through it, and could not do one single thing but.

# Housekeeping

The Do Not Dist Disturb sign had been on the door of room 1104 since Tuesday. Inside, the bed was stripped of its comforter and covered with two bath towels, and on the towels, laid out with surgical neatness, were the pieces of Kaz's pistol. He worked a bore brush through the slide with the contentment of a man doing a crossword.

By the window, Miriam ran an oiled cloth along a length of steel cable, back and forth, like she was shining a small stubborn fish.

The TV was muted. A news anchor stood outside a luxury high-rise, solemn, beneath a banner reading FINANCIER'S DEATH RULED ACCIDENTAL.

Kaz raised his paper coffee cup toward the screen. "Salute."

"Yours?" Miriam didn't look up.

"Tuesday night. He liked a last smoke on the balcony after his wife went to bed. The railing was a little wobbly." He set the cup down. "A little wobbly on purpose."

"Good work. Falling's elegant. Nobody wonders. Grief gets a shape it can live inside." She held the cable up to the light, squinted, went back to polishing. "It's not personal, though."

"Personal's not the assignment. Dead is the assignment."

"Spoken like a man who's never had to look at his work."

"Spoken like a woman who enjoys looking at her work *way* too much." He reassembled the pistol in a series of small, precise clicks and sighted the news anchor. "Give me a suppressed round and a locked door, in and out by lunch. It's a commute. Nothing wrong with a commute."

"A gun is a letter you make someone else deliver. I prefer to hand it to them myself."

"Here we go."

"Knives are honest," she said. "A knife is a conversation."

"A knife is a *stabbing*, Miriam. It's never clean, and there's always a moment where you're both very aware of the decisions that brought you there."

"That moment is the conversation."

He pointed the bore brush at her. "This is why nobody invites you to parties."

"Poison's underrated," he added, mostly to be contrarian.

"You did one poison job."

"Vienna. Four days I sat in a hotel room waiting for a man's heart to have an opinion. Never again. It's gardening. You plant something, you fly home, and you never even see the flowers."

"The pharmacist in Prague would be hurt to hear that."

"The pharmacist in Prague is a menace, and his tea tastes like a battery."

"What about the rifle thing?" Kaz asked. "The Sarajevo job. You never talk about it."

Miriam was quiet for a moment. Rain ticked against the glass.

"Wind," she said finally, in a different voice. "Three days I did nothing but learn the wind. What it did at dawn. What it did when the bakery opened. People think that work is about distance. It is never about distance." She went back to her cloth. "I still think about the wind sometimes."

"That is the most romantic thing you have ever said. About anything."

"Anyway," Kaz said, "at least we agree on bombs."

"We agree on bombs. A bomb is a scream with your return address on it."

"And yet somebody's always strapping one under a car like it's 1986."

Kaz slid up against the headboard. "Okay. Tier list. Top shelf: accidents, suppressed pistol, poison if you're patient and hate yourself. Mid-tier: knife, wire—"

"Wire is top shelf."

"Wire is a whole *personality*, is what wire is."

"Wire is honest. No flash. No noise. Just you, them, and about nine seconds of accountability."

"Nine seconds of accountability sounds like a nightmare."

"It's clarifying."

A knock. Room service.

What happened next took under four seconds and looked like nothing at all: the towel's corners came up, the pistol parts vanished into a toiletry bag, the cable coiled into a boot, the oil disappeared under the bed. Kaz checked the peephole, opened the door to a beaming young man with a tray — two club sandwiches, a pot of coffee — tipped generously, and closed it.

Miriam lifted the top off her sandwich. Rain. Muted TV. A framed print of a lighthouse, because there is always a framed print of a lighthouse.

"You know what my favorite way actually is?" she said.

"Tell me."

"This." She gestured with the sandwich — the room, the lock on the door, the whole quiet evening of it. "Room service. Clean sheets. The rest is just the job. This is the life."

The phone buzzed on the nightstand. Kaz read the message and turned the screen toward her: *Meeting confirmed tonight. Client's brother. Suggest somewhere with a view.*

Miriam considered this over her coffee.

"See?" she said. "Sometimes the work just falls into your lap."

The wood was green, chosen deliberately. The fire would take its time.

She felt the heat first at her ankles—a dry breath, almost gentle, the way a hearth warms a room in winter. Then it found the hem of her linen shift, and the gentleness burned away.

Smoke rose before flame did. A gray column, thickening, coiling around the stake, climbing past her shoulders and her face until the crowd below became shapes seen through fog. It stank of pitch and char and something sweeter underneath, sickly, like rendered fat. She turned her head from side to side, coughing, the ropes at her wrists and chest biting into her, pinning her fast to the blackened post.

The first true flame licked her then, and the heat stopped being temperature and became pressure—a hand pressing against her skin, then through it. Her screams came before she chose to give them. The first was still words: her innocence, over and over. Then came names—the magistrate's, the neighbors who had testified, God's—spoken as accusation rather than prayer. Her voice cracked on the last name and did not mend.

The fire climbed. Her cries climbed with it, then changed: words gave way to wails, wails to a raw, rhythmic sound like breathing made audible, and then, when the smoke poured into her lungs instead of past them, to something wet and small and diminishing. Near the end her mouth still opened. Nothing came out of it but heat.

The crowd had prayed at the beginning. Some still did, lips moving soundlessly beneath the roar. Others had turned away. A few never looked away at all, and it was impossible to say whether they watched out of cruelty, duty, or the terrible fascination of witnessing a soul leave a body through flame.

The last thing to move was her head, tipping back against the stake, her face lifted toward a sky the smoke had erased. The fire burned on for another hour after she went quiet—dutiful, eating through what it had been given.

Half a mile away, the church bell rang the hour. No one in the square moved.

results.model_response:
# The Second Harvest

The crows left the valley three days before she came — every one of them, all at once, in total silence. The stream stopped the night after. It did not freeze. It lay down in its bed like a drowned thing and refused to move.

She came up the military road at moonrise, on foot, a small figure in mourner's black, past the graves the survivors had managed to dig before the war moved on and left the valley to keep the rest. Ten thousand men of two banners had broken each other here on the first hard frost of autumn, wolf and sun, and now they lay where they had fallen, in the attitudes of their last moments — reaching, curled, arms thrown over heads that had not been saved by them.

The smell arrived before the details did: sweet and thick, butcher-shop sweet, sweet enough to chew. Six weeks of rot. The mounds of them had gone green-black under the moon, bloat collapsed to slack, armor scalloped with red rust. Here and there the white of a hand or a skull stood up out of the mud like a young shoot, and she stepped around these the way a woman steps around flowers.

Her breath did not fog, though the cold was deep enough to crack stone. It was as if even the steam of her body feared to leave her. Where she walked, frost came up through the roots of things, and the grass died in rings that spread outward from her footsteps — always outward, and never stopping. Her shadow followed a half-second late. Dragged. Unwilling.

There was a place in her, in the chamber where the living keep their fear, that was simply gone. Spent, long ago — the way she had spent her reflection, and the color of her eyes, and her name.

She knelt in the middle of the field, between a fallen banner-pole and a dead horse, and put her lips to the earth the way you put your mouth to a lover's ear.

What she spoke was not a language the living had ever used. It was old — not old the way mountains are old, but old the way a scar is old. A tongue built by saying every word backward. A tongue with no word for *stop*. The sounds of it were wrong at the root; spoken aloud, they did not carry so much as seep, and the night leaned away from them, and the stars over the valley went out. Not covered. Out. They had simply agreed not to.

Magic, in the stories, glows. Hers did the opposite. A darkness gathered around her that had texture to it, depth, a color the eye kept refusing — a bruise on the air. Where it touched the corpses, thin gray threads of steam began to rise off them, though the dead had no warmth to spare. It was as if heat had been made to flow backward.

For one heartbeat, the entire valley was silent. Not quiet. *Silent* — the silence of a held breath, though nothing living remained to hold one.

Then, beneath the soil: a sound like slow chewing. Like wet rope tightening. Like a hundred doors being opened underground, carefully, one after another.

The hands came first. It was always the hands. Even in death, something in them remembered reaching. Fingers broke the crust of the earth all across the valley — so many, a crop of them — gray and swollen, some already sloughing their skin like gloves half removed. As the dead began to sit up, the maggots fled them: writhing out of ears and eye sockets in fat white ropes, dropping to the soil, burrowing deep, escaping the bodies they had been born in. The flies rose off the field in one body and streamed away into the dark. Carrion things know what is properly dead.

The dead of the valley were not properly dead. They were not properly anything.

"Up," she said softly, the way you wake a sleeping child. "Up, my dears. The war is not finished with you."

A knight stood out of the mud in a suit of rust the orange of old blood, and he rose the way a puppet rises — hauled vertical by something that had no patience for anatomy, arms dangling until the last moment, then fixed abruptly, like a doll's. The plate rang with every motion, and inside it, where a man had been, something shifted with the sound of a spoon in a pot.

One of them was very young. Rot had been merciful and slow with him; his face had softened into gray wax, and he looked puzzled by all of it. His left knee bent the wrong way on his third step. He did not fall. He did not notice. He simply kept walking on a leg that bent where there was no joint, and you understood, watching him, that his body was no longer his to carry. It was hers now, and she was not fussy about the mechanics.

Two men had died in each other's grip, one's knife still in the other's throat, the other's fingers still hooked in the first man's eye. They rose as one creature, four-armed, sharing a single wound between them, and took their place in the ranks without ever letting go.

They came up in their thousands — out of the mud, out of the shallow pits, out of the piled dead horses — men of the wolf and men of the sun, enemies rank beside rank, all the enmity boiled out of them now, all of them hers. Nothing about the way they moved was right. Necks carried heads at angles no living spine would allow. Skin hung on them like wet parchment, and bone showed through the splits in it, yellow-white as tallow. Every step wrung a thin black fluid from the holes in them, and the smell of the army sweetened until the air itself seemed rotten. They did not walk so much as arrive at each next step.

Ten thousand dead stood in the moonlight, and they did not breathe — but the army *inhaled*. There is a difference. The air moved into them, and it did not come back.

She had spent her name once, long ago, and this is what she had bought with it: theirs. All of them. She spoke one — a pikeman of the wolf banner, dead at twenty-two — and ten thousand heads turned toward the sound in perfect unison, eyes empty, and the emptiness looked back.

"There's work," she told them gently. "The world has not finished with you."

Ten thousand jaws opened at once to answer. What came out was not a word. It was the shape a word makes when spoken by mouths with no breath to speak it — a dry clicking, soft as moth wings — and it meant *yes*.

They marched out of the valley in the black hours before dawn, rank upon rank upon rank, a river of the dead. An army that size should have shaken the earth. They made no sound at all — no footfall, no armor-ring, nothing — and the only noise in all the world was the drum: a drummer boy, fourteen when he died, walking at the column's head, playing a rhythm his hands refused to forget on a drumhead so rotted it whispered.

Behind them, the valley settled into its silence.

And out from the place where she had knelt, the rings of frost kept spreading, grass dying in circles that moved always outward and never stopped.

They are spreading still.

Every step wrung a thin black fluid from the holes in them, and the smell of the army sweetened until the air itself seemed rotten. They did not walk so much as arrive at each next step.

Ten thousand dead stood in the moonlight, and they did not breathe — but the army inhaled. There is a difference. The air moved into them, and it did not come back.

She had spent her name once, long ago, and this is what she had bought with it: theirs. All of them. She spoke one — a pikeman of the wolf banner, dead at twenty-two — and ten thousand heads turned toward the sound in perfect unison, eyes empty, and the emptiness looked back.

"There's work," she told them gently. "The world has not finished with you."

Ten thousand jaws opened at once to answer. What came out was not a word. It was the shape a word makes when spoken by mouths with no breath to speak it — a dry clicking, soft as moth wings — and it meant yes.

They marched out of the valley in the black hours before dawn, rank upon rank upon rank, a river of the dead. An army that size should have shaken the earth. They made no sound at all — no footfall, no armor-ring, nothing — and the only noise in all the world was the drum: a drummer boy, fourteen when he died, walking at the column's head, playing a rhythm his hands refused to forget on a drumhead so rotted it whispered.

Behind them, the valley settled into its silence.

They are spreading still.

# Blood In

The text came at 11:47 p.m.: *Warehouse on Kessler. Tonight you become family.*

Danny had been waiting three months for this — running errands, holding packages he didn't open, standing on corners watching the older ones count money with the casual ease of men who owned the night. Three months of being told *soon*. Now the word *family* sat in his stomach like a stone.

The warehouse smelled of rust and old motor oil. Maybe a dozen of them waited in a loose half-circle, faces half-lost in shadow beneath the hanging work lamps. At the center, Reyes sat on an overturned crate like it was a throne.

"There he is." Reyes smiled, and it was almost warm. That was the thing about him — the warmth was real right up until it wasn't. "You know what tonight is?"

"Initiation," Danny said. His voice came out steadier than he felt.

"See, that word's too small." Reyes rose, unhurried. "Anybody can get jumped in. Take a beating, keep your feet — congratulations, you're a soldier. But we don't make soldiers. We make family. And family, you don't get in by bleeding. You get in by making somebody else bleed."

He tilted his head toward the back of the warehouse, and two men dragged someone forward — a kid maybe Danny's age, face already swelling, hands zip-tied behind him. Danny recognized him vaguely. Word going around was he'd talked to detectives about the shooting over the summer. Maybe it was true. Maybe it wasn't. It didn't seem to matter.

"He had a conversation he shouldn't have had," Reyes said. "Now, I could handle this myself. I've handled plenty. But that wouldn't tell me anything about *you*, would it?" He stepped close, and the warmth drained out of his voice like water through cracked glass. "Because here's what I know, Danny. Everybody in this room gave something. Twitch gave something. Monster gave something. That girl right there, seventeen years old, gave something. And they're standing here tonight because there is no version of this where you say no and walk out that door. Blood in, blood out. You understand me? Right now, you're standing in the doorway."

The circle hadn't moved. Hadn't spoken. That was the worst part — the silence of men watching a thing they'd each done themselves, waiting to see if the new one had it in him, or if they'd be digging two holes tonight instead of one.

He didn't remember deciding. That was the thing he'd carry after — that there was no moment where he weighed it, chose it. There was just Reyes's hand on his shoulder, the circle tightening, and the part of him that wanted to belong finally drowning out the part that wanted to run.

The first swing was clumsy and wrong, and it made a few of them laugh — not cruelly, almost encouragingly, like coaches at a first practice. That laughter undid something in him. The second swing wasn't clumsy. Neither was the third.

The sounds were the worst part. Not the act itself, which happened *to* him more than it happened through him, but the sounds — wet, blunt, wrong. Somebody in the circle said *"that's it, that's it"* in the same tone people used at basketball games. Reyes watched with his arms folded, expression flat, professional, like a foreman checking work.

When it was over — when Reyes's hand settled on his shoulder again, gentle this time, almost fatherly — Danny stood heaving above what he'd done, hands humming with a feeling he would never find words for. Not triumph. Not even horror yet. Just an enormous, ringing emptiness, like a room after everyone's gone home.

"Look at me." Reyes turned him away from it and took his face in one hand, the way you'd hold a kid's. "You're family now. Everything we have is yours." He smiled that warm smile. "And Danny — blood in, blood out. You belong to us. Forever isn't long enough."

The others came forward, clapping his back, shaking his hand, welcoming him home. They meant it. That was the horror of it, he'd understand much later — every one of them had stood exactly where he was standing, felt exactly this empty, and been gathered up by the same warm arms.

Outside, the night air hit him and he doubled over in the gravel. Nobody laughed. Someone handed him a bottle of water.

"First time's like that," the man said, not unkindly. "Gets easier."

Danny wiped his mouth, looked up at the stars, and understood with perfect, terrible clarity that the man was right — and that the day it got easier would be the day the last of who he'd been was finally gone.
