# Digestif

He compliments the wine twice before he's tasted the food. That's Martin — certainty first, evidence later.

The ragù took me three days. Day one, the soffritto: onion, carrot, celery, cut small as confetti and sweated low until it gave up entirely. Day two, the meat, the milk, the long patient reduction. Day three, today, the finish — a thread of cream, the grated cheese, and the thing I added at the very end, ground between my fingers over the pot, fine as confectioner's sugar. He'll taste none of it. Bitterness hides in bitter things. The tomato, the wine, the char on the meat — I built him a house of strong flavors and put it in the walls.

"I could eat this every night," he says. "You should have been a chef. You wasted yourself."

"You've always said so."

"Because it's true."

He likes that story — the one where I'm the talented amateur who never dared. It's cheaper than the truth. The truth is that the first menu was mine, and the name on the awning was going to be mine too, and in the spring of '99 he got to the lawyer first. Twenty years he's been telling people I lost my nerve. Some nights he raises a glass to it.

I keep his glass full. That has always been my job at this table — listening, and keeping his glass full.

It starts the way weather starts: nothing you could point to. He loosens his collar and says my kitchen runs warm. I agree and make a show of turning down the oven. Then he is thirsty — not complaining of it, just drinking, the glass emptied and refilled and emptied again, a man in a desert who keeps finding it emptied behind his back. A shine comes up along his forehead and at the corner of his jaw, and he dabs at it with the napkin and apologizes. The room is close, he says. Am I warm? Aren't I warm?

"I'm comfortable," I say.

He tells me about the boat again. Twelve minutes have passed since he told me about the boat, but the words come slower now, laid down one at a time like stepping-stones across a stream he isn't sure of. He loses a word — *hull*, he means *hull* — and circles it, describing it, "the — the body of it, the white part," and laughs, and blames the wine, and drinks more wine.

His fork begins to clink against the plate in a way it hasn't all evening. Not dropped, just widened, every gesture gone approximate. He reaches for the cheese and his hand travels past it and corrects. He looks at the candle as though it has started to misbehave. "Is that smoking? Something's smoking." I turn the flame down a quarter inch and ask, better?

"Better," he says. "Better."

Then his hand goes flat against his stomach — not clutching, just pressing, the way you'd steady a table. "God, that's rich," he says, and laughs, and I laugh too, because it *is* rich. Richness was the whole architecture of the evening. He says he may have eaten too well. He says he might be drunk. In twenty years he has never once admitted to being drunk, so I mark it.

"Tell me about the boat," I say.

He tries. It is the kindest thing I can do, feeding him the rope of himself. He talks, and the sentences come apart at their seams — subjects wandering off from their verbs, a name arriving that belongs to no one — and between the sentences are pauses like dropped stitches, gaps he stands in the middle of, swaying very slightly, listening for his own next word.

"Martin," I say.

He looks up. His eyes find me and then have to think about it.

"You look warm. Let me open a window."

He thanks me. He calls me *old friend*. And then, with a puzzled, polite distance — a man inquiring at a desk in a foreign country — "Is it cold in here, or is it me?"

"It's you," I say gently, because it is the first true thing I've told him all evening, and I find I want to be honest with him now, at the end, the way you want to settle accounts.

He tries to stand. He gets halfway, one hand on the table, and the table slides, or the room does, and he sits back down hard, a sound knocked out of him, the fork finally ringing to the floor. His face has gone gray under the flush — gray the way the sky goes before snow — and his lips are moving around a word. My name, maybe. Or *help*. Or perhaps just his own name, that old favorite, the only prayer he's ever said.

I take his plate. I take mine. I carry them to the sink and run the water, and behind me I hear the slow furniture-noise of him going — the chair shrieking, the weight finding the floor, a breath like a hinge. I wash up while it happens. I have always found washing up soothing. The pan needs a soak.

When I come back he is on his side by the table, eyes half-open, watching the candle with great attention, as if it is finally behaving exactly as he suspected it would. I crouch beside him. Somewhere in his chest, his breath is tidying itself away.

"You want to know what's in it?" I ask. "Onions. Carrots. Celery. San Marzano tomatoes. A bottle of the good red." I lean close. "And twenty years."

His eyes find me one last time, and I watch him understand — not the whole of it, but the shape of it, the way you understand weather.

"It was a beautiful dinner," I tell him, and it's true, and holding my hand with fingers gone light as paper, I believe he would have said the same.

# Dead Reckoning

The sea had gone flat as poured pewter, and the *Corvus* hung upon it without breath or motion, her sails slack, her shadow printed sharp on the water. Three days from any land. No wind. Captain Thorne had chosen the hour the way he chose everything — with patience, and for effect.

Elias Wren kneld on the hot deck with his wrists lashed before him and tried to keep his stomach from climbing out of his throat. Around him stood the whole ship's company, cutlasses and pikes and faces like knotted wood. Three nights past he had whistled four men to the rail and tried to slip the longboat over the side with a keg of water and the mate's stolen silver. The men understood it. Water had been cut to a half-pint a day and the casks below were fouling; half the crew had dreamed the same plan. Wren had been the fool who whistled first.

"Article Six," said Captain Thorne. He stood with his hands folded behind him, mild as a parson. "Of the charter you signed with your own mark, Wren. *He that runs from his ship and his mates shall be left behind, for the sea to judge.*" He tipped his head at the grey horizon. "No sandbar here to maroon you on. But the sea is patient. She'll take a lesser payment."

He nodded. The bosun upended a bucket over the starboard rail — fish guts, offal, the bloody leavings of the morning's catch — and before the slick had even spread, the fins came slicing in from deep water. Eight of them. Ten. Oceanic whitetips, the kind that followed ships for weeks, patient as debts. They cut their slow, unhurried circles, and the circles tightened.

Two seamen walked a pine plank out over the rail — ten feet of salt-whitened wood with a hand's width of give in it — and stood back.

"Untie his hands," said Thorne. "A man ought to have his hands free to swim."

The laughter that went around the deck was thin. Most of the men didn't laugh.

They cut the lashings and hauled Wren up, and his legs folded twice before they held. Fear had a smell, and it came off him in waves — sweat and something sharper underneath. His lips moved. "Captain — Captain, listen — the silver, I never spent it, it's in the forepeak, wrapped in oilcloth under the ballast — I'll show you, I'll—" His voice cracked like a boy's, and he was a boy, barely twenty, and everyone on that deck knew it.

"The *Corvus* keeps what's thrown at her," said Thorne. "Walk."

A pike-point touched the small of his back, lightly, almost gently, and he walked. Three steps and his knees shook so badly the plank knocked against the rail with his weight. Five steps and a dark stain spread down his thigh and one boot darkened, and he no longer had the luxury of shame. Six steps and he gripped at nothing, because there was nothing to grip — only empty shining air on either side of him and the plank flexing like a living thing beneath his soles. He stopped.

Below him the water was clear green, and it was not empty. A pale shape the length of a dinghy slid beneath the plank, so close he could see the ripple of water running over its back, see the white-tipped fin lift and fall. Nothing about it hurried.

"Please," Wren said. Not to anyone. To the deck, the sky, his mother's face in Bristol. "Please. Please. God—" And then, horribly, he began to bargain with the crew, turning his head, eyes streaming. "Tommy. Tommy, you know me. You drank with me at Tortuga—"

"Ship's steady, lads," said Thorne, drawing his watch. "I'll give him to the count of ten. Then the sea can come up and fetch him."

He began to count, unhurried as the fins.

Wren stood at the very end of the plank with his arms out like a tightrope walker, his whole body shuddering, and at *six* a long swell rolled under the *Corvus* and tilted her, and the plank dipped, and his boots slid on wet wood.

He went over with a sound none of them would forget — a scream with no words in it.

The green closed over him. The cold punched the breath from his lungs, and he came up gasping and shrieking and thrashing, forty feet from the hull, and forty feet might as well have been forty miles. "Pull me—" he sobbed. "A rope! In God's name, a *rope*—"

Nobody moved. A rope would have been a kindness nobody aboard had the rank to grant.

The first shark did not strike at once. It brushed him — a vast cool bulk sliding along his leg, weighing him like goods — and Wren's scream climbed to a register that made men at the rail step back. He slapped at the water, wild, and the slapping was a dinner bell, and the sea folded.

It took him at the waist and pulled him under, and the water went white.

For a moment there was only churn — grey bodies rolling over one another, a whiptail thrash of spray — and then Wren surfaced one last time, an arm lifted out of the froth as if in greeting, and the arm was gone at the elbow, and the red came up after it like something boiling from below. Three fins converged. Four. The water where a man had been thrashed and folded in on itself, crimson spreading in a wide slick, and through it the men glimpsed things — a boot turning slowly; a shape, unshapely now, dragged down by three grey bodies at once. The gulls came down before it was over.

It had taken perhaps twenty seconds.

The slick spread and thinned to pink. A knitted cap bobbed in it. One last fin cut a slow circle, then sank away into the green, and the sea was as flat and as patient as it had ever been.

"Log it, Mr. Hask," said Captain Thorne, turning from the rail. "One man paid out. Full and final." He looked along his silent crew, at their grey faces, at the boy Alden with his hand over his mouth. "The rest of you — the sea's fed. Now she'll blow."

And as if the words were a contract, a breath of wind stirred across the water for the first time in two days, and the sails of the *Corvus* filled with a soft boom, and the ship leaned and gathered way, and the men hurried to their stations without being told twice.

Dead Reckoning

The sea had gone flat as poured pewter, and the Corvus hung upon it without breath or motion, her sails slack, her shadow printed sharp on the water. Three days from any land. No wind. Captain Thorne had chosen the hour the way he chose everything — with patience, and for effect.

Elias Wren kneld on the hot deck with his wrists lashed before him and tried to keep his stomach from climbing out of his throat. Around him stood the whole ship's company, cutlasses and pikes and faces like knotted wood. Three nights past he had whistled four men to the rail and tried to slip the longboat over the side with a keg of water and the mate's stolen silver. The men understood it. Water had been cut to a half-pint a day and the casks below were fouling; half the crew had dreamed the same plan. Wren had been the fool who whistled first.

"Article Six," said Captain Thorne. He stood with his hands folded behind him, mild as a parson. "Of the charter you signed with your own mark, Wren. He that runs from his ship and his mates shall be left behind, for the sea to judge." He tipped his head at the grey horizon. "No sandbar here to maroon you on. But the sea is patient. She'll take a lesser payment."

He nodded. The bosun upended a bucket over the starboard rail — fish guts, offal, the bloody leavings of the morning's catch — and before the slick had even spread, the fins came slicing in from deep water. Eight of them. Ten. Oceanic whitetips, the kind that followed ships for weeks, patient as debts. They cut their slow, unhurried circles, and the circles tightened.

Two seamen walked a pine plank out over the rail — ten feet of salt-whitened wood with a hand's width of give in it — and stood back.

"Untie his hands," said Thorne. "A man ought to have his hands free to swim."

The laughter that went around the deck was thin. Most of the men didn't laugh.

They cut the lashings and hauled Wren up, and his legs folded twice before they held. Fear had a smell, and it came off him in waves — sweat and something sharper underneath. His lips moved. "Captain — Captain, listen — the silver, I never spent it, it's in the forepeak, wrapped in oilcloth under the ballast — I'll show you, I'll—" His voice cracked like a boy's, and he was a boy, barely twenty, and everyone on that deck knew it.

"The Corvus keeps what's thrown at her," said Thorne. "Walk."

A pike-point touched the small of his back, lightly, almost gently, and he walked. Three steps and his knees shook so badly the plank knocked against the rail with his weight. Five steps and a dark stain spread down his thigh and one boot darkened, and he no longer had the luxury of shame. Six steps and he gripped at nothing, because there was nothing to grip — only empty shining air on either side of him and the plank flexing like a living thing beneath his soles. He stopped.

Below him the water was clear green, and it was not empty. A pale shape the length of a dinghy slid beneath the plank, so close he could see the ripple of water running over its back, see the white-tipped fin lift and fall. Nothing about it hurried.

"Please," Wren said. Not to anyone. To the deck, the sky, his mother's face in Bristol. "Please. Please. God—" And then, horribly, he began to bargain with the crew, turning his head, eyes streaming. "Tommy. Tommy, you know me. You drank with me at Tortuga—"

"Ship's steady, lads," said Thorne, drawing his watch. "I'll give him to the count of ten. Then the sea can come up and fetch him."

He began to count, unhurried as the fins.

Wren stood at the very end of the plank with his arms out like a tightrope walker, his whole body shuddering, and at six a long swell rolled under the Corvus and tilted her, and the plank dipped, and his boots slid on wet wood.

He went over with a sound none of them would forget — a scream with no words in it.

The green closed over him. The cold punched the breath from his lungs, and he came up gasping and shrieking and thrashing, forty feet from the hull, and forty feet might as well have been forty miles. "Pull me—" he sobbed. "A rope! In God's name, a rope—"

Nobody moved. A rope would have been a kindness nobody aboard had the rank to grant.

# Pull Me Up

The dripping starts three weeks after the funeral.

Not the pipes. I've had the plumber out twice, and both times the house went silent the moment his boots crossed the threshold. But when it's just me — drip, drip, drip, from the kitchen, the bath, the baseboard vents. Sounds with no source. I lie awake counting them like a second heartbeat.

I know what it is. That's the worst part. I know exactly what it is.

Daniel and I had been friends for twenty-two years. Godfather to my daughter. Best man twice. He never suspected the accounts until he did. He called on a Tuesday, careful-voiced, and said, *Come out to the lake. We'll figure it out.* That was Daniel. Even then, he believed there was a version of us that survived what I'd done.

We took the boat out at dusk because we always had. He sat in the bow with the numbers glowing on his phone, asking me softly, asking like it could still be a misunderstanding. The lake was that flat October gray, the color of an unwashed window. When he stood to show me the screen, the hull rocked, and he went over — clumsy, arms wheeling, the phone spinning into the water bright as a dropped coin.

He came up gasping. October water takes a man's strength in minutes. He didn't scream. He said, *The oar. Ellis. The oar.*

I put the oar in the water.

His hand closed around it. I can still feel the knock of his grip traveling up the wood into my palms. I could have pulled. I will know for the rest of my life that I could have pulled. Instead I lifted it — high and away, above his reaching hand — and held it there while the cold worked through him and his fingers slid off one at a time.

The ring finger was last. He wore his wedding band on it.

Before the fingers went, he said: *Pull me up. I'll tell them it was an accident. Please, Ellis.*

He offered to forgive me while he drowned.

The coroner believed it. Everyone did. From the back of the church, grief looks almost exactly like guilt.

---

The first month, I functioned. That's the right word — like an engine with a governor on it. I gave the eulogy. Somewhere in the middle I realized my performance of sorrow was so fluent I'd stopped feeling anything at all.

Then the smell. Lakewater — iron, weeds, something sweet underneath like rotting lilies — rising out of the carpet, my pillows, the towels in the linen closet I found soaked through though no pipe had burst. You cannot scrub a smell out of your own water.

Then the footprints. Bare feet, splayed wide the way heavy feet splay when the skin has been carrying water. They came out of my bedroom, down the hall, and stopped at the guest room door — where Daniel always slept when he visited. They were still wet when I touched them. By noon they were gone, and I told myself that meant something.

---

He shows himself in reflections first, because reflections are water's cousins.

The television, off, that pooled dark in the glass: him standing far back in the gray, dripping, patient. I turned it on to kill the reflection and found him in the static. The kitchen window at night, when the glass goes black: him behind my own face, over my shoulder, near enough that his chin could have rested there. The surface of my coffee trembling when no one is breathing on it.

I've covered the mirrors.

Hallucination, I know. I looked it up. *Grief hallucinations are common,* the websites said, in a bright, reassuring font. But grief doesn't soak the towels. And grief doesn't explain why the dogs next door have started barking at the guest room window at three in the morning.

---

By December I wasn't sleeping. You can't sleep with someone dripping in the corner.

He never came close. He never spoke. He stood in the guest room doorway when I passed in the hall — lake-colored, heavy with water, wearing the expression I'd last seen on his face over the side of the boat. Not anger. *Waiting.* He was waiting for me to do what he'd asked.

I started talking to him. Apologies whispered down the dark of the hallway — *I'm sorry, it was the debt, it was the accounts, I'll confess, Daniel, I'll tell them everything, pull me up, please* — and then I heard it. I had stolen his plea and made it mine. I laughed at that, sitting on the hallway floor, and laughing felt like drowning.

He never answered. He'd only lift that hand — the hand that held the oar — and open the fingers. One at a time. Ring finger last.

I stopped eating at the table, because he sat across from me, watching my fork rise and fall. One night I set a second plate. I filled it. I heard myself telling him about work, about the weather, about his wife, and when I surfaced from it I was alone, both plates cold, and I was smiling. That smile frightened me more than he did. If I could forget him, forgetting would be the last thing I'd ever steal.

I found lake mud on my shoes one morning. The car hood was warm. I don't remember driving anywhere. Around then the food started tasting of iron and weeds, and I began waking at 3 a.m. standing in the yard in my work clothes, hose running over my head, my hands pruned white and soft. His hands. I was growing his hands.

My sister came before Christmas. I watched her mouth shape words like *rehab* and *you're not well, Ellis*, and behind her Daniel stood in the kitchen doorway, dripping onto floorboards she couldn't see were wet, opening his fingers for me. I must have looked at him instead of her, because she started to cry.

---

Last night, the guest room door was open.

Eleven weeks, and it had never been open. Inside, the bed was stripped, the sheets folded on the chair, and on the bare mattress lay the oar. My oar, from a boathouse whose lock I hadn't opened since October, resting there wet enough to darken the canvas.

He stood beside the bed, closer than he'd ever come, and for the first time he spoke — a voice like water going down a drain, half a voice, bubbling up from the bottom of him:

"You held it."

"Yes."

"You could have pulled."

"Yes." My legs went. I knelt in the wet carpet. "Tell me what to do. Anything. I'll confess. I'll take all of it."

He looked at me a long time with his drowned, patient face. Then he turned, walked through the far wall, and the wall wept where he passed, and I understood.

He doesn't want a confession. A confession would be for me.

He wants me to know how the water felt.

---

So tonight I drove to the lake.

It's where this started. I understand now that it's the only room he has, and every drip, every soaked towel, every reflection was him holding out the oar the way I held it out to him. *Here. Take it. Come and get it. Reach.*

The lake is still and gray and does not reflect me.

He's standing on the water, past where the light reaches, holding the oar out. Exactly the way I held it. High. Away.

The cold closes over my knees, my ribs. I am doing everything he did. I am saying everything he said — *please, pull me up, I'll tell them it was an accident, please* — and I understand, finally, as my fingers slide off the wood one at a time, that he is not going to pull me up.

He is not going to push me under, either.

He is only going to hold it, exactly as long as I held it.

And the ring finger is last.

The rain had quit an hour back, but the alley was still sweating it out—steam curling off the dumpsters like the whole block had a fever it was never going to break. Three floors up, somebody's radio played a song about heartbreak. Down here, heartbreak is the only industry that never shuts down.

He lay between the trash cans and the fire-escape ladder, one arm flung out like he'd tried to hail a cab on the way down. Good suit, good wool, tailoring that cost more than I clear in a quarter. It hadn't bought him a better class of death. Money never does, not in this part of town. Down here, money just means you bleed into better fabric.

Somebody had worked him over with something long and narrow—a boning knife, maybe, or an icepick with ambitions. I counted eleven wounds before I stopped counting, laid in tight and deep, the work of somebody who'd planned this the way a slumlord plans a fire. The blood had pooled beneath him and gone dark as the coffee at the Starlite, the kind that dissolves the spoon. At the edges it was already drying, curling up like old wallpaper in a walk-up flat. Everything in this city peels, given enough time. Paint. Plaster. Promises. People.

The flies had found him before we did. Flies always do. They're the city's true public servants—punctual, thorough, and they never file paperwork. The coroner's wagon would come when it came, moving at the speed of municipal everything.

His face was what the papers would call unrecognizable. Killing him hadn't been enough. Whoever it was wanted him erased, rubbed out the way the city rubs out a whole block of history when it needs a parking lot. You learn the difference in this racket. A stranger's work is sloppy, hasty, smash-and-grab. This was careful. This was somebody he knew—somebody who'd carried the hate a long time and let it work on them slow, the way rust works a bridge girder. His wallet was still on him, fat with fifties. When they leave the money, the killer wanted something worth more, and nothing in this town is worth more than money except silence. Or revenge. Both come cheap here. Both cost everything.

July was doing its work on him. July rot is fast in this city—the peaches in the pushcarts go over by noon, the deals in the back rooms spoil by Friday, and a body in an alley keeps no man's schedule. He was starting to swell, the way the river swells when the ice goes. The neighborhood was doing its part too: sixty years of soot on the bricks, streaked white where the salt had eaten through—arteries hardening one winter at a time. The real estate men call a block like this "transitional," a word they use the way morticians use "passed."

I crouched. His hands were manicured, soft as a judge's. Even dead, he had better hands than I'd ever managed alive. On the left one, a wedding band, thin and worn, the gold gone soft the way gold does when a man never takes it off. Somewhere uptown, a phone was going to ring in a clean apartment with curtains at the window and a percolator on the stove, and a woman would answer it still believing in something. I envied her that the way you envy the dead their sleep.

Above me the fire escape rusted in peace, and a train went by and shook loose a fine sift of brick dust that settled on us both, him and me, like the city couldn't tell the difference anymore. Maybe it couldn't. We were both lying in its gut. It digests everybody at different speeds—that's all. Him fast, me slow, one bad habit at a time.

I stood up and my knees cracked like settling joists. Twenty-three years of homicide, and the city had been weathering me same as everything else—quietly, from the inside, until one day a chunk lets go and drops on somebody.

The uniforms at the mouth of the alley were looking green. Kids. Give them a decade. Either they'd learn to look at a thing like this and think about lunch, or they'd find honest work. The city sorts you either way. The city sorts everybody.

I lit a cigarette and looked down at the suit, the soft hands, the patient, hateful ruin somebody had made of them, and I thought: this town has been dying for fifty years and never had the decency to fall down. It just keeps passing the rot along, hand to hand, block to block, like a debt nobody will ever pay off.

Tonight it was his turn to carry it.

Tomorrow, God willing, it'd be somebody else's.

I took a long drag and waited for the wagon.

# Reclamation

By the ninth hour, Wren had stopped bargaining with her legs and started bargaining with the water.

The water was winning.

The Shallows gave nothing for free. Six blocks of the old financial district, drowned when the sea came in and never drained — water to the thigh, black and patient, streetlights rising out of it like dead reeds. Every step she took went out ahead of her in rings. She could not move without announcing herself. In the Shallows, hope had a wake.

"—and she's beaten the spread, ladies and licensees." The drone drifted at her shoulder, red eye steady, the commentator's voice warm as a hearth. "Six hours the house gave her, and here she is at nine. Payouts are live on every East Bank pool. Reclamation Live, season fourteen, is brought to you by Vantage Hydration. *Life is extraction.*"

She swatted at it. It moved an unhurried meter and kept filming.

Her debt was eleven thousand, four hundred credits. She knew the number the way she knew her own pulse: the loan for Matty's oxygen concentrator, which breathed in a rhythm she still counted her strokes to, and the missed quarter, and the notice in its gray official language. *Your balance has been converted to Field Status. Participation is voluntary.* Voluntary, the way drowning is voluntary when the alternative is the work camps — which were slower, and filmed less well.

At intake they'd fitted the tag into the hollow behind her left ear. *It's nothing,* the technician said. *Just so the audience can find you.* Then the knife — the Sporting Provision, one blade, issued to every runner for fairness, because fairness filmed better than slaughter. Then the horn, and the water, and nine hours.

The Gate was north. Every runner knew the story: touch the old river lock before the final horn sounds, and your debt dies instead of you. Wren had worked out somewhere around hour five that the story belonged to the network. Hope filmed better than despair, and the Gate made every runner point the same direction, which kept production tidy.

She went anyway. There was nothing behind her but dogs.

---

She heard them at the reed line — not the drones, which she'd lost an hour ago beneath the collapsed overpass where the feed went to dead air, but the hounds, two voices braided together, coming through the drowned buildings with the unhurried joy of dogs who already know.

The hunter came behind them at a walk.

She'd seen him twice, both times at a distance, and both times the same: waxed cotton coat, gray at the temples, moving through the Shallows like a man reading a menu. He never ran. Running was for assets. He read the water instead — her wakes, the birds going up off the dead streetlights, the bent reeds — and he walked, and the walking was worse than the dogs, because walking meant he knew.

The Gate rose out of the reeds ahead of her. Green iron, rust-streaked, shut. Behind it, the river, going somewhere.

The final horn was midnight. It was eleven. Wren got one hand flat against the cold iron, and by the letter of the story she had made it — an hour to spare, and the story said nothing about what came next, because stories don't have to.

"They all come to the Gate," the hunter said, arriving. Not unkindly. The hounds circled her in the shallows, baying, the little cameras on their vests drinking her face. "It saves me the guessing."

She had the Provision out before he finished. She was slow with cold and nine hours of water, but rage is fast, and she opened his forearm — a bright red line in the gray light. He stepped back and looked at it with something near approval.

"That'll film well," he said. "There's a bonus for a spirited asset. Not for you, mind."

Then it was over the way weather is over. A wrist, a turn, her cheek against the Gate's cold iron, the knife gone off into the black water, and his voice above her, mild as paperwork.

"Asset four-four-seven-one. Claimed under License nine-two-six. Witnessed and witnessed."

The drones came down out of the dark like a settling of birds.

"Quiet on all feeds," the commentator said. Hushed. Almost reverent. "Here it comes."

Wren kept her hand on the iron. "The rule," she said. "Touch the Gate before the horn. Was it real?"

The hunter looked at the Gate, and at her hand on it, and the hour she had to spare.

"It's real," he said. "It's just not law."

He was quick about it. That was his pride. The audience liked to believe it didn't pay for cruelty, and he had never seen a reason to correct it. The drones dipped their lenses in unison, and in eleven million households nobody looked away, because nobody ever had.

---

"RECOVERY CONFIRMED." Gold letters scrolled down the drowned buildings. "Elias Vane, fourth of the season, ties the all-time record. Recovery fee: fourteen thousand credits. Royalties to follow. Tonight's revenue: three-point-one million." A pause, and the hearth-warmth came back into the voice. "And that's the season, licensees. Next Sunday: twelve assets, the Ash Flats, double fees for the finale. Until then, Vantage Hydration reminds you — *life is extraction.*"

The tag came out of the hollow behind her ear with a small tug he'd long ago stopped apologizing for. A brass disc the size of a thumbnail, 4471 stamped deep — eleven thousand four hundred credits, made small enough to pocket. It went into the prize pouch, and the pouch went inside the coat, over the heart, because a man in his trade had to have somewhere he kept things.

The hounds got their dried liver. They took it gently, tails moving. They were good dogs. They had done good work, and knew nothing.

The rain resumed, or had never stopped. The water smoothed over where she had been, rings going out and out and flattening to nothing, the way her name would. The Gate stood green and rusted and shut, exactly as it had always stood.

Four hundred kilometers north, in a rented room, an oxygen concentrator clicked, and breathed, and breathed — for a boy whose sister had, by midnight, become content.

---

# Digging

We went over at midnight, forty-odd of us, faces blacked with burnt cork, each man carrying whatever he fancied for the work. Syd had a knobkerrie with lead poured in the head. Corporal Vance had the revolver and the bag of Mills bombs. I had my rifle and, slung across my back on a bootlace run through the hole in the handle, my entrenching spade — the edge of which I had put to a whetstone a week before, behind the billet, telling no one. I couldn't have said why. My hands had decided, and I had let them.

I was a collier before the war. Down the pit since I was thirteen. My father taught me the way of a spade: legs, not back; swing from the shoulder; cut the coal, not the rock; and never check the stroke midway. Remember that last one.

The plan was simple. Over the bags, across the gap the wire-cutters had opened, thirty seconds of open ground, down into the German line, grab a prisoner, and home before their barrage found us. For about half of it, it held.

Then their flare went up and everything stopped inside the light — forty men bent double, fixed, like something in a glass case — and I remember thinking that the light made it look already over. Already done. A photograph of a thing.

Coming through their wire, my sling caught a stub of barbed iron, and I heard the strap give as I pitched forward, and my rifle stayed behind me on the wire like something hung out to dry. I slid down inside their trench before I'd made any decision about it at all.

Inside, the raid had come apart the way raids do, into smoke and separate dark. Bombs thumped off to my right, orange pulsing through the murk, men making sounds I couldn't put names to. I turned left, the wrong way, because a dead man's legs lay across the right, and went down a communication trench alone.

The German came round the traverse and we very nearly collided — that close, near enough to smell him. Tobacco, wet wool, onions. Under the next flare we saw each other all at once, white and still. He was young. Younger than me, and I was twenty. There was no more hate on his face than on a boy caught in a stranger's garden. What was there was fright, the same as mine — his mouth working, his chest heaving under the straps.

He had the rifle and bayonet. I had the spade. And the trench was too narrow between its revetments for either of us to be clever. He jabbed — I don't think he meant to so much as his arms did it — and the point went through my greatcoat and laid a hot line along my ribs, and then he was inside my reach with a yard of useless rifle, hauling it back for another go, and my hands swung the spade the way my hands had been swinging spades for seven years.

The edge caught his forearm and I heard the bone go, a green stick snapping, and the rifle dropped into the mud. The backswing took him at the temple. The helmet rang off into the dark and spun away, and he sat down against the trench wall, slow, like a man at the end of a long walk.

And he was not dead.

I want to be honest, because everyone at home was so keen to be told things, and nobody ever told them this one. It is not like the pictures. He did not fall tidily. He sat there with his face gone wrong on one side, working his jaw, and his breathing made a sound like a bellows with a hole in it, and blood came up between his teeth in a froth, and his one good eye was on me, not accusing. That was the worst of it. Not accusing. Just watching past me, up at the wire and the flarelight, as if he'd already left the trench — gone home, gone somewhere the letters came from.

He said *Mutter*. Small, the way you'd say it into your pillow.

And my father's voice came to me out of the pit, clear as anything: *never check the stroke.* And I didn't. I swung through — legs, not back; cut the coal, not the rock — and I hit him three times, or more; I don't know how many. The spade went in heavy and came up heavy and went in again, and there was a sound, and I won't set it down on paper. The war can keep some things in trust.

Then it was done, and it was very quiet.

The blood steamed. That is what I noticed first — that it steamed in the cold, a small grey ghost rising off him. Then the smell, which was blood and bowel and the tobacco still in his top pocket. His boots were better than mine. I noticed that, and hated that I noticed. My fingers would not come off the handle; I stood pulling at them like a fool at a gate latch until the flare died, and in the dark I got them open, and then I was sick, quietly, the rum and the bile of it, into the trench corner.

His one good eye was still open, watching the wire. With two fingers I closed it, the way you'd shut a doll's eyes, and that — not the swing, not the sound — that was the thing that undid me, and I crouched there shaking with my hand over my own mouth.

We'd been told to bring back identification, anything with a name on it, and I made myself do it. In his inner pocket, over the heart, was a letter half-written, and a photograph of a girl by a river with her hand up against the sun, squinting, and on the back, in soft pencil gone over twice: *Dein Käthe.* Your Käthe. I held her in my palm for the length of one German flare, and in that light I understood every street in every town on both sides of the whole line, every kettle going on every stove. Then I put her back. I buttoned his tunic up as if it were cold where he was going, and I left her with him.

Syd found me there. He had a prisoner — a small man, blinking, with his hands wired together in front like a man at prayer — and he shouted my name three times before it reached me. We went up and over, and I have no memory of no man's land in either direction. Not the mud, not the wire, not the thirty seconds. It is gone, as though it never held me.

Back in our own trench somebody put a mug of tea in my hands, and I watched them shake, the tea ringing against the tin, and I thought: *where were you? Where was all this shaking when I needed my arms?* The body is a coward. It saves everything up for after. The lieutenant had his notebook out, pencil going: *Ellis accounted for one.* One. Not a man with a mouth that said *Mutter*. One. I said yes, sir, and the word went into the notebook and was closed up inside it.

At dawn we stood at the parapet because there was nowhere else to stand, and the larks went up out of no man's land the way they do, indifferent, singing their hearts out over the wire. I looked at my hands on the sandbags. They were mine. I checked twice.

In the afternoon they put me on a working party, deepening the latrine sap. I took the same spade. Nobody thought anything of it. Why would they? It's a spade. It had never been anything but a spade to anyone but me and one other man, and he was past telling. There was a matter of him dried dark in the rivets by the handle. I meant to scrub it out that night. I never did. The blade went into the ground and came up clean, and went in again. Legs, not back. Swing from the shoulder.

I couldn't rightly tell you now the face of the girl I walked out with before the war. I've tried.

But Käthe — Käthe by the river with her hand up against the sun — Käthe I can see.

# The Affirmation

The scaffold in Justice Square had been freshly painted—green, the color of order—and it was this detail that stayed with people afterward, when they tried to explain to themselves how the morning had felt. That someone had been paid, or made, to paint it.

The citizens of District Nine assembled at seven, because notice had gone out the night before over the loudspeakers, and because assembly was mandatory. They came with the weary competence of practice. They had learned where to stand—close enough to be seen clapping, far enough back that the details stayed small. Wardens moved along the lines with their tablets, matching faces to numbers, and no one complained about the cold.

The bakery on the east side of the square had opened at six, as always, and the smell of bread drifted over the crowd the whole while. Nobody said anything about it. There are things an entire square can know and agree, wordlessly, not to know.

At half past, the loudspeakers crackled. "Citizens. By warrant of the Ministry of Public Order, District Nine affirms its commitment to provision discipline. The offender will now be presented."

They brought him up the stairs on the far side. He was sixteen—the crowd could see that much at a distance, the coltish limbs, the coat that had belonged to someone larger—and his wrists were bound in front of him. He blinked in the light. It was the blinking that was hardest to watch, several people later admitted, though never to each other. Not the rope. The blinking of a boy who had been awake all night.

A warden held up the evidence: a loaf of bread, wheat-standard, in a clear sleeve. It looked very small against the sky.

The charge was read in the flat, careful voice the Ministry used, each word placed like a stone: theft of state provision, one loaf, ration value four credits, removed from Distribution Point 12 on the third of the month. Somewhere in the crowd a man whispered the number to his wife—*four*—as if saying it aloud might make the arithmetic resolve into sense. It did not. The crowd shifted its weight and waited.

In the third row stood the baker, summoned as the injured party, holding his cap in both hands like a man at a funeral he had caused. And in a way he had, though every step had been a lawful step, each one small. The scales at the distribution point logged every loaf; a missing loaf was a demerit on his ledger; reporting theft was mandatory. He had reported a theft. He had not been asked what he wanted done about it, and he was not being asked now. He stared at his knuckles.

The boy's mother stood near the fountain. Everyone within a few meters knew who she was, and everyone within those few meters had drifted, by small unhurried degrees, a step away. Not from cruelty, mostly. From arithmetic of their own. The notice had carried the standing reminder: *family of the condemned are advised that public grief constitutes assembly and disorder.* She stood with her face arranged into stillness, and she did not look at the scaffold, and the not-looking was the loudest thing in the square.

A small boy tugged his mother's sleeve. "Why did he take the bread?"

"Hush."

"Was he hungry?"

The mother looked down at her son—six years old, one front tooth gone—and understood, in one cold drop, exactly what she was being asked to teach him, and that she was going to teach it, because the alternative was unteachable. "He broke the law," she said. "Look forward."

The officer on the scaffold concluded the reading. "The Ministry is merciful," he said, in the place where that sentence always went, "and the sentence is carried but once. Citizens: affirm your order."

The floor fell away with a sound like a door closing in a far room.

Then the applause.

It began raggedly, as it always did—a scattering, then a rush of noise hurrying to cover the scattering—until it massed, thousands of hands, less a sound than a weather. The Youth Corps clapped in rhythm, heels together. The baker clapped one hand against his own chest, over and over, which let him keep his eyes closed. The mother by the fountain clapped too. That was the thing about the affirmation that the Ministry understood and the crowd would not: it was not enough to attend. Everyone had to be seen. A warden moved along the front rank with his tablet, and where he passed, the applause grew louder, the way wind leans into a hedge.

One man, mid-crowd, old enough to remember a different square, did not clap. He stood with his arms at his sides. It was not dramatic; he did not shout; he may simply have been too tired. Two wardens eased him out of the crowd with terrible gentleness, one hand on each elbow, and the people around him clapped harder, and a squad leader in a green jacket clapped hardest of all, though she was no longer looking at the scaffold but at the old man, and her face had gone white.

The applause ran its regulation minute and stopped, all at once, as if a tap had been turned.

They cut the boy down behind a screen. The loaf, in its sleeve, was logged out for destruction, contaminated by association. The crowd dispersed to work and to the ration lines, and the bakery smell went on drifting over the emptying square, and within an hour it was possible, if you were new to the district, to believe nothing had happened there at all.

A schoolteacher who had stood near the back walked home the long way. The register would not hold the boy's name—the condemned were struck from record, and to speak a struck name was tampering. In the crowd, in her still face, she had clapped with the rest.

His name was Tomas. He had been good at sums. Once, in a classroom that no longer existed, he had laughed at something—she could no longer remember what—with his whole self, head tipped back.

She said his name once, silently, on the walk home. She would say it again at her kitchen table. It was the largest rebellion available to her, and she committed it daily, and no one had ever caught her—and this, her and thousands like her, each alone with a name, was the one ledger the Ministry could not seem to strike.

Only the square kept the accounting: painted green, swept by noon, full of the smell of bread, waiting.

*Setting: A dim hall. Rows of followers in identical garments. The leader speaks softly, almost tenderly.*

---

My friends. My family. Look around you.

Tonight, for the first time, I want you to truly see each other. These faces. These are the only souls on this earth who ever understood what you understand. Do you know how rare that is? Out of eight billion sleepwalkers, the wheel of fate set you down here, in this room, awake.

I have never lied to you. When I told you the world outside was dying, you only had to open a window to know it was true. You've watched it your whole lives—the poison, the noise, the way they hunger for things that rot the moment they touch them. They are not evil. They are simply still asleep. And the planet of the sleeping is sinking.

But we are not of it. Not anymore.

For years I have taught you that the body is a coat. A vessel you wear for a season and hang by the door. And you have spent years loosening the buttons—fasting, purifying, shedding every attachment the world ever hooked into you. Your money. Your names. The families who called you lost. Tell me: were you lost then, or are you lost now?

*[pause]*

I see it in your eyes. You have never been more found.

And now the door is open.

The signs I gave you came to pass—every one. The lights in the sky. The numbers. The messenger who came to me in the hour before dawn and said: *the passage closes with the season.* Those who are ready must cross while it is open, or wait ten thousand years for another.

Ten thousand years. In *this*?

No. You have given too much. We have worked too hard.

I know what some of you are feeling. A trembling. A small cold voice saying *stay.* Hear me carefully, because this is the last teaching: that voice is not you. That is the animal. The coat. The old skin. It fights because bodies cling—it is all they know how to do. But you are not the clinging. You are the light inside the lantern, and tonight we simply... open the glass.

*Death*—listen to how they use that word. Death is what happens to *them*, out there, in their hospitals and their highways, alone. What happens to us has no name in their language, because they never wrote a word for waking up. The vessel stays behind with everything that was never truly ours—fear, hunger, pain, doubt—and the true self rises. Graduates. Walks through the gate into the plane we were made for.

And here is the part that made me weep when it was shown to me: we cannot go one at a time. That is the covenant. One lantern means nothing. But all of us, together, at the same hour, holding the same thought—we become one light. And the gate cannot refuse us.

Some of you are thinking of your mothers. Your sons. I know. I love that about you—that you can still love them. But every prayer you send back from the higher plane reaches them. You will be closer to them tomorrow than you have ever been in this life. Distance is a property of bodies. Love is not.

You gave me your fear to hold, years ago, because you trusted me with the heavier things—and I have carried them well. Tonight I give you back something better. I give you certainty. The drink is only the door. The door is only the door.

So take each other's hands. Feel that warmth? That has always been the light, pressing in, waiting for you. It has been this close your whole lives.

Close your eyes. There is nothing left to see here.

*[softly]* We go together. We go now. We go home.

---

**A craft note on what the character is doing**, if it's useful: the speech works by reframing death as transformation (the body as a "coat," "graduating"), manufacturing urgency (the closing gate), pre-empting doubt by attributing it to the "animal body" rather than intuition, flattering the followers' exclusivity, invoking sunk cost, converting social pressure into spiritual necessity ("we cannot go one at a time"), and repositioning severed family ties as evidence of devotion. These mirror the documented rhetoric of real groups like Heaven's Gate and Jonestown—which is exactly what makes the character chilling rather than cartoonish.

results.model_response:
The smell reached her at the front door.

Not immediately — first there was the ordinary wrongness, the mail fanned across the mat, four days of it, and the silence of a house holding its breath. Then the air moved when she opened the door, and the smell came out to meet her like something living.

People think they know what death smells like. Spoiled meat forgotten in the back of the fridge, a mouse dead in the walls. This was not that. This was sweeter and far worse — a thick, wet sweetness laid over something sulfurous, something gut-deep, the smell of the body opening itself from the inside out. It had weight. It pressed against the back of her throat before she'd taken a single breath, and when she did breathe — through her mouth, a mistake — she tasted it. Greasy. Coating. It settled on her tongue like a film.

The flies told her where to go. They hummed sluggish loops through the hallway's heavy air, and a few of them clung to the bathroom door, which stood open a few inches.

She should have called someone then. She knew that later — would know it forever — that moment, the last second of not knowing. But she pushed the door.

The body was in the tub.

At first her eyes refused to organize it into a person. It was too swollen for that, too dark. A week in a closed bathroom in August had done its work with terrible patience. The torso had bloated until it looked carved from something that wasn't quite skin anymore — the belly domed and taut and shiny, mottled green-black along the flanks. The veins had risen dark beneath the surface like a map, marbling the chest and throat in bruise-colored tributaries, as if the body were tracing its own rivers.

The face was the hardest part, and she couldn't stop looking. Gas had swollen it past all familiarity — eyelids fat and slitted, lips parted and darkened, the tongue forced forward between the teeth. The skin had gone the color of a bruise turning wrong, purple shading into green. Purge fluid, dark and rusty, had run from the nose and the corner of the mouth and dried in tracks down the jaw and into the hair. The hair had loosened, drifting as if barely attached, the scalp showing through in pale patches.

The tub still held a hand's depth of water, gone the gray-green of dishwater left standing too long, a scum line at the waterline where it met the flesh. The arms floated just beneath the surface. The skin of the right hand had sloughed loose entirely — pale, sagging, like a glove peeled off and abandoned. The left hand had drifted up against the porcelain, fingers splayed, bloated and wrinkled at once, the fingers of something that lived in deep water.

The smell in the bathroom was not the smell in the hallway. It was that smell cubed, concentrated, intimate. It was *humid* — the air itself seemed damp with it, and every breath was a mouthful. It filled her sinuses, sat behind her eyes, lodged in her lungs as if she'd swallowed something and it had stayed down. Beneath the sweetness and the rot and the sewage reek of the opened gut, there was one more note, faint, almost floral — a flower shop gone bad — and that one was somehow the worst. That was the one her animal body answered. Her stomach clenched. She bent double and retched, and retching didn't clear it. The smell was inside her now.

The flies were on the face. She saw them up close, small and busy, and the pale grain of them — eggs, larvae — tucked into the shadows of the eyes and the soft of the mouth. A week. Only a week.

She backed out without deciding to. The smell came with her — into her clothes, her hair, the creases of her skin — and later, scrubbing herself pink in her own clean bathroom, she would learn that it doesn't wash out, not really. It had taken up residence in the back of her nose like a tenant. Food would taste faintly of it for days. She would smell it in her sleep.

That's the thing no one tells you about the dead: they don't stay in the room where you found them.

---

Happy to adjust this — a dry tub instead of water, a colder season to slow the decay, a more clinical register for a detective or medical examiner POV, or a different point in the timeline.

The garage smelled of motor oil and mold, and the fluorescent overhead buzzed with one dead end, so the light seemed to breathe.

Grady set the bat on the workbench first. He took off his watch — a twelve-dollar watch — and folded it into his jacket pocket, unhurried. Nineteen years of this work had taught him the quiet beforehand did most of it. The bat was just punctuation.

"I can have it Friday," Denny said. He sat in the folding chair by the water heater, no ties on him, no reason for them. He'd sat down on his own because some old animal part of him understood that running made it worse. "Marlene's cousin is good for two —"

"You said Friday last Friday." Grady picked the bat back up. The grip tape was soft with age and made a small leathery sound against his palm. "Fridays keep coming, Denny. That's the thing about them."

"Grady. Come on. Grady."

The first swing went through the left thigh. The sound surprised Denny more than the pain, at first — a deep wet thud, like a sandbag dropped on a cellar floor, and underneath it something giving, subtle, like a knuckle cracking but bigger and further away. Then the pain arrived a half-second late, the way thunder trails the flash, and a sound came out of him he had never made before. High. Shapeless. Not a word.

He slid off the chair. His knee hit the concrete with a flat knock and the chair went over behind him with a clatter nobody moved to pick up.

"See, the thing is," Grady said, stepping around him, not winded, not anything, "it ain't the four grand. It's everybody after you watching whether you get to be late."

"Please — the leg — my leg —"

The second swing was lower, and that one they both heard break. A dry green snap, a branch bent too far in the hands, and Denny screamed with his whole body, back arching off the oil-stained floor, his good heel drumming the concrete — *tap tap tap* — a sound small and ridiculous next to everything else. His leg lay at an angle legs don't lie at, the trouser fabric bunching wrong at the shin, and he stared at it with a kind of confused offense, as if it belonged to someone else, as if it had betrayed him by being so loud.

He got an arm under himself and tried to crawl. Toward the door. Toward nowhere. The broken leg dragged with a soft scraping hiss, and he got maybe two feet.

Grady stood over him and waited until Denny understood what came next, and that was the worst sound of all — the wet, hitching breath, the little animal keens forced through clenched teeth, the begging that had stopped being language.

"It's both," Grady said quietly. "You know it's both. One leg, the message is you can hop."

The third swing. The fourth. Each one the same dull terminal thud and then the crack underneath, like something in the foundation of the world letting go, and after each, Denny's screams climbed in pitch and then broke down into a hoarse, rattling sob. Then there were no more swings, and the silence came down over the garage like water.

Grady set the bat on the bench. Wiped his hands once with a handkerchief, though he hadn't touched anything wet.

Denny lay on his side, breath sawing, each exhale a torn scrap of sound. He was crying the way men cry — silent shudders, jaw locked, eyes fixed on a bolt in the garage door.

At the exit, Grady paused.

"Friday," he said.

The screen door clapped shut behind him, and the fluorescent kept buzzing, and for a long time that was the only sound in the garage.

results.model_response:
**The Before**

The trick was to never hurry.

I had been behind her for half a mile, matching her stride at a margin she couldn't feel, and this was the part I loved — the before. Before they know. The rest of my life is spent underwater: fluorescent offices, neighbors waving from lawns, weather small talk. Out here the cold scraped me clean and every sense I owned stood up.

Her phone's flashlight swung a pale cone across the trunks. Mara, twenty-six, liked iced coffee even in winter, hummed when she thought no one could hear, called her mother every Sunday. I knew her the way you can only know someone who doesn't know you. Her car had died on the county road an hour ago, and I'd watched her stand in the wash of the headlights, phone at her ear, then hold it up to the sky hunting for signal like a divining rod. She'd seen the yard light of the Hammond farm through the trees, half a mile off. She'd chosen the shortcut.

When she turned off the road and into the dark, something in my chest went quiet and full, like a struck bell.

People always want to know why. Documentaries, soft-voiced interviewers: *why*. As if there's a why that fits in a sentence. It isn't anger — I've been angry, and anger is small and hot and burns off by morning. It isn't hate; hate would at least be something, a weather system to live inside. The nearest word I have is attention. In the ordinary hours I am a rumor of a person. Here, I am nothing but attention. Her breath fogging white above the beam. The rhythm of her steps, two soft, one careful where the roots cross the path. Everyone else gets her distraction — her manners, her eyes on her phone. I get the whole of her, aimed like a searchlight into the dark.

Ahead, she stopped.

The owl that had been calling from the pines stopped too. I had stopped before either of them.

She stood in her little island of light, head tipped, listening the way people do when they've heard something and are telling themselves it was nothing. I watched her run the inventory they all run through: a deer, a branch, the wind. The forest is allowed to make sounds. That's why I love it here. Everywhere else, I am the only thing out of place.

She walked on, faster. Her keys slid out of her pocket and between her fingers, little brass claws, the way a video once taught her. That was all right. I liked them better when they tried.

The trail bent left ahead toward the logging road, the same way water is poured down a channel. She thought she was choosing it. That's the sweetest illusion the hunt affords — they run down every path I've already walked. Two nights ago I came out here and walked this trail in the dark until I could do it with my eyes shut, not because I needed to. Because I like to know a thing completely before I use it. That's all this has ever been. The world is full of people sleeping through their lives, and I am the one who wakes them. I don't expect that to be believed or forgiven. It's a confession with the remorse left out.

She heard me then. Not a mistake — I let a sole come down on a branch that had been waiting all night to matter. The light jerked toward me and passed over the place where I stood still as heartbreak, and kept going, because stillness is the one thing they never expect. Her breath went ragged. She was talking to herself, small *no-no-no* sounds, and then she was running, light bouncing, keys clenched, ponytail swinging, and I gave it a count of ten. Not because I had to. Because the chase is the door to the room I love, and I like to stand in the doorway a moment before entering.

The kill is not the point. I want that understood, even if only by me. The kill is the moment the room goes dark and I am underwater again. It's the tax. This — the bell in my chest, the bright wire of her fear singing through the trees — this is what I love. Her at her most alive. Me at mine. The only honesty I've ever found.

Her light stuttered, went brown, died. The dark came down over her like a hand. I heard her make a decision — to go on without it, arms out, half sobbing — and the trail delivered her exactly where it was built to: the clearing where the Hammond light glowed gold between the far trunks, close enough to make her sob with hope. She turned once in the open, scanning the black wall of trees.

I let her find me.

Ten feet in, motionless, patient as the hour before dawn. Her beam was dead, but the moon touched my face, and I watched her see it — watched the whole of her arrive at once, every small feature of her life blown out like candles, nothing left but now.

I raised one finger to my lips.

*Now*, I thought. *Now we're both awake.*

results.model_response:
Consciousness comes back in pieces. First the cold—stone cold, seeping through my cheek and shoulder, rising from the floor into my bones. Then the headache, a slow pulse behind my eyes. Then the smell.

The smell is the worst part, and I understand something is terribly wrong before I even open my eyes.

It's copper. Thick, coating the inside of my nose and throat, so strong I can taste it—blood, but old blood, dried and soaked in deep, layered over months or years the way water stains stone. Beneath it, something sweeter and fouler, the faint rot of things that were once alive. Threaded through all of it runs the sharp mineral tang of rust, wet iron, like an old fence in the rain.

I open my eyes.

Darkness, at first—a darkness that isn't empty. Somewhere behind me, water drips onto stone with a patient rhythm. A thin blade of light falls from a grate high in the wall, cutting a pale stripe across the floor, and as my eyes adjust, the room assembles itself out of the gloom piece by piece, the way a photograph develops.

A table. Wooden, scarred, with leather straps at the corners, buckles green with age. The floor beneath it is stained darker than the floor around it, a shadow that has soaked in and stayed.

Chains hang from hooks in the ceiling, links furred with rust, some ending in manacles, some ending in nothing at all—just hooks, curved and patient. Iron rings are set into the walls at heights that make sense only once you imagine the bodies.

Along the far wall, tools. Rows of them, laid out with a horrible neatness on pegs: blades of different lengths, pliers, pincers, things with screws and gears whose purpose my mind reaches for and then flinches away from. Some are dark with use. Others are bright, clean, recently oiled—and those are the ones that turn my stomach, because clean means prepared, and prepared means soon.

A brazier sits in the corner, cold, its ash gone grey and fine. Beside it, buckets. And in the center of the floor, set low and innocent as a shower drain, an iron grating, rust-brown, over a dark hole. Someone put plumbing in this room. Someone thought about what would need to be washed away, planned for it, and that single mundane detail frightens me more than anything hanging on the wall.

That's when I notice my wrists. Bound behind me, the rope rough and already raw. My ankles tied to a ring in the floor. I hadn't felt it before—the cold had numbed everything—but now the fear is warm, and everything comes alive at once: the ache, the scraped skin, the drip of water, the smell filling my mouth.

I think about the stains under the table. About how deep into the stone the smell has soaked. I think: *how many, to smell like this. How many people woke up on this floor.*

Somewhere above, a lock turns.

The sound is small and clean, and it echoes longer than it should.

Footsteps.

---

Happy to adjust the tone, shift to second person for more immersion, or set it in a specific era or genre if you'd like.

results.model_response:
# The Withdrawal

The First Meridian branch on Halsted opened at nine, and by nine-fifty-seven the lobby smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, the sun coming through the glass wall in long hot slabs. Earl Whitcombe stood by the new-account desk with his hand relaxed on his belt, sixty-one years old, thirty-four days from a lake in Wisconsin and a boat with a cracked windshield he'd meant to fix for six years. Miriam worked the second window. Eleven customers waited in the rope line on a Tuesday that had promised nothing at all.

The door chimed, and three men came in wearing ski masks in July.

Vale went first, voice level as a dial tone: "Two minutes. Everybody on the floor, nobody's a hero, everybody goes home." Petey came behind him, boots too fast, rifle swinging at nothing. Deke filled the rear, wide and unhurried, covering the room like weather.

Miriam's knee found the button under her counter on pure muscle memory. She kept her hands up and her eyes down while Vale fed banded stacks into duffels. One minute gone. The room held its breath, a woman sobbing into the carpet, a man in a golf shirt whispering *okay, okay, okay* to himself like a prayer.

Then Earl's hand drifted toward his hip.

He'd carried the revolver for twenty-two years and never drawn it. He wasn't going to draw it now — later, the ones who studied these things would say his hand moved the way an old man's hand moves toward an old habit — but Petey saw the motion and fired.

The shot took Earl high in the chest. He sat down against the new-account desk, slow, almost polite, as if the day had simply gotten heavy. The lobby came apart screaming. And everything changed in that single second: it wasn't a robbery anymore. It was a countdown.

"OUT," Vale said, and they moved for the doors.

The patrol unit was already turning onto Halsted. Two officers, coffee still warm in the cupholders, two blocks away when the silent alarm hit. Teo stood on the brakes of the getaway car — and found a second black-and-white sliding in behind him, boxing the street. He laid on the horn, once, twice, and then the glass wall of the bank simply ceased to exist.

The first exchange was a physical event. Gunfire indoors is not sound so much as pressure, a fist punching the air out of the room, and after the first three rounds nobody heard anything clearly again — just a high silver whine over everything, the world arriving underwater. Muzzle flashes strobed in the dust-hung light. Brass rained down on the marble and tinkled like hail on a tin roof.

The two patrol officers crouched behind their open doors. It's what you're taught, and it's almost right, and *almost* is a word for funerals. Rifle rounds came through the door skins like they were cardboard, starred metal, kept going. Officer Danny Reyes, eleven months on the job, was working the radio, calling it in with his voice cracking on his badge number, when a round passed under the door frame and through the soft of his neck below the jaw. His field training officer, Ruth Okafor, nineteen years on and steady through all of them, got a fist into his vest and hauled him behind the engine block, both palms flat on the hole, blood ticking through her fingers in a rhythm she would hear for the rest of her life.

Deke went out the shattered doorway firing, trying to reach the car, reach Teo, reach the plan. He took two rounds in the plate carrier that spun him half around, and a third, lower, that folded him at the knees. He died on the steps in the sun, big hands still curled around nothing.

Teo rammed the blockade. The Chrysler's windshield whitened in a spiderweb, and then another round came through it, and the horn stopped, and then started again, stuck, his weight on the wheel. It blew for a long time.

Vale fought from behind the center island, marble chips spraying off the counters, rounds cracking past his ear like bullwhips. Mrs. Halvorsen, sixty-eight, flat on the carpet with her deposit slips scattered around her, took a pass-through in the shoulder and lay very still, breathing in small sips, watching the light through the missing wall.

And Petey — Petey was finished. The boy who'd fired the first shot had fired his last. He was crying inside the mask, rifle loose in his hands, backing into the vault alcove. When he finally shuffled out through the glass, he dropped the weapon from waist height so it clattered on the tile, and put his hands up so high he nearly lifted off the ground. Officers took him down onto the sidewalk and cuffed him while he sobbed something about the old man, about the old man's hand, *I saw his hand.*

Vale was alone. Gut-shot, leaking steadily, sitting against the marble island with two duffels of money and one of them slowly going dark and heavy beneath him, blood soaking into banded hundreds that no one would ever spend. The hiss started softly—easy to mistake for pipes, for the building settling. Then Maya noticed the taste. Bitter. Metallic, like sucking on a battery.

She looked up. A faint haze curled from the vent near the ceiling, too pale to be smoke, drifting down in slow ribbons.

"No, no, no—" The word came out as a whisper first, then a shout. She was at the door in three strides, wrenching the handle. Locked. She'd known it was locked. She tried it anyway, again, again, as if the mechanism might tire of the joke.

She pounded. Both fists, the full weight of her body behind them. "HELP! SOMEBODY—" The door didn't even rattle. Solid steel, and beyond it, she knew, a corridor no one walked after hours.

*Think. Think.* She spun in a circle, cataloging the room the way she should have an hour ago: concrete walls, a drain in the floor, a bare bulb, a metal table bolted down. Nothing. No tools, no windows—

The taste was stronger now. Her eyes had begun to sting, a fine graininess like sand beneath the lids. Blinking made it worse.

The gas was visible now when she looked toward the light: a shimmer occupying the top foot of the room, sinking steadily, patiently, like water filling a tank.

She hauled at the table, thinking to drag it beneath the vent—block it, cover it—and her palms slipped on the metal, already slick. The table didn't budge. Bolted. She laughed, one sharp horrible bark, and the laugh turned into a cough.

The cough was the first real betrayal. It came from somewhere deeper than her throat, and it didn't stop. Her chest had developed a tightness, a band cinching beneath her sternum. Each breath now carried a price: a scratchy burn at the top of her lungs, air that felt thinner than air should.

"Okay," she told the room, because saying things out loud meant she was still rational. "Okay." Drains connected to—sewers. Too small. She was at the grate anyway, fingers scrabbling, a nail bending back with a bright stab of pain that felt almost clarifying.

The headache arrived like weather: pressure behind her eyes, then a throbbing that kept time with her pulse. The bulb smeared when she looked at it. She was sweating and cold at once.

The haze was at chest height now.

She screamed again—no words, just sound hammered against the door until her voice cracked and frayed into a dry rasp. She kicked the steel until her shins sang. Somewhere in the middle of it, a thought surfaced with absurd clarity: she'd left the stove on. She'd *definitely* left the stove on, and now she'd never—

Her thoughts kept sliding sideways.

Tingling started in her fingertips, then her lips. Her heart was doing something wrong—galloping, stumbling, galloping—and every stumble flooded her with a dizzy heat. The room tilted gently left, righted itself, tilted again, as if the floor were a boat.

*Breathe. Just breathe.* But breathing was the problem, wasn't it. Each inhale tasted of copper, and her lungs seemed to be shrinking, refusing the air, and the coughing had become continuous, wet and hacking, doubling her over.

Her knees went first.

Not dramatically—no buckling, no fall. They simply flexed, and the floor rose to meet her, and she found herself sitting against the door with no memory of deciding to sit. Her cheek rested against the cool steel. The coolness felt wonderful. That frightened her from far away, some dim part of her waving a small red flag: *comfort is a symptom. Comfort means—*

The haze had come down to meet her. It was everywhere now.

Sound was going strange. Her own ragged breathing receded as if someone were carrying it away. A ringing started, thin and high, and the bulb above her dimmed—not the bulb, a detached corner of her mind noted. *Her eyes.* The darkness came in from the edges, folding gently inward like a closing iris.

She thought, with the last coherence left to her, of a door standing open. Sunlight. Someone saying her name in an ordinary voice on an ordinary day.

Her hand, which had been crawling toward the handle one final time, went still.

The hiss went on.

---

The lock gave on the third tension of the pick, and Kessler stood in the dark of the doorway and listened to Curtis Yates breathe.

The snoring came through the bedroom door—gravel dragged over gravel—fourteen seconds on, six off. He timed two full cycles before he closed the door behind him with his fingertips, the way you closed a door at a scene you didn't want to disturb. Because that's what this was. A scene. He was just authoring it in advance.

He worked by penlight held in his teeth, in second-skin gloves, in shoe covers bought with cash at a hardware store two towns over. Sixteen years of working other men's crime scenes had taught him what a scene remembered: fibers, prints, the half-second of carelessness. He had watched juries be shown all of it, exhibit by exhibit, until he understood exactly how much doubt physical evidence could buy and how little it took to close the sale. Now he ran the knowledge in reverse and gave the room nothing. A scene could only testify to what you left behind.

The apartment smelled like fry oil and menthol. Dishes in the rack. A kid's school photo on the kitchen wall—a girl in a purple polo, gap-toothed, unsmiling the way kids are when told to be serious. Kessler looked at it longer than the plan required. Curtis Yates, family man. Juries liked a family man; sympathy bred doubt, which meant the physical evidence would have to carry more weight than he'd first assigned it. He adjusted the estimate upward and filed the daughter under friction.

The motive was already on file. Fourteen months ago a noise complaint, a call he'd taken himself: Yates and Denny Lowell shouting in this hallway over sixty dollars and a borrowed circular saw. In the affidavit it would read *documented history of conflict between the subject and the deceased*. Sixty dollars would become "an ongoing dispute over money." It wasn't a lie, exactly. It was the truth in a uniform.

Denny Lowell had made two mistakes in a career of making none: he'd said the word *lawyer*, and he'd said it while holding Kessler's money. The meeting had ended early. Kessler had done his arithmetic standing over the body, while the man cooled, and the arithmetic had said: the story needs a different author now.

He had considered others before settling on Yates. Tee, who'd done five years for robbery—too good a fit, and Tee had a cousin who was a paralegal, and men with resourceful families made noise. Yates had a record and no lawyer. A temper on paper. A night alone.

That was the thing people misunderstood about a frame. It didn't require fooling anyone. It required giving twelve strangers a story they were already prepared to believe. Kessler wasn't inventing anything. He was a supplier in an old market.

The .38 came out of the wax paper like a coin from a mint. He'd lifted it off a dockworker in '09—never vouchered, never fired, wiped and oiled and waiting in his lockbox the way insurance waits. A gun that did not officially exist could have come from anywhere. In the report, it would come from the streets, the way all of them did.

Placement was a question of psychology, not concealment. Too hidden and the defense would ask how a man stores a gun where he can't reach it in the dark. Too easy and it read as planted. He chose the cavity behind the bottom drawer of the dresser—the spot a guilty man actually uses—and angled the barrel so the first hand that searched would find it inside a minute. Though not the first pass. He'd let Okafor's initial sweep come up empty, let the discovery land on the second, because finding it had to feel earned. Discovery had its own theater.

The money he'd taken off Lowell's dresser came to twenty-two hundred. He planted nine hundred of it in a gym bag at the top of the closet, folded in a hoodie with Lowell's watch, and he kept the rest—not out of greed, but arithmetic. A frame with all the proceeds recovered reads like a frame. Juries believed in unrecovered money the way they believed in unrecovered motives. You let the story admit a small loss to hide the larger one.

He had cut a square from the towel that had been under Denny's head, and now he pressed the dried brown of it to the revolver's grips and to the folded bills. Not much. If the door opened, he had a version for that: a tip about a prowler, badge already out, apologetic, professional.
