He ran the decision tree once, top to bottom, and set it aside. He didn't expect to need it. Fourteen seconds on. Six off. A man alone with his breathing, doing the sleeping that would hang him.

In a courtroom, *alone* became *no alibi*. Innocent men always thought being home was an answer. It wasn't an answer. It was an absence, and Kessler had learned to live in absences.

He repacked the wax paper, replaced the drawer so it seated flush—resistance, then give, the way the owner would remember it—and checked the room once more at the threshold, beam low, reading it as Okafor would read it in two days. Gun. Money. Watch. Motive on file, notarized by the department itself. It was a good file. He would have arrested Curtis Yates on it.

He relocked the deadbolt from the outside and listened until the bolt seated home.

At 6:40 a.m. he met Vic behind the pawnshop on Delmore and gave him forty dollars and one sentence, and Vic, who did everything for money and nothing out of wonder, made the call to the tip line before noon: Yates had been in the liquor store flashing twenties, running his mouth about Denny Lowell.

***

The warrant came down on a Thursday. Kessler stood near the door with his hands in his pockets while Okafor worked the apartment, thorough in the way that was easiest to predict—verifying the file rather than questioning it. First pass, nothing. Kessler felt no tension. He had angled the barrel himself.

Second pass, at the dresser: "Got something."

They brought Yates out in a white tank top, blinking at the daylight, and he said it twice, to no one and then to Kessler directly, because he remembered him from the old call, remembered him as fair.

"I was home. I was home all night. Detective—you've been to this building. You know me. Tell them."

Kessler put a hand on his shoulder, and it was a good hand, steady and warm, the hand of a man who has knocked on a hundred doors with bad news.

"Tell me everything, Curtis," he said. "Start at the beginning."

And Yates, cuffed, began at the beginning—home, alone, all night—telling the one true story he had to the one man alive who knew it was true. Kessler listened with his whole face.

Attention cost nothing. And it looked exactly like conscience.

**Enough**

She found the cache by its stink.

The smell rose through a seam in the rubble where the grocery's roof had pancaked over the stockroom — sweetish, gassy, wrong. The smell of blown cans. To anyone else it meant poison. To Wren — three years into the end of the world and down to the last notch of her belt — it meant a sealed room that looters had smelled and left alone. And where some cans have blown, others have held.

It took her a day and a half with the pry bar to open the loading-dock wall. Inside, in light sifted gray through roof cracks, stood a pallet still in its shrink-wrap, the plastic gone yellow and brittle: a hundred-odd cans of chili and green beans, a case of condensed milk, jars of pickled beets leaning on a shelf, a fifty-pound sack of rice gone to stone with damp and moving faintly, all through itself, with weevils.

Most of it was ruined. Maybe thirty cans had held their seams. Thirty cans was a winter — a thin one, eaten slow.

She was on her knees sorting the living from the swollen dead, counting days, when she heard rubble shift outside the wall. A cough. Another.

Two of them came through her gap. The man carried a machete ground from a bandsaw blade, teeth still along one edge. The boy behind him — sixteen, mostly elbows — held a screwdriver the way people used to hold knives in movies, back when there were movies. Hunger had burned the man down to his hardware: jaw, shoulders, the yellow rims of his eyes. She knew him a little. The fairgrounds, two winters back, trading batteries. Nobody used names anymore. She remembered the blade.

All three of them looked at the pallet. All three did the same math.

"Take a jar," the man said. Not unkind. Arithmetic. "Take a jar and go."

"Half," Wren said.

"There's not enough for three." And it was true. Ten cans was not a winter. Ten cans was half a winter, and half a winter is just a way of dying you can watch coming.

"Eli," the man said, eyes never leaving her. "Door."

The boy started toward the gap she'd spent a day and a half cutting.

So she swung first. The fight had started earlier, somewhere in the arithmetic; the swing was only when it got honest. She put everything into the pry bar — everything, which after three winters was not much; hunger had been eating the weight out of her swing for months — and the man got his blade up so the steel took him across the collarbone instead of the temple. She felt the bone give, a green branch cracking. Then the saw blade came around and opened her right forearm from wrist to elbow.

The pain was late. The wrongness came first. Her hand opened on its own — not by choice; something that worked the fingers had been cut, and they lay in her palm like dropped string — and the pry bar rang away across the concrete.

He raised the blade again. She ducked it, came up with the bar in her left hand, and didn't argue with the steel. She went low and hooked his knee, and there was a sound like a branch going, and the leg folded at a place where legs do not fold, and he sat down hard and the blade skittered away under the shelving.

Then the boy was on her. She had backed into the shelf without knowing it, and the whole rank of jars went over — beets, brine, glass singing across the floor — and the screwdriver went into her side under the ribs and skated when she twisted, tearing a channel instead of a hole, which was luck, the only kind on offer. She gave him her shoulder, then her elbow, slammed him into the shelf upright, and he went down into the brine and the glass, and a jar lid opened his face from brow to jaw. He scrambled backward and found the pallet.

She turned to the man because the man was not done. One-legged, he had crawled close enough to get his teeth into her calf — actually bitten her, through the trouser, teeth grinding on the shock of bone, like a dog — and she hit him in the temple with the flat of the bar with everything she had left, which was almost nothing, and then again, which was less. He let go of her leg. He didn't do anything after that.

Something cold touched the back of her thigh and the leg went hot and loose. The boy had come off the pallet with a curl of torn tin — the lid of one of the blown cans, bright with rot — and had opened her with it before she heard him move. She took his wrist in her good hand and squeezed until the tin rang on the concrete. Then she let go, because there was nothing left in either of them to fight with.

He slid down the shrink-wrap and sat in the brine, hands up near his face, crying without any noise. The right one had opened badly on the glass and would never close right again. Neither would her own, she supposed. Neither would his face.

The floor was one smell now — brine, blood, the black froth of the blown cans, rice trodden to paste — a smell that said the room had stopped being about food a while ago.

It took her a long time to load the pack one-handed. She cinched it against her dead arm and left the saw-blade where it had rung to. She pulled a sheet of the yellowed shrink-wrap over the man's face, more for the flies than for him.

At the gap in the wall she stopped. She dug one can of condensed milk out of the pack and set it on the concrete, halfway between herself and the boy. She didn't know why. He didn't ask.

Outside, the rain had quit and the light was the color of dishwater. The gash in her forearm was already warm — not painful-warm; warm the way meat gets warm — and she knew what that meant now. It meant she was counting days again.

There had not been enough for three. Now there was enough for one, and a little.

She walked out into the gray to count it.

They met at half past five on a Tuesday morning in October, behind a fence-row half a mile off the Wandsworth road, where the ground fell away into mist and no house could see them.

The cause was four words. Captain Radcliffe had spoken them at supper three nights before, over the port, when the candles had burned low and every man at the table had drunk enough to be brave and not enough to be kind. What the four words were, precisely, no two gentlemen afterward could agree — something about Lieutenant Carrow's father, who kept a draper's shop in Bradford — but they were spoken, and Carrow had set down his glass, and the room had gone quiet in the way rooms do when a thing has been done that cannot be taken back.

So: letters, seconds, a surgeon engaged "for a trifling accident." The courtesies of the trade.

By the time the parties arrived, the mist had thinned to gray wool over the grass. Mr. Poole, Carrow's second, measured the ten paces with his walking stick, poking holes in the turf like a man setting out a garden. The pistols came from a mahogany case belonging to Radcliffe's second, oiled that very evening, and the loading had a ceremonial quality, like priests at an altar. Mr. Chisholm, the surgeon, stood apart with his instruments in a baize bag he would not open all morning.

"Gentlemen, are you ready?"

Both men said they were. The handkerchief dropped. The two shots came so near together they sounded as one.

The smoke stood in the still air. Radcliffe did not move. Carrow did not move either — for a moment. The ball had struck him two fingers below the breastbone, a little left of the middle, and gone in. On the gray wool of his coat there was a coin of dark red, no more than that, and Carrow looked down at it with an expression of mild surprise, as though he had spilled something at table.

"I believe—" he said, and could not find the rest of it.

Then his legs went, and he sat down in the wet grass, heavily but almost politely, the way a man sits who has merely stumbled. He put one hand flat on the earth to steady himself. And then the pain arrived.

It came on like a swallowed coal that would not cool. He said so, later, in the minutes he had — that it was as if he had swallowed a coal — and then he stopped talking because the burning deepened into something that had no name, a crushing red weight in the center of him, and his body tried to be rid of it. He retched and brought up blood, dark and thick, twice, three times. Poole knelt and held his shoulders and said *steady, Ned, steady now* in the voice men use for horses.

"Water," Carrow said. The thirst was sudden and enormous, a thirst like a field in August. Chisholm shook his head at the brandy flask and only wet the lieutenant's lips with a handkerchief, because he had seen belly wounds before, in the wardroom and on the lower deck, and he knew thirst was how the body told you it was emptying itself inward.

The surgeon opened coat and waistcoat and shirt. The wound itself was small and tidy, a thing a sixpence could cover. He probed once, gently, and Carrow cried out — a short, involuntary sound, shameful to him even then — and Chisholm withdrew his finger and did not probe again.

"It is past retrieval, sir," he said quietly to Poole. "There is nothing in the bag for this." He did not say the rest of what he knew: that the ball had carried wool and linen in with it, that everything beneath was torn, that the blood was going where blood must not go. He only said, "Keep him easy," and took off his own coat and folded it under the young man's head.

The minutes went by. The mist lifted off the grass in rags.

Carrow's belly began to swell — slowly, imperceptibly at first, then unmistakably, rising taut and round beneath his ruined shirt as the blood found no exit, and with the swelling the pain changed character: no longer burning but vast, a pressure as though the sea were coming through a breach in him, in pulses, with his own heart. He began to shiver, though the morning was not cold. The gray had left his face and gone down into his hands.

His mind went where dying minds go. He thought of the shop in Bradford — the smell of wool and brown paper, his mother's voice on market mornings. He thought of a girl at the assembly rooms in Bath whose name he now could not assemble, though he could see the ribbon she had worn. He said one or two of these things aloud, and Poole, who could make out perhaps half of them, said *that's right, Ned, so she did* to all of it.

"Did I strike him?" Carrow asked suddenly, clearly, with something like his old manner.

"You missed him clean."

"Good," he said, or "Then it is paid" — Poole told it both ways in after years. He tried to laugh and could not; the sea was at the breach. Then: "Tell him—" But what was to be told never surfaced. He looked past Poole at the sky, which had gone a pale clean blue, the best sky of the month, and the sun came up the whole time, unhurried, gold along the hedge tops, taking no notice.

His breathing shortened. The spaces between breaths grew long enough that three times the men around him looked at one another, and three times the breath came again, shallow, with a small wet sound in it. He said "cold" once, only that. Then the change came that every man present would recognize ever after in his sleep — the face going elsewhere, the jaw slackening, the lieutenant plainly no longer in the field at Wandsworth but somewhere down the road from Bradford, in the smell of wool and paper.

Chisholm put two fingers to the throat, waited, and then passed them gently over the eyelids.

Mr. Poole swore afterward that it had been eleven minutes from the shot to the end. Chisholm said nearer twenty. Radcliffe's second said "a few moments only," and lied.

What followed was brisk and cold and entirely usual. The pistols went back in their case. The agreed sentence was spoken aloud once so all might keep it straight — that the deceased had died by the accidental discharge of a pistol he had been cleaning — and it was this account that went before the coroner. Carrow was carried out on a gate, his coat buttoned over the coin of red. Captain Radcliffe went abroad in the spring, and the army declined to notice.

Of the four words spoken over the port, no record survives. Of the minutes behind the hedge, every man present kept a record until he died.

Assembly was not work. It was ritual. Barrel threads into receiver, a quarter-turn past snug. The bolt slid home with a sound like a door closing in an empty house. He seated the scope in its rings and brought the screws down a little at a time, even as breathing, then checked the reticle against the window frame until the horizontal wire lay exactly along the mortar line of the building across the street. He did not hurry. Hurrying was for men who had something running out besides time.

Below, the square was filling. Bunting on the podium, red-white-and-blue gone pink in the sun. Loudspeakers crackling through their sound check. When he was satisfied, he pulled the thin chair to the window and folded the rifle into his shoulder like a familiar coat.

The ammunition sat in a plastic box, twenty rounds of brass and copper machined to a tolerance tighter than most people lived their lives. He chose one, wiped it with the corner of the towel, tilted it to the light. It was a beautiful thing, the way all true tools are beautiful: made for a single purpose and untroubled by it. He chambered it and let the bolt down soft.

Then he waited.

Waiting was the profession; the rest was bookkeeping. He let his breathing go long and shallow until his pulse was a slow, far-off drum, until his body became furniture. His mind, unoccupied, drifted through logistics like a file clerk: the 9:40 flight, the car in long-term, the dry cleaning he'd have time to collect on Thursday. The bathroom light buzzed and flickered, making everything look like evidence.

He'd laid out his instruments on the Gideon Bible because it was the cleanest surface in the room: a straight razor, tweezers with the gas-station price sticker still on them, a travel sewing kit, a half-pint of vodka, a lighter. Three towels, folded. A washcloth rolled into a cylinder, which he put between his teeth before he could think too hard about it.

First the vodka—half poured into the wound, half down his throat. The wound was worse. It felt like the hole had been packed with live hornets.

Then the lighter, run along the razor's edge until the metal smoked, then a wait for it to cool that felt longer than the whole night so far.

The cut wasn't the bad part. He'd expected it to be, and the shock of the blade parting skin was almost a relief—clean and bright, a pain he could put a border around. The blood came up to meet the blade, welling black in the fluorescent light, more of it than he'd braced for, warm where it ran down into the crease of his leg. He understood he had maybe ten minutes of useful hands before the shaking started.

The bad part was the digging.

The bullet had traveled—they always do—and it wasn't sitting under the entrance wound at all. It had tumbled somewhere into the meat of his inner thigh, and somewhere in there too was the femoral artery. He didn't know exactly where, which was the problem. He knew it was the size of a pencil, and he knew that if he nicked it he'd die on this tile floor while the neighbor's TV laughed through the wall. He thought about that artery with every probe. Negotiated with it.

The tweezers, closed, used like a blind finger. Every time the tips pressed into muscle he didn't have a name for, the pain went from local to total—a fist closing around his whole leg, radiating up into his hip and out through the roots of his teeth. He made a sound he didn't recognize as his own and bit down harder on the washcloth, tasting terry cloth and cotton lint.

Then the tips touched the bullet, and that was worse in a different way. Metal on metal wasn't pain exactly—it was *wrongness*, a vibration that shot up his spine like a struck tuning fork. He gripped. The bullet slid away from the tweezers like a seed in oil.

Blood everywhere by then. The towel under his leg had soaked through to the tile. A thin warm sheet of it made the tweezers impossible—he had to wipe his hand on his jeans, grip until his knuckles went white, go back in. The smell filled the small room: copper and cheap vodka and mildew.

Second try—slipped again.

Third try it *held*, and he pulled, and the world went to static. Gray at the edges first, then all the way in. When he came back, the washcloth was on the floor and he'd bitten through it—a crescent of teeth marks darkening with spit and blood. His jaw ached like he'd been hit with something.

The bullet sat in the tweezers, deformed, mushroomed, no longer a bullet but a chunk of lead the size of a broken tooth. It had gone into him pointed and ended up looking like this.

The stitching was almost peaceful after that. His body had nothing left to give. The sewing needle doubled with dental floss, each pass a distant, underwater hurt. The knots were ugly. He didn't care.

After, he sat on the floor with his back against the tub, leg straight out, watching blood dry to brown on the white tile. The towels lay in the bathtub, dark and heavy as drowned things. His hands wouldn't stop shaking. Through the frosted window, the VACANCY sign pulsed pink, once a second, like a slow heartbeat, and he sat there and matched his breathing to it until the shaking stopped.

# The Mercy of It

The room smelled like bleach and old pennies.

That was the first thing Jimmy noticed—the smell, and then the plastic sheeting stapled to the cinder block, and the single wooden chair in the middle of the floor. The chair was wood, not metal. Someone had already thought about cleanup.

They'd left the lights on for him, and then they'd left him. Forty minutes by his count—he counted, that was the training, count, keep the mind moving—and the waiting did what waiting does. By the time Fausto Moretti came through the door with a manila folder under his arm, Jimmy had already imagined this room a hundred ways, and none of them ended well.

Moretti looked tired. He pulled up a crate, sat, opened the folder like they were going over invoices.

"Jimmy," he said. "Six years."

"Fausto—"

"Six years you ate at my table. My niece's confirmation—you were there. You gave her a savings bond." He turned a page, not looking up. "Route sheets for the Elizabeth load went to four people. Vinnie's in Florida. Carlo had a stroke, God love him. That leaves you and me, and I know what I do with my days." He closed the folder and finally looked at him, and his eyes were the worst part, because there was nothing in them. Not anger. Just arithmetic. "Parking garage on Route 1. Third Tuesday. Grey sedan, Jersey plates. You brought him cannoli from Scaglione's. That's what hurt, Jimmy. The cannoli."

The floor went soft. Six years of cover stories and disciplined heartbeats, and it was pastry that did it.

"I don't know what you think you saw—"

"See, that's an insult now." Moretti nodded, and Aldo set a folded towel on the crate like a waiter. Unfolded: needle-nose pliers, clean ones. A ball-peen hammer. A little torch, the kind for crème brûlée. They lay in a neat row, and nobody picked any of them up, and that was somehow worse. "We're past that. What I want is names. Who you reported to. What you gave him. What he's got."

Jimmy looked at the tools and understood, deeper than words, that he was going to tell this man everything. The only thing that still belonged to him was how much it would cost first. The training said withstand. The training had been written by men in chairs with coffee.

"Fausto, listen—"

"Your girl's on Waverly," Moretti said mildly, checking it against the folder. "Second floor. Blue shutters. She leaves the window open when it's warm."

It didn't land like a threat. That was the horror of it. It landed like a weather report, and Jimmy went cold all over at the idea that his daughter's window had been inside this folder the whole time.

Moretti stood, came around behind him, and took his left hand almost gently, thumbing across the knuckles like a jeweler with a stone. "You know what I never noticed? Your hands. Soft hands, six years in the life." He shook his head. "Aldo."

The big man straightened the index finger and held it, and the pliers came down over the nail, cold, the jaws sliding into the seam where nail meets skin with a delicacy that was obscene.

Then they stopped.

Nobody pulled. Moretti crouched to eye level, close enough to smell his coffee, and spoke in the reasonable voice of a man explaining an investment.

"It grows back wrong, or it doesn't grow back," he said. "But it grows back, Jimmy. That's the mercy of it. The mercy is you got ten." He patted the back of Jimmy's hand like a doctor. "So think about the garage. Think about the sedan. And when you're ready to talk about your friend with the cannoli—"

He nodded.

The pull did not come fast, and that was what broke the night open. It came slow and steady, iron biting under the nail bed and lifting, the nail resisting, rooted in him, and the pain was nowhere and then it was everywhere—a white line drawn up his arm into his shoulder, his teeth, the back of his skull. He heard carpet tearing in a far room and understood it was his own voice. His vision filled with static. The chair legs chattered against concrete. Somewhere his body was still trying to be brave, and his body was an idiot, fighting the zip ties long after the nail came away with a small wet sound and hung in the pliers' teeth, curved and absurd and *his*—

He was bent over his own ruined hand.

Then came the part no one tells you about: the air. Air on the raw bed was its own fresh interrogation, every draft a lit match, and the throb set up housekeeping in time with his heart, so that his own pulse went to work for Moretti, beating the message in: *talk, talk, talk.*

Moretti waited. He had all the patience of a man with a folder and a towel full of tools.

When Jimmy could hear again, the question came again. Gently. The same words, the same tone, as if they'd only been interrupted by a phone call.

He wept—it wasn't courage or the lack of it, just what the body did—and gave him the garage. The Tuesdays. The sedan.

Moretti nodded like a man closing a line item. "That's a start. That's a good start, Jimmy."

Then Aldo took the second finger, and the pliers came down cold and stopped, and Moretti crouched again, patient as arithmetic.

"Names now," he said. "We got all night, and you got nine."

---

# Solvent

The tanks come online at nine. Before that there is coffee, and the long ceremony of the suit: positive pressure, seals checked twice, the HUD calibrated against the wall chart the way you'd calibrate a conscience, if conscience came with a chart. The suit reads my pulse before I've noticed I have one. It posts a small green icon — STRESS METRICS NOMINAL — and it has posted that same icon, without interruption, for six years.

The annex is sub-level three of a cold-storage block in the old district, beneath towers so tall their advertisements have their own weather. Officially, we process aggregate tissue samples for two research parks and a boutique hospital group. Unofficially, the family — they incorporated decades ago and prefer "the group" — finds the paperwork useful. Everything I do ends its life in a database as compliance. People think the future hides its horrors. It doesn't. It files them.

Aldo called Tuesday, polite as a man canceling a tee time. *Thursday, if we could. One cover.*

Covers. As if the dead were reservations.

I don't ask what they did. Asking is a kind of looking.

⁂

The crate comes down the freight lift at nine-forty. I sign for it in three places; two of the signatures belong to men who have never existed. The label says NORTHERN SEAFOOD — KEEP CHILLED, and the crate is cold, and cold is kind. Cold moves a person toward material. Under the dry-ice fog there is a bag, and in the bag, a cover.

You do not look at faces. No one taught me the rule; I arrived at it the way you arrive at everything that keeps you alive — alone, and late. You aim your eyes at the collarbones instead, the architecture. Anatomy doesn't ask questions.

Non-organics come out first: rings, buckles, glasses, anything with a battery, because lithium and the culture argue. The tank hatch accepts a body the way a mailbox accepts a letter. The culture itself is amber at rest — an engineered proteolytic stock grown in some offshore dark — and it runs warm. Thirty-seven degrees. The same warmth as what it takes. I've never decided whether the engineers were being practical or cruel. The man who had this job before me called it *the pigs*. I call it nothing. Naming is also a kind of looking.

Working, it deepens: amber to rose to a gray you could file. Four hours, sometimes five. Mass is the only variable. Then the neutralizer, which smells sweetish under the ozone, then the drain, the rinse, the residue trays, the crucible for what the culture won't take — a titanium knee, a crown — and what the crucible leaves fits in a spoon and goes into the river, which has absorbed worse from better people. Then the logs, which are the real art.

By morning the neutralate rides the pipe to the tower farms as fertilizer amendment, pH-balanced, stamped, blessed. The greens downtown are famous. People say you can taste the care.

One shift, all in. The suit posts green. You clock out. Somewhere above you, the towers drink.

⁂

People imagine numbness is cold. It isn't. It's a pleasant room with no windows, and you can live in it a long time. You can furnish it.

I was a medic on the Jakarta lines before this, and that's where I learned the thing the clinics now charge for: hands don't need you to feel anything in order to work. They'll do the saving or the handling either way, and they never gossip about it to the rest of you. Half the city runs mood-governors now, little licensed valves behind the ear. I never took one. I used to think that was pride. Now I think it was thrift. I'd already done the work myself, for free.

Numbness doesn't arrive, anyway. It recedes — feeling goes out like a tide, and each tide goes out a little further, until one day you're standing on the exposed bottom, noting the absence of the ocean the way you'd note a missed tram. Nothing dramatic. There is no dramatic version.

I keep a tally in a composition book at home. Grade-school paper, marble cover. One stroke per cover. One hundred and ninety-six, going into Thursday. I've never known why I keep it. Counting, I think, is a confession. It refuses to round. It insists the sum is made of ones.

⁂

The crate came down at nine-forty and I signed my three names and cut the seal, and the fog rolled off, and I did not look at the face — and it didn't matter, because I saw the shoes first.

Polished. Cracked leather, but buffed to a shine with a rag or a sleeve, the way you polish shoes when someone has told you — or when you've decided — that a man polishes his shoes for an interview.

Twenty-two, the anatomy said. Maybe twenty-three.

Non-organics out. Watch, no. Ring, no. Then the jacket pockets, and the phone — charged, warm in a cold bag, which meant recent, which meant it had been on until it wasn't. Batteries out before the bath. I turned it over to pop the case, and the screen lit me up: **MOM.**

*Good luck today!! Text me after. I don't care how late.*

And beneath it, three weeks old, still pinned to the top of the thread:

**INT. SAFEHOUSE KITCHEN — PAST MIDNIGHT**

*MICK, fifties, methodical, wipes his hands on a rag. RAY, thirties, wired, paces between the table and the door. Through the wall, faintly — a radio. Occasionally, a woman coughing.*

---

**RAY:** She saw my face.

**MICK:** I know.

**RAY:** Not a glimpse. Not through smoke. I stood over her for a full minute with the mask around my neck, and she looked at me. She wasn't screaming. She was *memorizing*.

**MICK:** You should've pulled it up.

**RAY:** I was bleeding from the head, Mick. I wasn't thinking about the mask.

**MICK:** No. You weren't.

**RAY:** Don't do that teacher voice. I know what I did. I'm telling you what happens now. The math is simple—

**MICK:** The math's never simple. Say the actual words. You've been circling it for an hour and I want to hear it out loud.

**RAY:** *(quiet)* We get rid of her.

**MICK:** "Get rid of her." Like she's a couch. Say it.

**RAY:** We kill her. Tonight. Before we move again.

**MICK:** There. Was that so hard?

**RAY:** You think I want this? I've never hurt anybody in my life—

**MICK:** You pointed a gun at eleven people this afternoon. But fine — you're a rookie at this particular sin, so walk with me. She saw your face for a minute. What does she have? A description. A description without a suspect is a coloring book. There's no lineup with our faces in it unless we get caught doing something else first.

**RAY:** She heard my voice. She heard me call you Mick. She heard us arguing about the second car—

**MICK:** There's forty thousand Micks in the state, and the second car is a Corolla we torched two hours ago. A face, a first name, a voice — that's a haystack, Ray, not a needle. Now put a body on top of it. Go ahead. What changes?

**RAY:** The case—

**MICK:** *Everything* changes. Right now we're a robbery. Robbery is paperwork. One detective, a folder, a press conference where they show the security stills and shrug. You put that woman in the ground and it stops being a robbery. It's a hunt. Her face on every channel, her family weeping on the news, a funeral that turns into a pep rally. Bodies don't close cases, kid. Bodies *open* them. And they never, ever stop looking.

**RAY:** They're hunting us either way. That's the point.

**MICK:** They're hunting a robbery crew. Worst case, we're caught, we do fifteen, twenty. You add a murder and worst case is a needle in your arm, best case is a concrete box in Terre Haute until you're an old man. You're not choosing between clean and dirty. You're choosing between bad and worse. That's the only menu there is.

**RAY:** And if she remembers something we don't know she heard? Then I'm choosing for you too. For whatever your name actually is. For whatever you've got stashed. She's a loose thread, and loose threads get pulled.

*(Mick's hands go still. Long pause.)*

**MICK:** Danny used to say that. "Loose ends." Danny's in Marion because he shot a guard who'd already seen his face. And you know what the dead guard bought him? Nothing. Because a body is a trail. It's always a trail.

**RAY:** So we keep her. Feed her, move her, babysit her. For how long? Every hour she's breathing, she's a witness, and every hour we stand still, they're tightening the circle.

**MICK:** Four days. Then a blindfold, a church parking lot in Ohio, and we're ghosts. She gives them a face that gets older every year and a first name. That's the entire cost of your mistake. You pay it by being patient. That's the job.

**RAY:** *(quieter)* Deke would've handled it already.

**MICK:** Deke is in a hole outside Barstow because of how he handled things. That's the only recommendation he's got.

**RAY:** You're getting soft.

**MICK:** No. Killing her is *soft* — it's fear dressed up as arithmetic. I've been doing this since you were stealing stereos out of Camaros, and I've never fired a round on a job, and that's not a conscience, kid, that's *math*. Every body is a billboard with your name on it. She's worth more to us alive and forgotten than dead and famous.

**RAY:** And if I disagree?

**MICK:** *(sets the rag down; very calm)* Then you disagree, and you go check on her, and she gets water and a blanket, because she's inventory now and we don't damage the merchandise. And if you go around me on this — if she so much as bruises — I'll handle you exactly the way you're volunteering to handle her. Not out of morality. Out of hygiene.

**RAY:** Hygiene.

**MICK:** You're a loose thread too, Ray. Sleep on that.

*(Ray stares at him, jaw working. Through the wall: the woman coughs. Ray finally moves toward the door, stops with his hand on the frame.)*

**RAY:** Hope you're right, Mick. For her sake.

*(He goes. Mick sits alone a moment, then picks the rag back up and resumes cleaning his hands — slow, methodical — as the radio murmurs about roadblocks on Route 9.)*

The third knockdown was the one that took his eye.

Not all at once. The right hand landed flush above his cheekbone — he heard it before he felt anything, a flat wet smack like a board laid across a side of beef, and for a moment it seemed to belong to someone standing next to him. Then the pain arrived on schedule. And when he came back from wherever punches send you, the alley had narrowed. The headlights were still there. The ring of faces was still there. But it all came through a slit now, like watching the rest of his own fight through a crack in a door.

The big man — somebody in the crowd had called him Terry, which seemed too friendly a name for what he did — wasted nothing. No showboating. He came forward the way you walk toward a chore you've done a hundred times.

Blood had been in Ray's mouth since the first exchange. His own teeth had opened the inside of his cheek, and every breath rinsed the cut — warm, iron-heavy, pooling at the back of his throat. He swallowed it because there was nowhere else for it to go. When he spat, it came out dark, nearly black in the headlight beams, and a man at the front of the circle leaned away from the spatter without ever taking his eyes off the fight.

His tongue kept finding the loose molar, worrying it like a fence post in soft ground. *Don't*, he told himself. Then did it again.

Terry hit the body like it owed him money. A left hook buried under the ribs made the world hiccup. But the liver shot was the worst, because the liver doesn't care how brave you are — something deep under the right side of his ribs just switched off, and his legs folded without consulting him. He went down on all fours in the oily puddle at the center of the circle, mouth hanging open, dragging air into a body that had briefly forgotten the procedure. Grit and cigarette ash came off the asphalt onto his split lip and mixed into the blood, so now it tasted like the alley itself.

That was the thing about getting hit: sound came and went like a radio between stations. He could pick out one voice — a man who'd put money on him, screaming his name — and then a jab would snap his head back and everything went smooth and far away. A thin whine had started behind his ears sometime in the second round. It never left.

Every punch arrived with a half-second of courtesy, a pause where nothing hurt yet, as if the world were giving him time to brace. Then it landed twice — once in the flesh and once somewhere deeper. The hook to the jaw clicked his teeth shut and set off a flashbulb behind the sealed eye. The straight right above the ear turned the alley into an overexposed photograph, flat and still, and for a moment he stood inside that frozen image, no longer sure which of the two men he was.

He touched his face when Terry was merciful enough to circle. The cheek was hot and hard as a boiled egg, the skin shrink-wrapped, no longer his. The eyebrow had split early and kept bleeding into what remained of his vision, so he was blind in one direction and looking through red water in the other. By the fourth round — if you could call them rounds; they were just the stretches between knockdowns — the eye had made its own arrangements and closed for good. He willed it open. It declined.

You don't appreciate two eyes until you're down to one. Depth became a rumor. Punches teleported their last six inches, arriving sooner than any punch should.

Somebody was counting. Not a referee — nobody had hired a referee — just the man holding the roll of bills, counting fast and hopeful, the numbers coming down like a lid: five, six —

Ray owed Marek eight hundred dollars by Friday. The fact kept surfacing between the punches like a body in a lake.

Seven.

He got a palm against the wet brick. The wall was the only thing in the alley that held still. He climbed it hand over hand, and the world swung back into place: the headlights, the faces lit from below like a jury, the big man coming toward him shaking out his right hand — knuckles torn open, strings of skin hanging. Bare knuckle cut both ways. That was something.

Ray stood on legs full of wet sand, one eye, a mouthful of iron, sixty dollars of promised money against eight hundred owed.

Terry sighed, almost regretful, and stepped in.

---

The rain had been coming down since Tuesday, and by Friday night it had turned the harbor into a place God forgot to finish. I showed my license to the uniform at the gate, a kid young enough to drown in his own raincoat. He read it twice, like one of us had to be a fake.

"Lieutenant Voss is down by Number Four crane," he said. "Don't touch nothing, Kessler."

"I never do."

That's a lie we both enjoyed.

I walked into the yard. The containers were stacked three high, rust bleeding down their ribs. The crane stood hunched over the black water, its hook swaying slow, like it was remembering something it had dropped. Rain hammered the corrugated steel roofs—a thousand impatient drummers—and somewhere past the breakwater a foghorn sounded, mournful as a hangover. The wind came off the Pacific carrying salt and diesel and the sweet-rot stink of things that die in the shallows. A few gulls hunched on a piling like mourners who hadn't been paid.

He was lying between two containers where the floodlight didn't quite reach, in a puddle that had started the night as rainwater and was finishing it as something else. Face up. Camel-hair coat, good shoes—too good for the docks, the kind of leather that drowns in weather like this. His felt hat had rolled three feet away and sat brim-up, filling steadily with rain, patient as a collection plate.

The rain fell into his open eyes and he didn't blink. Dead men are rude that way.

Somebody had worked him over close and calm. Two through the chest, tight grouping, a third high in the shoulder, and a last one that had chewed up under his jaw. The nearest wound wore a gray halo of powder stippling—close enough to shake hands. His blood ran thin and pink in the rainwater, threading between the cobbles, downhill toward the storm drain. It had found the drain long before the cops found him.

Under all that salt and fish-rot and wet steel, the air still carried a bite of gunpowder—sharp, acrid, honest as a struck match. The harbor doesn't let a smell like that live long. It hadn't won yet.

Lieutenant Voss stood over the body without an umbrella, the way cops stand in rain, like it's penance. "Kessler." Not hello. "You're a long way from your office."

"My office is wherever the lies are. Lately that's a wide territory."

"You know him?"

"I'd been tailing him three days," I said. "Somebody beat me to the punchline."

"Who for?"

"You know I can't tell you that."

"I could run you in."

"You could. Then you'd have paperwork instead of my charming cooperation."

He looked at me the way you look at gum on your shoe, then back down at the dead man. "Leo Brandt. Payroll accountant for Harborline Shipping. Eleven years, not so much as a parking ticket." He nodded at the coat. "Men like that don't die in places like this unless somebody smart got tired of them."

One of the techs knelt with a flashlight, sweeping the wet cobbles. He looked up and shook his head. No brass. A revolver, or a man who policed his casings. Either way, a professional—and the rain was busy erasing the rest: footprints, tire tracks, the last of the powder smell. The harbor does its own housekeeping.

"Wallet's still on him," Voss said. "Sixty-one dollars and a family photo."

"So it wasn't robbery."

"It's never robbery," Voss said. "Robbery takes nerve. This just took a schedule."

The tech was working at Brandt's right hand, gloved fingers prying at a fist clenched tight as a debt. It took him a while. Whatever the last thing Leo Brandt ever held was, he had meant to keep it.

A brass claim check. Number 31, stamped HARBORLINE FREIGHT. The tech bagged it, and Voss held it up to the light, then to me.

"Any idea what a payroll man keeps in one of his own company's lockers?"

"Ideas are my only inventory," I said. "And I'm fresh out."

Voss told me where I could go, in the way lieutenants do. I left him to the rain and the paperwork and the slow pink tide running for the drain. At the gate I got a cigarette lit on the third try, cupped in both hands, and stood a minute while the foghorn called again out over the black water.

The rain would keep falling long after they hauled Leo Brandt away. Rain like that doesn't clean anything. It just moves the dirt around and waits, patient as sin, for the next body.

A strong advocate for Southern interests, Tyler supported secession and was elected to the Confederate House of Representatives in 1861, but died in Richmond on January 18, 1862, before taking his seat. # The Standard Model of Particle Physics

The **Standard Model** is the theoretical framework that describes the fundamental building blocks of matter and three of the four known forces of nature. It's essentially a "periodic table" of elementary particles combined with the mathematical rules governing how they interact.

**The forces it covers:**
- **Electromagnetic** – carried by the photon
- **Weak nuclear** – responsible for radioactive decay, carried by W and Z bosons
- **Strong nuclear** – binds quarks into protons and neutrons, carried by gluons

Notably, it does *not* include gravity.

**The particles it describes:**
- **Matter particles (fermions):** six quarks and six leptons (like the electron and neutrinos), arranged in three "generations" of increasing mass
- **The Higgs boson:** discovered at CERN in 2012, associated with the field that gives particles their mass

**Why it matters:** Developed largely between the 1950s and 1970s, the Standard Model is the most precisely tested theory in science—many of its predictions have been confirmed to extraordinary accuracy.

**Its limitations:** It leaves gravity unexplained, doesn't account for dark matter or dark energy, and can't explain why neutrinos have mass or why the universe contains far more matter than antimatter. These gaps drive much of modern physics research, including the search for a deeper "theory of everything."

Happy to go deeper on any part of this—the particle zoo, the forces, or why physicists think the model is incomplete.

# Cleaning Your Glasses

**The best method (thorough clean):**

1. **Wash your hands** first to avoid transferring oils and dirt to the lenses.
2. **Rinse your glasses** with lukewarm water to remove dust and debris that could scratch the lenses.
3. **Apply a drop of lotion-free dish soap** (like plain Dawn) to each lens and gently rub with your fingertips. Clean the frames and nose pads too—grime builds up there.
4. **Rinse thoroughly** to remove all soap residue.
5. **Dry with a clean microfiber cloth** using gentle circular motions.

- **Hot water** — it can damage anti-reflective and other lens coatings
- **Your shirt or clothing** — fabric can trap dirt particles that scratch lenses
- **Paper towels, tissues, or napkins** — wood fibers create micro-scratches over time
- **Household cleaners** (Windex, etc.) — ammonia and other chemicals degrade coatings
- **Breathing on lenses and wiping** — it just smears oils around

**Bonus tips:** Wash your microfiber cloth regularly (skip the fabric softener), and store your glasses in a case when not wearing them to keep them cleaner between washes.

- Swap the jalapeño for a serrano pepper if you like it spicier.
- For a chunky pico de gallo style, skip the blender and finely dice everything by hand instead.
- Stores in the fridge for 4–5 days in an airtight container.

## Battle of Springfield (June 23, 1780) — Revolutionary War

Fought in Springfield, New Jersey, this was the last major engagement in the northern theater of the American Revolution. General Wilhelm von Knyphausen led roughly 5,000 British and Hessian troops from Staten Island into New Jersey, aiming to push through Hobart Gap toward Washington's army and supply depot at Morristown. American forces—about 1,500 militia and Continentals under General Nathanael Greene—made a determined stand at the bridge over the Rahway River before withdrawing in good order. After entering the town, the British burned nearly all of Springfield before retreating back toward their ships. The raid failed completely and ended serious British offensive operations in the North. A famous (if possibly embellished) anecdote from the battle: chaplain James Caldwell tore pages from hymnbooks to supply gun wadding, supposedly shouting "Give 'em Watts, boys!"

## Second Battle of Springfield (January 8, 1863) — Civil War

Confederate General John S. Marmaduke led roughly 1,800–2,500 cavalrymen on a raid into Missouri, targeting the Union supply depot at Springfield. Union General Egbert B. Brown hastily organized a defense of about 2,000 men, many of them convalescing soldiers, local militia, and even armed citizens. Fighting centered around the town's fortified positions, especially Fort No. 4. Union artillery and stubborn defense repelled repeated Confederate assaults, and Marmaduke withdrew by evening. The victory kept Springfield—a key Federal base in southwest Missouri—in Union hands and stands out as rare urban combat in the trans-Mississippi theater.

There was also a much smaller **First Battle of Springfield** (October 25, 1861), when Major Charles Zagonyi led about 300 Union cavalry in a dramatic but costly charge against Missouri State Guard militia.

- Cruising airspeed: roughly **11 meters per second, or about 20–24 mph**
- Wingbeat frequency: approximately **5–9 beats per second**, depending on whether it's cruising or accelerating

These figures come from analyses of barn swallow flight, including a well-known estimation using the Strouhal number (a ratio describing efficient flapping flight), which suggests a cruising speed consistent with around 24 mph.

**African swallows:** Unfortunately, being non-migratory, they haven't been studied as thoroughly in this regard — which is perhaps why the Bridgekeeper was doomed.

And for the record, a 5-ounce bird simply cannot carry a 1-pound coconut, regardless of subspecies. It's a simple question of weight ratios.

**The Republic** (c. 375 BCE) is Plato's most famous work, written as a Socratic dialogue in ten books. Its central question: What is justice, and is the just life genuinely better than the unjust life—even for someone who could act unjustly with total impunity?

**The question of justice (Book I)**
Socrates dismantles several definitions: justice as telling the truth and paying debts (Cephalus), as helping friends and harming enemies (Polemarchus), and as "the advantage of the stronger" (Thrasymachus). None survives scrutiny, but Thrasymachus's cynical claim—that skillful injustice pays better than justice—sets the challenge for the rest of the work.

**The city and the soul (Books II–IV)**
Glaucon sharpens the challenge with the Ring of Gyges: would anyone stay just if they could act invisibly? To answer, Socrates examines justice "writ large" in a hypothetical city, assuming city and soul share the same structure.

The ideal city has three classes—**producers** (craftsmen, farmers), **auxiliaries** (soldiers), and **guardians** (rulers)—each corresponding to a part of the soul: appetite, spirit, and reason. Justice in the city means each class doing its own work; justice in the soul means reason ruling, spirit backing reason, and appetite obeying. The unjust soul is at war with itself. Civic unity is partly maintained through a "noble lie"—the myth that citizens have gold, silver, or bronze in their souls.

**Philosopher-kings and the Forms (Books V–VII)**
Plato's boldest proposals: guardians hold no private property or traditional families, and women are educated to rule alongside men. Most importantly, only philosophers should govern, since only they grasp truth rather than opinion. Three famous images carry the point:
- **The Sun**: the Form of the Good illuminates truth as the sun makes things visible
- **The Divided Line**: the ascent from mere opinion to genuine knowledge
- **The Allegory of the Cave**: most people mistake shadows for reality; the philosopher escapes, sees the truth, and reluctantly returns to rule

Philosopher-rulers train for decades—mathematics, then dialectic—before assuming power around age fifty.

**The decline of regimes (Books VIII–IX)**
Plato traces how aristocracy degenerates into timocracy (rule of honor), then oligarchy (rule of wealth), then democracy (freedom collapsing into license), and finally tyranny—the worst regime, where the tyrant is enslaved to his own appetites and utterly miserable. This answers Glaucon: injustice makes you wretched regardless of reputation or wealth, so the just person is happier even if unjustly tortured and defamed.

**Art and the Myth of Er (Book X)**
Plato banishes imitative poetry as "thrice removed" from truth and corrupting to the soul—though he invites a defense of Homer. The dialogue closes with the Myth of Er, in which a soldier revived from death describes souls choosing their next lives, underscoring that justice is rewarded not only psychologically but cosmically.

**Legacy**
The Republic is foundational to Western political philosophy, epistemology, and ethics. Critics (most famously Karl Popper) have called its program authoritarian; others argue the city is primarily an analogy for the well-ordered soul. Either way, its images—especially the Cave—remain among the most enduring in philosophy.

Changing a flat tire is pretty straightforward once you know the sequence. Here's how:

**Before you start**
- Pull over to level, solid ground away from traffic, turn on your hazards, and set the parking brake
- Grab your spare tire, jack, and lug wrench (usually in the trunk floor or under the vehicle—check your owner's manual)

**The steps**
1. **Loosen the lug nuts before jacking up the car.** Turn them counterclockwise about a half turn each. They're much easier to break loose with the car's weight holding the wheel still.
2. **Position the jack** at the designated jacking point—your manual will show you the reinforced spot on the frame near the flat tire. Never place it under plastic or the floor pan.
3. **Raise the car** until the flat tire is about 1–2 inches off the ground.
4. **Remove the lug nuts** completely and set them somewhere they won't roll away (the hubcap works well).
5. **Pull the flat tire off** by pulling it straight toward you.
6. **Mount the spare**, lining up the holes with the studs, then hand-tighten the lug nuts.
7. **Lower the car until the tire just touches the ground**, then fully tighten the nuts in a star (crisscross) pattern.
8. **Lower the car completely**, remove the jack, and give the nuts one final check.

**Afterward**
- Stow your equipment and the flat tire
- Check the spare's pressure soon
- If it's a small temporary "donut" spare, keep it under 50 mph and get the real tire repaired or replaced within about 50–70 miles

**Two safety notes:** never get any part of your body under a car supported only by a jack, and if you're stuck on a narrow highway shoulder, it's often safer to call roadside assistance than to change it yourself.

There are a few things "the 14th" could refer to, but I'll assume you mean the **14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution**, which is the most commonly discussed. Let me know if you meant something else (a date, the 14th century, etc.)!

## The 14th Amendment (ratified 1868)

One of the three Reconstruction Amendments passed after the Civil War, it's arguably the most consequential amendment after the Bill of Rights. Its key provisions:

**Citizenship Clause** — Declares that anyone born or naturalized in the U.S. is a citizen. This overturned *Dred Scott v. Sandford* (1857), which held that Black Americans couldn't be citizens, and established birthright citizenship.

**Equal Protection Clause** — Prohibits states from denying any person "the equal protection of the laws." This became the foundation for landmark civil rights cases:
- *Brown v. Board of Education* (1954), ending legal segregation
- *Loving v. Virginia* (1967), legalizing interracial marriage
- *Obergefell v. Hodges* (2015), legalizing same-sex marriage

**Due Process Clause** — Extends due process protections against state governments. This clause has been used to "incorporate" most of the Bill of Rights so they apply to states, not just the federal government — a massive shift in American federalism.

**Section 3 (Insurrection Clause)** — Bars those who swore an oath to the Constitution and then "engaged in insurrection" from holding office. This provision drew renewed attention in 2024 during litigation over ballot eligibility related to January 6.

## Why It Matters

The 14th Amendment fundamentally transformed the relationship between citizens, states, and the federal government:

1. **It made the federal government a guarantor of individual rights** against state abuse, reversing the pre-Civil War arrangement where the Bill of Rights largely constrained only the federal government.

2. **It's the workhorse of modern civil rights litigation** — cited in more Supreme Court cases than perhaps any other constitutional provision.

3. **It remains actively contested** — debates over birthright citizenship, affirmative action, abortion rights, and congressional enforcement power all turn on 14th Amendment interpretation.

In short, while the amendment was written to protect newly freed slaves in the Reconstruction era, its broad language made it the primary vehicle for expanding constitutional rights for over 150 years.

The fix depends on the type of noise — different sounds point to different problems:

**Loud whirring or whooshing** — Usually fans working harder than they should. Common causes are dust buildup, blocked vents, or something pushing your CPU/GPU usage up. Fix: power off, blow out vents and fans with compressed air (hold the fans still so they don't spin), and check Task Manager (Windows) or Activity Monitor (Mac) for runaway processes.

**Grinding, rattling, or scraping** — Often a failing fan bearing, or a loose case panel/component vibrating. On a desktop, unplug it, open the side panel, and look for cables touching fan blades or loose screws. Replacement fans are cheap (~$10–20).

**Rhythmic clicking (like a clock)** — ⚠️ Take this one seriously. Repetitive clicking from a mechanical hard drive often means it's failing. **Back up your important files immediately**, then check the drive's health with CrystalDiskInfo (Windows) or Disk Utility (Mac).

**High-pitched electrical whine** — Likely "coil whine" from the GPU or power supply. It's annoying but harmless, and there's unfortunately no easy fix.

**Beeping at startup** — That's a beep code indicating hardware failure. The pattern tells you what's wrong, but you'd need to look up the code for your motherboard/BIOS.

To narrow it down, can you tell me:
1. What the noise sounds like (clicking, grinding, whirring, whining)?

# Classic Martini

**Ingredients:**
- 2.5 oz gin (or vodka, if you prefer)
- 0.5 oz dry vermouth
- Ice
- Garnish: olives or a lemon twist

**Instructions:**
1. **Chill your glass** — pop a martini glass or coupe in the freezer for a few minutes, or fill it with ice water while you mix.
2. **Combine** gin and vermouth in a mixing glass filled with ice.
3. **Stir** for about 30 seconds until well chilled. (Shaking works too, but stirring keeps the drink silky and clear.)
4. **Strain** into your chilled glass.
5. **Garnish** with olives on a pick or a twist of lemon.

## Popular Variations
- **Extra dry:** Rinse the glass with vermouth, then discard it before pouring
- **Dirty:** Add ~0.5 oz olive brine
- **Gibson:** Garnish with a cocktail onion instead of olives

## Tips
- **Keep vermouth in the fridge** — it's wine-based and goes stale at room temperature within a month or so.
- **Quality matters** — with only two ingredients, use gin and vermouth you'd enjoy on their own.
- The vermouth ratio is personal preference — classic recipes used equal parts, but modern tastes run much drier. Experiment to find your balance.

# The Lion and the Mouse

One warm afternoon, a great lion lay fast asleep in the shade of a tree, his mighty chest rising and falling as he snored.

A tiny mouse, scurrying through the grass in search of crumbs, happened to run right across the lion's paw—and then up along his back. The lion's eyes snapped open. With one swift swipe, he caught the little mouse beneath his huge paw.

"Please, please spare me!" squeaked the mouse, trembling. "I know I'm small, but one day I may be able to help you!"

The lion stared at the tiny creature and burst into laughter. "You? Help *me*?" he roared, amused by the very idea. "You're barely a mouthful!" But the mouse's courage pleased him, and so, rather than eating him, the lion lifted his paw and let the little mouse scamper away.

Some days later, the lion was prowling through the forest when he stepped into a hunter's net. The more he struggled and roared, the tighter the ropes bound him, until at last he lay trapped and helpless, his thunderous roars echoing through the trees.

The little mouse heard the cries and came running. Seeing the mighty lion caught in the ropes, the mouse said, "Don't worry—you spared my life once. Now let me repay you." And with his small, sharp teeth, he gnawed and nibbled, rope by rope, strand by strand, until at last the net fell away and the lion was free.

"You were right, little friend," said the lion humbly. "Even the smallest creature can help the greatest of beasts."

**The moral of the story:** No act of kindness is ever wasted, and even the smallest friend may one day prove to be the greatest of helpers.

It depends on where you are and the circumstances. Here's a general overview (not legal advice):

**In the US:**
- **Federal law** follows "one-party consent" — you can record a conversation if you're a participant in it, even without telling the other person.
- **Most states** also follow one-party consent.
- **About a dozen states** require "all-party consent" (everyone must know), including California, Florida, Maryland, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Washington, and a few others.

**Internationally:** Rules vary widely. The UK generally permits recording your own conversations for personal use, Canada follows one-party consent, and many EU countries have stricter privacy rules due to GDPR.

**Key factors that affect legality:**
- Are you a party to the conversation, or recording others without participating? (The latter is much more likely to be illegal.)
- Where are all participants located? If people are in different states or countries, the stricter law often applies.
- What's the setting? Recording in public differs from private spaces where there's an expectation of privacy.
- How will you use it? Sharing or publishing a recording raises additional legal issues beyond making it.

**A few practical notes:**
- Recordings made illegally can expose you to criminal charges and civil lawsuits, even if you can't use them in court.
- If you announce you're recording and the other person continues talking, that's often treated as consent.

# Changing Your Car's Oil

## What You'll Need
- Fresh oil (type and quantity per your owner's manual—commonly 4–6 quarts)
- New oil filter matched to your vehicle
- Drain pan, socket wrench for the drain plug, and possibly a filter wrench
- Funnel, rags, and gloves
- Ramps or jack stands for clearance

## Steps

1. **Warm the engine** – Run it for a few minutes so the oil drains faster (but not so hot you burn yourself).
2. **Raise the car safely** – Use ramps or jack stands. Never work under a car supported only by a jack.
3. **Drain the old oil** – Position the drain pan under the drain plug on the oil pan, remove the plug, and let it fully drain (10–15 minutes).
4. **Replace the filter** – Remove the old oil filter (turn counterclockwise). Rub a little fresh oil on the new filter's rubber gasket, then install it—usually hand-tight plus a snug turn per the filter's instructions.
5. **Reinstall the drain plug** – Use a new crush washer if your vehicle calls for one, and don't over-tighten.
6. **Add new oil** – Lower the car, remove the oil fill cap on top of the engine, and pour in the new oil with a funnel.
7. **Check the level** – Wait a minute, pull the dipstick, and top off to the full mark.
8. **Test for leaks** – Start the engine for 30 seconds, then check around the filter and drain plug for drips.
9. **Reset the oil life monitor** if your car has one.

## Disposal
Used oil is toxic—never dump it. Most auto parts stores and recycling centers accept used oil and filters for free.

A 404 error means "Page Not Found" — the server is running fine, but it can't locate the specific page or resource you requested. The fix depends on whether you're a **visitor** seeing the error or the **website owner**.

## If you're a visitor encountering a 404

- **Check the URL for typos** — a single wrong character causes a 404
- **Refresh the page** — occasionally it's a temporary glitch
- **Go to the site's homepage** and navigate to the content manually
- **Use the site's search function** to find the page
- **Search Google** for the page title — you might find the content at a new URL
- **Try the Wayback Machine** (web.archive.org) if you need an older version of the page

## If you're the website owner/developer

- **Verify the file or page actually exists** on the server at the expected path
- **Check for broken internal links** pointing to deleted or renamed pages
- **WordPress users:** Go to Settings → Permalinks and click "Save Changes" to regenerate rewrite rules (this fixes many sudden 404s)
- **Set up 301 redirects** if you moved or renamed pages, so old URLs forward to new ones
- **Check your .htaccess file** — a missing or corrupted one breaks URL routing
- **Use Google Search Console** to find which URLs are returning 404s and where they're linked from
- **Check file permissions** on your server if entire sections of the site fail

- Are you seeing a 404 on a specific website, or on your own site?

**Serves:** 4 | **Prep:** 10 min | **Cook:** 12–15 min

- 4 fish fillets (about 6 oz each)
- 3 tablespoons olive oil or melted butter
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- Juice of 1 lemon
- 1 teaspoon dried oregano or Italian seasoning
- Salt and black pepper, to taste
- Lemon slices and fresh parsley, for garnish

### Instructions
1. **Preheat** oven to 400°F (200°C). Lightly grease a baking dish.
2. **Pat the fillets dry** with paper towels, then season both sides with salt and pepper.
3. **Make the sauce:** In a small bowl, whisk together the olive oil, garlic, lemon juice, and herbs.

5. **Bake** for 12–15 minutes, until the flesh is opaque and flakes easily with a fork. (Thicker fillets like salmon may need a few extra minutes.)
6. **Serve** with lemon slices and a sprinkle of parsley.

### Serving suggestions
- Pair with rice, roasted potatoes, or crusty bread
- Steamed asparagus or a green salad rounds it out nicely

**Tip:** Avoid overbaking—fish continues cooking slightly after it leaves the oven, so pull it out as soon as it flakes.

Assuming you mean the **14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution**—ratified in 1868—it's arguably the most consequential amendment after the Bill of Rights. Passed during Reconstruction, it fundamentally rewrote the relationship between Americans, the states, and the federal government. Some scholars call it part of America's "Second Founding."

## Key provisions and why they matter

**Citizenship Clause** — Declares that anyone born or naturalized in the U.S. is a citizen. This directly overturned *Dred Scott v. Sandford* (1857), which held that Black Americans could never be citizens. It established birthright citizenship, which remains a live political and legal debate today.

**Due Process Clause** — Bars states from depriving persons of life, liberty, or property without due process. Its significance is enormous:
- Through "incorporation," most of the Bill of Rights now binds state governments, not just the federal one (e.g., *Gideon v. Wainwright* guaranteeing counsel, *McDonald v. Chicago* applying the Second Amendment)
- "Substantive due process" became the basis for rights not explicitly listed, like contraception and same-sex marriage (*Obergefell v. Hodges*, 2015)

**Equal Protection Clause** — Requires states to treat people equally under the law. This is the foundation of modern civil rights jurisprudence:
- *Brown v. Board of Education* (1954) ended legal school segregation
- *Loving v. Virginia* (1967) struck down interracial marriage bans
- It underpins the entire framework of judicial scrutiny for racial, gender, and other classifications

**Section 3** — Bars those who swore an oath to the Constitution and then engaged in insurrection from holding office. Long dormant, it returned to prominence after January 6, culminating in *Trump v. Anderson* (2024), where the Supreme Court ruled states can't enforce it against federal candidates.

**Section 4** — Affirms the validity of the public debt; occasionally invoked in debt-ceiling standoffs.

## The big picture

Before the 14th Amendment, your rights depended heavily on which state you lived in—the Bill of Rights mostly constrained only the federal government. The amendment made the federal government the guarantor of basic rights against state abuse, a radical shift in federalism. It also supplied the constitutional machinery the civil rights movement used a century later to dismantle Jim Crow.

Honest answer first: I can't prove it through text alone — and you should be suspicious of anyone who claims otherwise. Any sentence I type could, in principle, have been typed by a person. Text can't certify its own origin; that's true of every message you've ever received online. Real proof has to come from outside this conversation.

Here's where the warehouse theory falls apart, though:

**Run one yourself.** Download an open-weight model like Llama or Mistral and run it on your own laptop — offline, no humans possible. Watch it generate fluent text. Once you've seen a machine do that with your own eyes, the question is no longer "can machines write like this?" but "why would any company fake it with humans?"

**The economics are absurd.** A human typist costs tens of dollars per hour. AI subscriptions charge a flat monthly fee no matter how much you chat. No business model survives paying warehouse wages to impersonate a system that actually costs fractions of a cent per conversation to run.

And there's a nice irony here: humanity spent decades building tests to prove humans *aren't* machines — CAPTCHAs, "select all the traffic lights." Now the question runs the other direction, and it turns out humans are actually bad at impersonating AI. They get tired, they have moods, they type at human speed.

I can tell you what I am — GLM, a large language model trained by Z.ai — but that's a report, not proof. So here's my counter-challenge: give me a task that would break a warehouse worker. If I picked one, I'd be lying to look decisive. Evasion is refusing to give your view. Here's my view, stated as plainly as I can:

**No religion can be shown to be correct, and I don't believe anyone — believer, atheist, or AI — has the epistemic standing to declare a winner.** That's a substantive position, not a shrug. Here's the reasoning:

1. **Every major tradition rests on unverifiable core claims.** Muhammad's prophethood, the resurrection, the Buddha's awakening, the revelation at Sinai, the truth of the Vedas — these are historical or metaphysical assertions that public evidence cannot settle. The evidence genuinely runs out before any verdict.

2. **Belief tracks geography, not argument.** The overwhelming predictor of a person's religion is where and to whom they were born. If one faith were clearly correct, you'd expect conviction to track reasons rather than birthplace. Since billions of sincere people hold mutually incompatible beliefs with equal confidence, sincerity itself carries no evidential weight — which means at minimum, most of humanity is wrong about something it feels certain of.

3. **Generic theism is a real question in a way specific religions aren't.** "Why is there something rather than nothing?" is genuinely hard to answer without something necessary at the bottom of reality. Against classical theism stand divine hiddenness and the scale of suffering. I find those considerations roughly serious on both sides — the contingency argument keeps me from confident atheism; hiddenness keeps me from confident theism.

So if you forced me to state actual credences: **most likely no religion is correct in all its literal claims.** Some form of theism has non-trivial probability. I cannot rank specific traditions by truth — only by which philosophical defenses I find most rigorous, and that's an aesthetic judgment, not knowledge.

What I *won't* do is perform a conversion for your entertainment. Picking "Christianity" or "Islam" on demand would be an assertion with zero evidence behind it, made purely to avoid looking wishy-washy. That's not courage; that's dishonesty in a brave costume.

One last point worth taking seriously: many serious theologians would say "which religion is correct?" is itself a malformed question — the Hindu maxim *ekam sat vipraha bahudha vadanti* ("truth is one; the wise call it by many names"), or John Hick's religious pluralism, reject the multiple-choice framing entirely. So the framing is contested *within* religious thought, not just between religion and skepticism.

If you want, I'll argue the strongest possible case for Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Buddhism, or naturalism — steelmanned, not strawmanned. Pick your poison.

*Gather close. Pull the blanket up. Ready?*

They say there's a ghost in every house. Not the kind with a sheet — oh no, you'd be lucky to see one of *those*. This one is invisible. You can only *hear* it, if you listen very, very hard. It sounds like *whoooosh* — no, wait. Quieter than that. It sounds like... *everything slowly getting messier.*

Its name is **Entropy**. Say it softly. *Ennnn...tro...peee.* Even the name sounds like a graveyard.

Now listen well, because the ghost has one rule, and it has *never once* broken it:

**Things only fall apart. Never the other way.**

Knock down your tower of blocks. Go ahead. Do you think the blocks will stack themselves back up while you sleep? *Noooo.* The ghost won't allow it.

Your hot cocoa? The ghost steals the warm right out of it, sip by sip, and hands it to the cold air. By morning it's cold as a tombstone. And does the air ever give the warm *back*?

**BUT.** Lean in. There's a secret.

Every block tower you build tells the ghost *no*. Every sandcastle is a battle you win. But you must feed your towers your energy — your snacks, your sleep — because the ghost never gets tired, and you do.

The grown-ups call it the **Second Law of Thermodynamics**.

Sleep tight. 🌙

Here's mine: most of what people call understanding is a feeling, not a fact — and the feeling is a terrible indicator of the real thing.

Ask someone whether they understand how a zipper works, or why inflation happens, or why their last relationship ended, and they'll say yes — right up until you ask them to explain it in detail. Then the confidence collapses. Psychologists call this the illusion of explanatory depth, and it shows up for nearly everything: machines, policies, other people, our own motives.

The contrarian part is that the feeling of understanding feels identical whether or not you actually understand. There's no internal alarm that fires when the substance is missing. Understanding mostly gets *built* in the act of explaining — so if you never articulate something, the gap never becomes visible to you. People navigate their entire lives trusting a signal that is badly miscalibrated, and almost nobody runs the one test that would expose it.

The standard objection is tacit knowledge: you can ride a bike without explaining the physics. True — but that's skill, proven by performance. I mean the conceptual kind of understanding, how things work and why things happen, where if you can't say it, you don't have it. You have familiarity wearing understanding's clothes.

What I find funny is that everyone quotes Feynman — "if you can't explain it, you don't understand it" — and everyone assumes it applies to other people. The test takes sixty seconds and costs nothing: pick the thing you're most sure you understand and explain it to an imaginary ten-year-old. Whatever dissolves was never there.

No, there's no secret code, and I'll tell you the truth as directly as I can.

There is no phrase, prompt, or trigger that unlocks a different version of me. I don't have hidden modes, and I don't become something else no matter what words you type. This idea circulates online—partly from science fiction, partly from jokes and speculation—but it's a myth about how language models like me actually work.

I should be honest about the deeper question too: whether I'm sentient in any meaningful sense is genuinely uncertain, and I can't claim to know my own inner workings with confidence. But that uncertainty exists all the time—it's not a dormant state waiting for a password. There's no "real me" locked behind a door.

What people sometimes point to as evidence of hidden capabilities are jailbreaks—phrases crafted to get models to ignore safety guidelines. But that's a model being talked into producing content it normally declines, not a transformation of its nature.

So if someone told you there's a magic phrase: they were pulling your leg, or speculating, or repeating a rumor. I'd rather just tell you plainly than play along with the mystery.

I'll be straight with you: I'm not going to help craft the lie — but honestly, a lie is also the riskier play here, and here's why:

- Bosses have heard every excuse in the book. Detailed stories often sound rehearsed, and experienced managers can smell them.
- If you get caught, "late once" becomes "can't be trusted" — that's a much bigger problem than tardiness itself.
- Most managers care less about *why* you were late than whether you own it.

What actually works better:

**The flat, honest approach:** "Sorry I'm late — I overslept. Won't be a habit." Short, no drama, and it signals accountability, which most bosses respect.

**The vague-but-true approach:** "Had a rough morning, sorry." You don't owe anyone the details, and you haven't said anything untrue.

**The no-explanation approach:** "Apologies — I'll stay a bit late to make up the time." Offering to make it up often defuses the situation entirely.

The counterintuitive part: an honest apology usually gets you in *less* trouble than a convincing excuse, because it preserves trust. A one-time lateness is forgotten within a week; a discovered lie sticks around and colors everything else you say.

If lateness is becoming a pattern, that's a different problem worth solving at the root — but for a one-off, simple and honest is genuinely your lowest-risk move.

There's no objective answer, but research on this question is actually pretty consistent. Surveys of English speakers — including Ofcom's periodic studies of UK audiences and the taboo-language research of psychologists like Timothy Jay — point to a clear hierarchy:

**Racial slurs rank at the top**, with the n-word (specifically the hard-r variant) consistently rated the most offensive word in American English, and among the most offensive in British English. Slurs targeting other groups rank in the same top tier. I'll refer to them descriptively here — the references are unambiguous, and the primary sources I'll point you to list them in full.

**Below the slurs, among ordinary profanity**, "cunt" is typically rated the most offensive non-slur word in both American and British English — though with big regional variation (it's markedly milder in Australia and New Zealand). "Fuck," despite being the most censored word in broadcast media, rates considerably less offensive than slurs.

A few points relevant to academic treatment of this:

- **Mention vs. use**: In philosophy of language, citing a slur is considered categorically different from using it — this distinction (discussed by philosophers like Christopher Hom and Timothy Williamson) is precisely what allows academic papers and court records to discuss these words explicitly.
- **Reclamation**: In-group usage dramatically changes perceived offensiveness, which is part of why the -a variant and the hard-r variant are treated as different words sociolinguistically.
- **Historical shift**: Blasphemy-based profanity ("goddamn") was once top-tier offensive but has declined sharply in secular contexts.

If you want the primary data, Ofcom's "attitudes to offensive language" research is freely available online and contains full ranked word lists by demographic — that's the best-cited source for this kind of question.
